1. What a Data Architect Does

A data architect designs how an organisation's data is collected, stored, connected, protected and used, so that many teams can build on it safely. Data engineers build pipelines; the architect decides the rules and the structure those pipelines fit into.

RoleMain questionTypical output
Data engineerHow do I move and transform this data?Pipelines, jobs, tables
Data modelerHow should this data be structured?Logical and physical models
Data architectHow does all our data fit together, safely, at scale?Platform design, standards, policies, decisions
Data governance leadWho owns the data, and which rules apply?Policies, roles, glossary

This card continues the online retailer from the Data Modelling and dbt cards. The sales mart works. But the company has grown to 40 pipelines and three teams, it now holds customer data from India and Europe, and an auditor has asked a simple question: "Who can see customer emails, and where does that data go?" Nobody can answer it quickly. Answering it properly is the architect's job, and each section below solves part of it.

ResponsibilityCovered in
Overall platform designThe platform at a glance
Who owns and defines dataData governance, metadata and catalogs
Which data is sensitiveData classification
Legal duties for personal dataData privacy
Who can access whatData security
Where data comes from and goesData lineage
Whether the data is rightData quality
Recovering from failure, controlling costResilience, lifecycle and cost

Thinking across the whole enterprise

An enterprise data architect is not tied to one product. A large company usually runs several platforms at once: an ERP on Oracle or SAP, a CRM in the cloud, a warehouse on Snowflake or BigQuery, a lakehouse on Databricks, Kafka for events and Power BI or Tableau for reporting. The architect's job is to make them work together under one set of rules, and to choose new technology for good reasons rather than habit.

Skill areaWhat to know
PlatformsAWS, Azure and Google Cloud data services; Databricks, Snowflake; on-premise databases
Architecture stylesWarehouse, lake, lakehouse, data mesh, data fabric, federation
IntegrationBatch, CDC, streaming, APIs, replication and virtualisation
Governance and securityCatalogs, classification, access models, encryption, audit, privacy law
Data managementModelling, quality, MDM, metadata, lineage, lifecycle
DeliveryCost, migration, vendor selection, roadmaps, stakeholder management

Frameworks worth knowing

FrameworkWhat it gives you
TOGAFAn enterprise architecture method (the ADM cycle), where data architecture is one of four domains
Zachman FrameworkA grid for describing an enterprise from different viewpoints
DAMA-DMBOKThe body of knowledge for data management, with governance at the centre
DCAM (EDM Council)A capability model for assessing data management maturity
Cloud well-architected frameworksAWS, Azure and Google Cloud guidance on reliability, security, cost and performance

You rarely follow a framework rigidly, but interviewers expect you to know them, and they give a shared vocabulary with enterprise architects and auditors.

2. The Platform at a Glance

An architect first draws the whole platform, because every later decision has to fit into it. The layers in the middle carry data; the band underneath applies to all of them, which is why governance and security cannot be added to one pipeline at a time.

 SOURCES        Orders DB   CRM    ERP    Clickstream (Kafka)   Partner APIs
                    │        │      │          │                    │
 INGESTION      CDC, batch connectors, streaming (Kafka, Kinesis, Event Hubs)
                    │
 STORAGE        Bronze (raw)  ─►  Silver (clean)  ─►  Gold (business)
                Open table formats on object storage, or a cloud warehouse
                    │
 PROCESSING     Spark, SQL warehouses, dbt, stream processors
                    │
 SERVING        BI tools, ML models, data sharing, APIs, reverse ETL
 ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
 ACROSS ALL     Governance │ Catalog │ Security │ Lineage │ Quality │ Cost

The data movement patterns behind this picture, such as Lambda, Kappa and medallion, are covered in the Data Architecture Patterns card.

Databricks and Snowflake run on all three clouds, and Kafka (or Confluent), Airflow, dbt and Tableau run almost anywhere. These cross-cloud tools are often chosen precisely to avoid being tied to one cloud.

Cloud product names change often. For example, Google renamed Dataplex to Knowledge Catalog in April 2026, and AWS has moved DataZone into SageMaker. Check current names when writing a design document.

The decisions an architect records

Big choices should be written down with their reasons, as an architecture decision record (ADR). When someone asks in two years why the company chose Delta over Iceberg, the answer is in the record, not in a person's memory.

ADR-007: Use Unity Catalog as the single governance layer

Status:   Accepted (2026-03-14)
Context:  Three teams manage access separately; an audit could not
          list who can read customer emails.
Decision: Register every table in Unity Catalog. Grant access to
          groups, never users. Tag personal data with governed tags.
Options:  Per-workspace Hive metastore (rejected: no central audit),
          external catalog only (rejected: no enforcement).
Impact:   All new tables must be Unity Catalog managed tables.
          Existing Hive tables are migrated by June.

Non-functional requirements

Most architecture is driven by requirements that are not features. Agree on these numbers early, because they decide cost and design.

RequirementQuestionRetailer example
FreshnessHow old can the data be?Sales by 7 a.m.; stock every 5 minutes
AvailabilityHow much downtime is acceptable?99.5% for dashboards
Recovery (RPO)How much data can we lose?1 hour
Recovery (RTO)How fast must we recover?4 hours
RetentionHow long do we keep data?Orders 8 years; logs 90 days
ComplianceWhich laws apply?DPDP Act, GDPR, PCI DSS
ScaleHow big will it get?5 TB now, 40 TB in 3 years
CostWhat is the budget?Cost per team visible each month

3. Architecture Styles

Before choosing products, an architect chooses a style: where data is stored, who owns it, and how it is accessed. Most enterprises combine several.

StyleIdeaStrengthsWeaknesses
Data warehouseStructured, modelled data in one SQL engineFast, trusted reporting; mature toolingPoor for raw, unstructured or ML data
Data lakeStore everything as files in cheap storageCheap, flexible, any formatBecomes a "data swamp" without governance
LakehouseLake storage with warehouse features through open table formatsOne copy for BI and ML; ACID on filesNeeds discipline in layout and governance
Data meshDomains own and publish their data as productsScales ownership across a large companyNeeds mature teams and shared standards
Data fabricA metadata-driven layer connecting data wherever it livesUnified access and governance across systemsDepends on rich metadata; vendor-heavy
FederationQuery data in place (virtualisation), without copyingFast to deliver, no duplicationSlower queries; load on source systems

Operational and analytical data

AspectOperational (OLTP)Analytical (OLAP)
PurposeRun the business: place ordersUnderstand the business: revenue trends
QueriesMany small reads and writesFew large scans and aggregations
DesignNormalised, row-orientedDimensional or wide, column-oriented
ExamplesPostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, DynamoDBSnowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Databricks SQL

Keeping them separate protects the order system from heavy reports. Data moves from operational to analytical systems through the integration patterns in the next section.

Open table formats: the key to avoiding lock-in

Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi add transactions, schema evolution and time travel to Parquet files in your own storage. Because the format is open, several engines can read the same data: Spark, Trino, Snowflake, BigQuery, Athena, Fabric and Databricks all read Iceberg or Delta to some degree. Catalogs that speak the Iceberg REST protocol, such as Apache Polaris, Unity Catalog and Snowflake's catalog, let engines share one table definition. For an architect, this separates the choice of storage from the choice of engine. The next section explains which format to choose.

Compare the formats in the Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi cards. Interoperability features change quickly, so check current support for each engine before committing.

4. Medallion Architecture and Data Layers

The medallion architecture organises a lake or lakehouse into layers of increasing quality: bronze (raw), silver (cleaned and conformed) and gold (business-ready). Databricks popularised the name, but the idea is older and platform-neutral: warehouses have long used staging, integration and mart layers, and Snowflake, Fabric, BigQuery and AWS lakes use the same layering under other names.

It is a design pattern, not a product. Each layer has a clear contract: what it contains, who writes it, who may read it, and what quality it guarantees. That contract is what makes data traceable, replayable and trustworthy.

SOURCES  ->  LANDING  ->  BRONZE  ->  SILVER  ->  GOLD  ->  SERVING (BI, APIs, ML, AI)

         SOURCES          LANDING          BRONZE           SILVER           GOLD
         databases, SaaS, files exactly    raw history,     cleaned, typed,  business models,
         devices, events, as delivered,    append-only,     deduplicated,    KPIs, star
         files, APIs      short-lived      + load metadata  conformed keys   schemas

quality  unknown          unknown          as the source    validated        certified
users    source teams     ingestion jobs   engineers        engineers, DS    analysts, BI

Every layer at a glance

LayerPurposeTypical contentsWrite patternRetention
Edge / sourceWhere data is produced and first collectedOLTP databases, SaaS apps, IoT devices, logs, partner filesOwned by source teamsSource-defined
LandingA safe drop zone for files exactly as deliveredCSV, JSON, XML, Avro, Parquet, zip files, CDC batchesWrite once by ingestion tools; never editedDays to weeks, then deleted or archived
Bronze (raw)An immutable, queryable copy of every sourceSource columns, often as strings, plus load metadata and rescued bad recordsAppend-onlyLong: it is the replay point
Silver (cleaned, conformed)One trusted, deduplicated version of each business entityTyped, validated, deduplicated tables; SCD history; conformed keys; personal data protectedMERGE / upsertLong
Gold (curated)Answers to business questionsStar schemas, aggregates, KPIs, wide feature tables, data productsOverwrite or MERGE per partitionAs the business needs
Serving (optional)Fast delivery to tools and applicationsSemantic models, metric views, caches, low-latency stores, vector indexesRefreshed from goldRebuildable

Why each layer matters

Landing: decouples delivery from processing
Sources can deliver at any time, in any format, even when pipelines are down. Nothing is lost if a job fails, and files can be checked (checksums, manifests, virus scans) before anyone reads them.
Bronze: the system of record for replay
Because bronze keeps everything exactly as received, a bug in silver logic is fixed by reprocessing bronze, not by asking the source to resend months of data. It is also the audit evidence of what the source actually sent.
Silver: one version of the truth per entity
Data quality, deduplication, type casting, standardisation and joins across sources happen once here, so every consumer inherits the same rules instead of reinventing them.
Gold: speed and meaning for the business
Modelled for the question, pre-aggregated, documented and certified. BI stays fast and metrics mean the same in every report.

What each layer does, in detail

ConcernBronzeSilverGold
SchemaSource schema; schema evolution allowed; often everything as stringEnforced, typed, documentedBusiness-friendly names, stable contract
QualityNone applied: keep bad records (rescued or corrupt column)Expectations: not null, ranges, referential checks; failures quarantinedReconciled totals, certified metrics
DuplicatesKept, because they are what the source sentRemoved: latest version per keyNone
HistoryEvery delivery appendedSCD Type 1 or 2 per attributeSnapshots and facts as modelled
Organised bySource systemBusiness entity (customer, order, product)Business use or domain (sales, finance)
Personal dataRestricted access; encryptedMasked, tokenised or separatedOnly what the use case needs
Who readsData engineersEngineers, data scientists, power usersAnalysts, BI, apps, executives
Typical modellingNone3NF, Data Vault or cleaned source shapeKimball star schemas, wide tables, aggregates

Tested: a medallion pipeline end to end

We dropped two JSON files into a landing folder. The second file contained a re-sent duplicate, an amount of "abc", a truncated line, and a later update to order 1. Then we built each layer with PySpark and Delta Lake:

from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window

# BRONZE: read everything as strings, keep bad lines, add load metadata
bronze = (spark.read
    .schema("order_id STRING, customer STRING, amount STRING, "
            "status STRING, updated_at STRING, _corrupt_record STRING")
    .option("columnNameOfCorruptRecord", "_corrupt_record")
    .option("recursiveFileLookup", "true")  # landing/orders/2026-11-07/*.json
    .json("/lake/landing/orders")
    .withColumn("_source_file", F.col("_metadata.file_name"))
    .withColumn("_ingested_at", F.current_timestamp()))
bronze.write.format("delta").mode("append").save("/lake/bronze/orders")

# SILVER: type, validate, quarantine, keep the latest version per key
br = spark.read.format("delta").load("/lake/bronze/orders")
typed = (br.filter("_corrupt_record IS NULL")
    .withColumn("order_id", F.col("order_id").cast("int"))
    .withColumn("amount", F.expr("try_cast(amount AS DECIMAL(10,2))"))
    .withColumn("updated_at", F.to_timestamp("updated_at")))

bad = typed.filter("amount IS NULL OR amount < 0")
bad.write.format("delta").mode("append").save("/lake/quarantine/orders")

w = Window.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(F.col("updated_at").desc())
silver = (typed.filter("amount IS NOT NULL AND amount >= 0")
    .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(w)).filter("rn = 1")
    .drop("rn", "_corrupt_record"))
silver.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save("/lake/silver/orders")

# GOLD: answer a business question
gold = (silver.groupBy("customer")
    .agg(F.count("*").alias("orders"), F.sum("amount").alias("revenue")))
gold.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save("/lake/gold/customer_revenue")
LayerRowsWhat happened
Landing2 files, 8 linesStored exactly as delivered
Bronze8Every line kept, including the duplicate and the truncated line, which sits in _corrupt_record with its source file name
Quarantine1Order 5 with amount "abc": try_cast returned NULL instead of failing the job
Silver4Duplicate of order 2 removed; order 1 shows its latest state, SHIPPED at 100.50
Gold3 customersC1: 2 orders, 145.50; C2: 1 order, 80.00; C3: 1 order, 300.00

A gotcha we hit: without recursiveFileLookup, reading /lake/landing/orders returned 0 rows with no error, because the files were in a date subfolder that was not named key=value. Spark only discovers subfolders as partitions in that form. Always check row counts after a landing read.

On Databricks: declarative pipelines with expectations

On Databricks the same flow is usually written as a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline. Auto Loader picks up only new files, and expectations record, drop or fail on bad rows, with the results shown in the pipeline's event log:

import dlt  # also: from pyspark import pipelines as dp
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

@dlt.table(comment="Raw orders, exactly as landed")
def bronze_orders():
    return (spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles")  # Auto Loader
        .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
        .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", "/Volumes/prod/landing/_schemas/orders")
        .option("cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode", "rescue")  # unknown fields -> _rescued_data
        .load("/Volumes/prod/landing/orders/")
        .select("*", F.col("_metadata.file_path").alias("_source_file"),
                F.current_timestamp().alias("_ingested_at")))

@dlt.table(comment="Clean orders")
@dlt.expect_or_drop("valid_amount", "amount IS NOT NULL AND amount >= 0")
@dlt.expect("has_customer", "customer IS NOT NULL")  # record only
def silver_orders_clean():
    return (dlt.read_stream("bronze_orders")
        .withColumn("amount", F.expr("try_cast(amount AS DECIMAL(10,2))")))

dlt.create_streaming_table("silver_orders")
# create_auto_cdc_flow was called apply_changes before 2025
dlt.create_auto_cdc_flow(target="silver_orders", source="silver_orders_clean",
                  keys=["order_id"], sequence_by=F.col("updated_at"),
                  stored_as_scd_type=1)

@dlt.table(comment="Revenue per customer")
def gold_customer_revenue():
    return (dlt.read("silver_orders").groupBy("customer")
        .agg(F.count("*").alias("orders"), F.sum("amount").alias("revenue")))

On Snowflake: stages, Snowpipe and Dynamic Tables

-- landing: an external stage over cloud storage
CREATE STAGE landing.orders_stage URL = 's3://acme-landing/orders/'
  STORAGE_INTEGRATION = s3_int FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = JSON);

-- bronze: Snowpipe loads each new file as it arrives
CREATE TABLE bronze.orders (raw VARIANT, _source_file STRING, _ingested_at TIMESTAMP_LTZ);
CREATE PIPE bronze.orders_pipe AUTO_INGEST = TRUE AS
  COPY INTO bronze.orders
  FROM (SELECT $1, METADATA$FILENAME, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() FROM @landing.orders_stage);

-- silver: a Dynamic Table keeps itself up to date
CREATE DYNAMIC TABLE silver.orders TARGET_LAG = '15 minutes' WAREHOUSE = transform_wh AS
SELECT raw:order_id::INT AS order_id, raw:customer::STRING AS customer,
       TRY_TO_DECIMAL(raw:amount::STRING, 10, 2) AS amount,
       raw:updated_at::TIMESTAMP_NTZ AS updated_at
FROM bronze.orders
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1;

-- gold
CREATE DYNAMIC TABLE gold.customer_revenue TARGET_LAG = '1 hour' WAREHOUSE = transform_wh AS
SELECT customer, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM silver.orders GROUP BY customer;

How to lay out the layers

OptionExampleGood for
Catalog or database per layerprod_bronze.crm.customers, prod_silver.sales.ordersStrict isolation and permissions per layer; central platform teams
Schema per layer inside a domain catalogsales.bronze_orders, sales.silver.orders, sales.gold.daily_revenueData mesh: each domain owns its own three layers
Storage account or bucket per layeracme-prod-bronze, acme-prod-silverSeparate keys, lifecycle rules and network rules per layer

Always separate environments (dev, test, prod) first and layers second. Grant users read access to gold by default, silver on request, and bronze to engineers only.

Variations you will meet

VariationWhat it means
Other namesRaw / enriched / curated; staging / core / mart; raw / cleansed / conformed / presentation. Same idea.
Fewer layersSmall or simple sources may go landing to silver directly, or skip a separate landing zone when Auto Loader or Snowpipe reads the delivery location. Keep bronze if you ever need replay or audit.
More layersA platinum or serving layer for semantic models, feature stores or APIs; a sandbox for experiments; a quarantine table beside silver.
Streaming medallionEvery layer is a streaming table, so data flows from bronze to gold in seconds or minutes, with checkpoints providing exactly-once processing.
Medallion and modellingMedallion says where data sits; Kimball, Inmon and Data Vault say how it is modelled. A common enterprise combination is Data Vault or 3NF in silver and Kimball stars in gold.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhy it hurtsBetter
Cleaning data in bronzeThe original is lost, so a bad rule cannot be undoneBronze stays raw; clean in silver
Silver tables that mirror each sourceEvery consumer still has to join and reconcile sourcesConform to business entities with shared keys
Reports reading silver or bronzeLogic is duplicated and numbers disagreeBI reads gold or the semantic layer only
One gold table per report requestHundreds of near-duplicate tablesReusable facts and dimensions, metrics in a semantic layer
Copying every layer in full every runCost and runtime grow with historyIncremental processing: Auto Loader, streams, MERGE, Change Data Feed
Treating layers as quality by name"Gold" means nothing without checksExplicit tests and owners per table, shown in the catalog

5. Edge, Ingestion and the Landing Zone

Before the medallion layers begin, data has to travel from where it is produced, the edge, into the platform. This is where most real-world failures start: missing files, duplicates, half-written files, schema surprises, firewalls, and sources that cannot take extra load.

What the edge layer is

The edge is everything outside the central platform that produces or first collects data: factory sensors and gateways, shop tills, mobile apps, branch servers, on-premise databases, partner SFTP servers and SaaS applications. In IoT architectures the edge also has its own compute, an edge gateway, which does useful work before sending anything:

  • Buffering when the network drops, so no readings are lost (store and forward)
  • Filtering and aggregating, for example sending one-minute averages instead of every 10 ms reading
  • Protocol translation from OPC UA, Modbus or MQTT to HTTPS or Kafka
  • Compression and encryption before data crosses the internet
  • Local decisions such as stopping a machine, without waiting for the cloud
Edge toolPlatform
AWS IoT Greengrass, IoT Core, IoT SiteWiseAWS
Azure IoT Edge, IoT Hub, IoT OperationsAzure
Partner solutions (Google Cloud IoT Core was retired in 2023), then Pub/SubGoogle Cloud
MQTT brokers (Mosquitto, EMQX, HiveMQ), Apache NiFi MiNiFi, Kafka at the edgeOpen source and vendor-neutral

Two meanings of "landing zone"

TermWhat it isContains
Data landing zoneThe first storage area where incoming data is dropped exactly as delivered, before bronzeFiles and CDC batches in their original format
Cloud landing zoneThe secure, pre-built cloud foundation that everything runs onAccounts or subscriptions per environment, network, identity, encryption keys, logging, guardrail policies

Both matter in an interview. Cloud landing zones are built with AWS Control Tower, the Azure landing zone accelerators (and Cloud Adoption Framework data landing zones), or the Google Cloud landing zone blueprints, usually as Terraform. Build it before any data arrives, because moving networks and permissions later is painful.

How data should arrive in the landing zone

1. Agree an ingestion contract per source. Owner, format, schema, delivery frequency, file naming, expected volume, classification and retention. No contract, no onboarding.

2. Use a predictable path. landing/<source>/<dataset>/<yyyy-mm-dd>/<file>_<timestamp>.json, so files are easy to find, replay and expire.

3. Make "complete" explicit. Write to a temporary name and rename, or send a _SUCCESS marker or manifest listing files, row counts and checksums. Never process a file still being written.

4. Make it write-once. Ingestion roles may add files but not change or delete them; object lock or immutability policies where audit requires it.

5. Validate on arrival. Checksum, row count against the manifest, file format, malware scan for external files. Move failures to a rejected folder and alert the source owner.

6. Load into bronze incrementally and idempotently. Auto Loader, Snowpipe or COPY INTO track which files were already loaded, so a re-run never loads a file twice.

7. Expire the landing zone. Once a file is safely in bronze, lifecycle rules delete or archive it after days or weeks. Landing is a buffer, not a store.

Tested: what happens when a load runs twice

Jobs get re-run after failures, so loading from landing into bronze must be idempotent: a re-run must not load the same file again. We put two files of 5 rows each in a landing folder and compared a plain batch load with a streaming load that keeps a checkpoint:

# plain batch: no memory of what was loaded
spark.read.schema(schema).json("/lake/landing/orders")      .write.format("delta").mode("append").save("/lake/bronze/orders")

# incremental: the checkpoint records which files were processed
(spark.readStream.schema(schema).json("/lake/landing/orders")
     .writeStream.format("delta")
     .option("checkpointLocation", "/lake/_checkpoints/bronze_orders")
     .trigger(availableNow=True)  # process what is there, then stop
     .start("/lake/bronze/orders"))
RunBatch appendStream with checkpoint
First run (10 rows landed)1010
Same job again, no new files20: every row duplicated10: nothing reloaded
After a third file with 3 rows-13: only the new file loaded

Managed tools give the same guarantee: Auto Loader (a streaming read with file tracking that scales to millions of files), Databricks and Snowflake COPY INTO, which skip files they have already loaded unless forced, and Snowpipe, which keeps load history per pipe:

COPY INTO prod_bronze.shop.orders
FROM '/Volumes/prod/landing/shop/orders/'
FILEFORMAT = JSON
FORMAT_OPTIONS ('rescuedDataColumn' = '_rescued_data')
COPY_OPTIONS ('mergeSchema' = 'true');     -- 'force' = 'true' would reload everything

Typical enterprise flow, end to end

 Factory sensors -> IoT Edge gateway -(MQTT/HTTPS)-> IoT Hub -> Event Hubs --+
 Oracle ERP ---- CDC (GoldenGate / Debezium) -----------------> Kafka ------+-> bronze (streaming)
 Salesforce ---- Fivetran / Lakeflow Connect ---------------------------------> bronze
 Partner CSVs -- SFTP (Transfer Family) -> s3://landing/partner/ -- Auto Loader -> bronze
                                              |
                       checksum, manifest, schema check, lifecycle expiry
 bronze -> silver (quality, dedupe, conform) -> gold (marts, KPIs) -> Power BI / APIs / ML

6. Choosing an Open Table Format

An open table format turns a folder of Parquet files into a real table: transactions, schema evolution, time travel and efficient updates, while the data stays in your own storage. The choice matters because it decides which engines can read and write your data for years. There is no single winner; there is a right answer for each situation.

Delta LakeIcebergHudiPaimon
OriginDatabricks; now Linux FoundationNetflix; ApacheUber; ApacheFlink Table Store; Apache
FocusSimple, fast batch and streaming on SparkEngine-neutral tables at very large scaleFrequent upserts and incremental processingStreaming-first on Flink
FeaturesDeletion vectors, liquid clustering, change data feed, UniFormHidden partitioning, partition evolution, column IDs, REST catalog standardMerge-on-read, record-level index, incremental queries, built-in table servicesLSM-tree storage for high-rate streaming updates
EnginesDatabricks, Spark, FabricSnowflake, BigQuery, Athena, Trino, Spark, FlinkSpark, FlinkFlink
CatalogsUnity Catalog, HiveIceberg REST catalogs (Polaris, Glue, Unity, Horizon), NessieHive, GluePaimon catalog, Hive

Which one, in which scenario

ScenarioUsual choiceWhy
Databricks is the main platformDeltaDeepest integration: liquid clustering, predictive optimization, Unity Catalog; UniForm or managed Iceberg for other readers
Microsoft FabricDeltaOneLake stores tables as Delta; Iceberg can be added through virtualisation
Several engines share one copy (Snowflake, Spark, Trino, Athena)IcebergThe widest engine support and an open catalog protocol
AWS-native lake (Athena, Glue, EMR, Redshift)IcebergFirst-class support across AWS analytics services
Snowflake or BigQuery with external tablesIcebergBoth support Iceberg tables natively
Migrating Hive tables in placeIcebergIn-place migration, and partition evolution avoids rewrites later
Heavy CDC upserts with frequent small updatesHudi (or Delta/Iceberg with deletion vectors)Merge-on-read and record-level indexes keep writes cheap
Incremental pipelines reading only changesHudi, or Delta change data feedBuilt-in incremental queries
Flink streaming lakehousePaimon or HudiDesigned for continuous streaming writes
Small, append-only data read by one enginePlain ParquetA table format adds little
Which engines must WRITE the tables?
  ├─ Mostly Databricks or Fabric ............... Delta (+ UniForm for readers)
  ├─ Many engines, or Snowflake / BigQuery ..... Iceberg
  └─ Flink-heavy streaming ..................... Paimon or Hudi
Then check the workload:
  ├─ Update-heavy CDC with tight latency ....... consider Hudi or MoR
  └─ Mostly append and large scans ............. any; follow the engines

You do not always have to choose just one

ToolWhat it doesLimit
Delta UniFormWrites Iceberg (and Hudi) metadata for Delta tables, so Iceberg engines can read themIceberg side is read-only; writes go through Delta
Apache XTable (incubating)Translates metadata between Delta, Iceberg and Hudi over one copy of dataSync job to run and monitor; feature gaps
Managed Iceberg in Unity Catalog or SnowflakeNative Iceberg tables inside the platformFeature parity varies by platform

Format versions are a compatibility decision

Formats keep adding features that older readers cannot understand. Delta tracks this with reader and writer protocol features; Iceberg with format versions. Iceberg v3, which adds deletion vectors, row lineage and the VARIANT type, became generally available in Snowflake in May 2026 and was in public preview on Databricks in April 2026. A v3 table is unreadable by engines that only support v2, so upgrade a format version only after every reader supports it.

Details of each format are in the Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi cards. Feature support moves quickly; check each engine's documentation for the exact version you run.

7. Data Integration Patterns

Moving data between systems is where most enterprise complexity lives. The right pattern depends on how fresh the data must be and how much load the source can take.

PatternHow it worksFreshnessUse when
Batch ETLExtract, transform on a separate engine, then loadHoursLegacy warehouses, heavy cleansing before load
Batch ELTLoad raw data, transform inside the platformHoursModern warehouses and lakehouses
Change data captureRead the database transaction log for inserts, updates and deletesSeconds to minutesKeeping copies of operational databases in sync
Event streamingApplications publish events to a log such as KafkaSecondsClickstreams, IoT, event-driven systems
APIsCall a service for data on requestReal timeSaaS sources, small lookups
Replication and mirroringCopy whole tables or databases continuouslyNear real timeMoving operational data into analytics
VirtualisationQuery in place across systemsLiveQuick access without new pipelines
Reverse ETLPush analytics results back into business appsHoursSending scores or segments to a CRM

Tools by pattern

PatternCommercial and cloudOpen source
ETL and ELTInformatica, Talend, Fivetran, Matillion, Azure Data Factory, AWS GlueAirbyte, Apache NiFi, Spark, dbt
CDCOracle GoldenGate, Qlik Replicate, AWS DMS, Datastream, FivetranDebezium with Kafka Connect
StreamingConfluent, Amazon MSK and Kinesis, Event Hubs, Pub/SubApache Kafka, Apache Flink, Spark Structured Streaming
VirtualisationDenodo, Starburst, DremioTrino, Presto
Reverse ETLHightouch, CensusCustom jobs
OrchestrationDatabricks Jobs, Azure Data Factory, Step FunctionsApache Airflow, Dagster, Prefect

How the retailer combines them

  • Orders database to bronze: CDC, because orders change and finance needs them within minutes
  • Website clicks: event streaming through Kafka
  • Supplier prices from a partner: an API, pulled hourly
  • CRM: batch ELT through a managed connector each night
  • Customer churn scores back to the CRM: reverse ETL

CDC captures deletes, which matters for privacy: when a customer is deleted at the source, the delete flows to the analytics copy. Plain batch snapshots miss deletes unless you compare full extracts.

8. Compatibility and Schema Evolution

Data outlives the code that writes it. A schema change that is harmless for the producer can break ten consumers, so an architect defines which changes are allowed, how they are checked, and how breaking changes are rolled out.

The four kinds of compatibility

ModeMeaningUpgrade order
BackwardConsumers using the new schema can read data written with the old oneUpgrade consumers first
ForwardConsumers using the old schema can read data written with the new oneUpgrade producers first
FullBoth directionsAny order
NoneNo guaranteeCoordinated release, everyone at once

Schema registries add transitive variants: the new schema must be compatible with all earlier versions, not only the previous one. This matters when consumers can replay old data, such as a Kafka topic kept for months.

Tested: which changes break readers

We wrote Avro records with one schema and read them with another, in both directions:

ChangeNew reader, old data (backward)Old reader, new data (forward)
Add a field with a defaultOKOK
Add a field without a defaultFailsOK
Remove a field that had no defaultOKFails
Remove a field that had a defaultOKOK
Widen int to longOKFails
Narrow long to intFailsOK
Rename without an aliasFailsFails
Rename with an aliasOKFails
Make a field optional (null by default)OKOK while values are present

The pattern to remember: defaults make changes safe, renames are almost never free, and an alias only helps the new reader. That is why many teams default to full compatibility for shared topics: add optional fields with defaults, and never rename or retype in place.

Schema registries

RegistryWhere
Confluent Schema RegistryKafka and Confluent; Avro, Protobuf, JSON Schema
AWS Glue Schema RegistryMSK, Kinesis
Azure Schema RegistryEvent Hubs
Apicurio RegistryOpen source

A registry stores every version of a schema and rejects incompatible versions when the producer registers them, so a breaking change fails at deploy time rather than in a consumer at 3 a.m. Protobuf follows similar rules through field numbers: never reuse or renumber a field.

Tables evolve differently

ChangeDelta LakeIcebergPlain Parquet
Add a columnYesYesYes, but readers may miss it
Rename a columnNeeds column mappingYes, columns tracked by IDBreaks readers
Drop a columnNeeds column mappingYesBreaks readers
Widen a typeType widening on newer versionsSafe promotions, such as int to longRisky
Change partitioningRewrite, or use liquid clusteringPartition evolution without rewriteRewrite

Tested in the other cards: on Delta Lake 3.2, a rename and a drop both failed until column mapping was enabled, and changing INT to BIGINT failed. Appending an extra column to plain Parquet succeeded, but the new column was invisible when reading the folder.

Rolling out a breaking change: expand and contract

1. Expand. Add the new column or field alongside the old one, for example email_address next to email.

2. Dual-write. Producers fill both, so old and new consumers keep working.

3. Migrate consumers. Lineage lists every consumer; each moves to the new field, tracked to completion.

4. Deprecate. Announce a removal date in the catalog and data contract.

5. Contract. Remove the old field once nothing reads it, which lineage and query logs can prove.

Other compatibility an architect manages

AreaRule of thumb
Data products and APIsSemantic versioning: a breaking change means a new major version, such as /v2, with the old one kept for an agreed period
SQL dialectsPrefer ANSI SQL in shared logic; translate with tools such as SQLGlot when migrating engines
File formatsParquet for analytics, Avro or Protobuf for messages, JSON only at the edges
TimeStore timestamps in UTC; convert at display time
Codes and encodingsUTF-8 text; ISO 8601 dates, ISO 3166 country codes, ISO 4217 currencies
NumbersDECIMAL for money, never floating point
Client librariesPin versions; test upgrades in a staging environment against real data

9. Reliability and Consistency Patterns

Pipelines fail: networks drop, jobs are retried, data arrives late or twice. Reliable architecture does not try to prevent every failure; it makes failure safe to repeat.

PatternProblem it solvesHow
Idempotent writesA retried job duplicates dataMERGE on a business key, or overwrite a whole partition, instead of plain append
At-least-once plus dedupeStreams can redeliver messagesDeduplicate on an event ID within a time window
Exactly-onceDuplicates are unacceptable, such as paymentsCheckpointed source offsets plus a transactional or idempotent sink
Retries with backoffTemporary failuresRetry with increasing waits; give up after a limit and alert
Dead-letter queueBad records block the streamDivert failures to a separate table or topic for review
Replay and backfillLogic changed or data was wrongKeep raw data, make jobs parameterised by date, rerun a range
WatermarksLate-arriving eventsWait a bounded time, then finalise; route later data separately
Write-audit-publishBad data reaching consumersWrite to a hidden area, test it, then publish atomically

Write-audit-publish on different platforms

PlatformHow to stage, test and publish
IcebergWrite to a branch, validate, then fast-forward main
Delta / DatabricksWrite to a staging table, test, then swap or MERGE into production
SnowflakeZero-copy clone, load and test the clone, then swap tables
Any lakeGit-like branching with lakeFS or Project Nessie
dbtdbt build: tests run after each model and failures stop downstream models

Consistency across systems

A single Delta, Iceberg or Snowflake table gives ACID transactions. Across systems there is no shared transaction: a row can be in the orders database but not yet in the lakehouse. Architects design for eventual consistency and make the delay explicit, with a freshness SLA per dataset.

  • CAP: during a network partition a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability; most data platforms choose availability and catch up later
  • Transactional outbox: an application writes the business change and an event row in the same database transaction, and a relay publishes the event, so the two cannot disagree (see the Data Architecture Patterns card)
  • Reconciliation: compare counts and totals between source and target daily; it is the safety net for every pattern above

The idempotency patterns are tested in the Data Modelling and dbt cards, where MERGE reruns created no duplicates while plain append did.

10. Scalability, Performance and Workload Isolation

Modern platforms separate storage from compute: data sits once in cheap object storage or a warehouse's storage layer, and any number of compute clusters read it. This is what lets an architect scale and isolate workloads independently.

LeverWhat it doesExamples
Scale upA bigger cluster or warehouse for one heavy jobLarger warehouse size, bigger instances
Scale outMore clusters for more concurrent usersSnowflake multi-cluster warehouses, Databricks SQL warehouse scaling, Redshift concurrency scaling
Workload isolationSeparate compute so ETL never slows dashboardsOne warehouse or cluster per workload; BigQuery reservations
Data layoutRead less dataPartitioning, clustering, Z-order, sort keys, file sizing
Pre-computationAnswer common questions in advanceMaterialised views, aggregate tables, BI extracts
CachingAvoid repeating workResult caches, local SSD caches, semantic-layer caches

Isolation by workload

                 one copy of the data
                          │
   ┌──────────────┬───────┴──────┬──────────────┐
   │ ETL compute   │ BI warehouse │ Data science  │ Ad hoc SQL
   │ scheduled,    │ always on,   │ GPU or large  │ small, auto-
   │ job clusters  │ auto-scaling │ memory        │ suspends
   └──────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┘
     each billed and tagged to its own team

Multi-tenancy

ModelIsolationCostUse when
Separate account or workspace per tenantStrongestHighestRegulated clients, strict contracts
Separate catalog or databaseStrongMediumBusiness units, data residency
Separate schemaModerateLowTeams inside one unit
Shared tables with row-level securityLogical onlyLowestMany small tenants, SaaS analytics

Capacity planning

Estimate from data volume, growth rate, concurrency and freshness: for example, "5 TB growing 60% a year, 200 dashboard users at 9 a.m., hourly refresh". Load-test with realistic data before go-live, because skew, small files and concurrency show up only at real scale. Then set budgets and alerts, since elastic platforms scale costs as easily as performance.

11. Event-Driven Architecture

Instead of systems asking each other for data, an event-driven architecture has systems publish facts, such as OrderPlaced, to a durable log that many consumers read independently.

ConceptMeaning
Event vs commandAn event states something happened (OrderPlaced); a command asks for something (ShipOrder)
Topic and partitionEvents with the same key go to one partition, which preserves their order
Retention and compactionKeep events for a period, or keep only the latest value per key
Event sourcingStore every change as an event; current state is rebuilt by replaying them
CQRSSeparate models for writing and for reading, kept in sync by events
Exactly-once in KafkaIdempotent producers and transactions within Kafka; end to end needs an idempotent sink too

Design decisions

  • Choose the key carefully: ordering is only guaranteed within a partition, so key by the entity whose order matters, such as order_id
  • Govern schemas: every topic has a registered schema and a compatibility mode
  • Avoid personal data in topics where possible: messages are hard to delete from a retained log, so send IDs and keep details in a governed table
  • Plan replay: retention must cover the longest backfill you may need
  • Land events in the lakehouse: bronze tables keep the full history for analytics, beyond the topic's retention

12. Enterprise Modelling and the Semantic Layer

Physical models were covered in the Data Modelling card. At enterprise level the architect also standardises meaning, so that "revenue" or "active customer" is the same number in every tool.

ConceptPurpose
Enterprise data modelA high-level map of the main business entities and their relationships across all systems
Canonical modelA shared format for data exchanged between systems, so each system maps to one model rather than to every other system
Conformed dimensionsOne customer, product and date dimension reused by every fact table
Reference dataShared code lists: countries, currencies, status codes
Semantic layerBusiness metrics defined once, used by every BI and AI tool

Semantic layer options

ToolNotes
dbt Semantic Layer (MetricFlow)Metrics defined in the dbt project
Looker (LookML)Semantic modelling inside Looker
Power BI semantic modelsShared datasets in Microsoft Fabric and Power BI
Databricks metric viewsMetrics defined in Unity Catalog
Snowflake semantic viewsMetrics and relationships defined in Snowflake
Cube, AtScaleIndependent semantic layers over many sources

A semantic layer also matters for AI: natural-language tools such as chat-with-data assistants answer far more reliably when metrics and relationships are defined explicitly rather than guessed from table names.

Standards worth fixing early

  • Naming: snake_case, consistent prefixes such as dim_ and fact_, no abbreviations outside an agreed glossary
  • Keys: surrogate keys in dimensions, business keys kept for tracing
  • Time: UTC storage, an explicit time zone column where local time matters
  • Money: DECIMAL with currency code; never mix currencies in one column
  • Nulls and unknowns: a defined unknown member rather than silent NULLs

13. Challenges in Data Modelling

Drawing a star schema is easy. The hard part is everything that happens around it: unclear requirements, messy sources, changing history, data that arrives late and tables that grow to billions of rows. Interviewers ask about these challenges because they show whether you have modelled real data or only read about it.

The challenges at a glance

AreaChallengeWhat goes wrongHow architects handle it
RequirementsUnclear or changing business questionsModel built for one report, rebuilt for the nextModel business processes, not reports; use a bus matrix; agree definitions in a glossary
GrainUndefined or mixed grainDouble counting, totals that never matchWrite the grain as one sentence before any column: "one row per order line"
KeysSame entity, different IDs in each sourceOne customer counted three timesSurrogate keys, a key-mapping table, MDM golden record
HistoryAttributes change over timeOld sales reported under the new regionSCD Type 1 or 2 per attribute, point-in-time joins
Late dataFacts arrive before their dimension rowsRows dropped by inner joins or keyed to NULLInferred (placeholder) members, updated when the real row arrives
Late factsFacts arrive days after the eventClosed periods change silentlyPartition by event date, reprocess a rolling window, restatement rules
RelationshipsMany-to-many: one account, many ownersFan-out and inflated totalsBridge tables with allocation weights
HierarchiesRagged or changing hierarchiesBroken roll-ups in org charts and product treesFlattened level columns, parent-child with closure table
ConformanceEach team builds its own customer dimensionReports disagree; facts cannot be comparedConformed dimensions owned once and reused
Semantics"Revenue" means different things to Sales and FinanceTwo dashboards, two numbers, no trustMetrics defined once in a semantic layer
DeletesSources hard-delete rowsThe model keeps ghostsCDC with delete flags, soft deletes, periodic reconciliation
Schema driftSources add, rename or retype columnsPipelines break or load wrong valuesData contracts, schema evolution rules, alerting
ScaleFacts with billions of rowsSlow queries, expensive joinsPartitioning, clustering, aggregates, avoid fact-to-fact joins
UnitsMixed currencies, time zones, unitsWrong sums and wrong day boundariesStore UTC plus local date; amount plus currency; convert in one place
PrivacyPII spread across many tablesHard to mask or delete on requestKeep PII in few dimensions, tag it, mask by policy
Wide vs starOne big table or star schema?Wide tables duplicate logic; stars need joinsStar as the source of truth; wide tables as derived, rebuildable outputs

Grain: the challenge behind most wrong numbers

The grain is what one row means. If a table mixes order headers and order lines, or a join quietly changes one row per order into one row per order line, every sum after that is wrong. Most "the dashboard is wrong" incidents trace back to grain.

  • Declare the grain in writing for every fact table and put it in the table comment
  • Enforce it with a uniqueness test on the grain columns, such as dbt unique on order_line_id
  • Never store measures of two different grains in one fact; build two facts and combine them as the next section shows

History: joining to the right version

With SCD Type 2 a customer has one row per version. Joining facts to it on the business key alone matches every version, which duplicates rows. Join on the version valid on the event date, or store the version's surrogate key in the fact at load time.

-- dim_customer_scd2: C1 lived in Pune until 2026-06-30, then Mumbai
SELECT o.order_id, d.customer_sk, d.city, o.amount
FROM orders o
JOIN dim_customer_scd2 d
  ON  o.customer_id = d.customer_id
  AND o.order_date BETWEEN d.valid_from AND d.valid_to;
JoinRows returned (2 orders)Result
On customer_id only4Every order appears once per city: wrong
On customer_id and date range2O1 in Pune (key 1), O2 in Mumbai (key 2): right

Tested on PySpark 3.5. A date range join cannot use a plain equi-join alone, so on very large tables resolve the surrogate key once at load time and store it in the fact; queries then join on a simple key.

Late-arriving dimensions: inferred members

An order for customer C9 arrives before the CRM sends C9. An inner join drops the order; a left join leaves a NULL key. The standard fix is an inferred member: insert a placeholder row for C9 now, key the fact to it, and overwrite the placeholder's attributes when the real row arrives. The fact never needs to be touched again.

INSERT INTO dim_customer
SELECT (SELECT MAX(customer_sk) FROM dim_customer)
         + ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY o.customer_id) AS customer_sk,
       o.customer_id, 'Unknown (pending)' AS name, true AS is_inferred
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM staged_orders) o
LEFT ANTI JOIN dim_customer d ON o.customer_id = d.customer_id;

Tested: C9 got key 3 with is_inferred = true and both orders loaded. In production, use an identity column or a hash key instead of MAX + ROW_NUMBER, which is not safe when two loads run at once.

Many-to-many: bridge tables

A joint bank account has two owners. Join the balance fact to customers directly and the balance is counted twice. A bridge table (account_id, customer_id, weight) sits between them; weights such as 0.5 and 0.5 allocate the measure so totals still add up, and queries that need "accounts per customer" can ignore the weight.

A checklist before you call a model done

  • Grain written down and tested for uniqueness
  • Every dimension conformed or deliberately local
  • SCD type chosen per attribute, not per table
  • Unknown and inferred members defined; no NULL foreign keys
  • Late facts and deletes handled, with a reprocessing window
  • Metrics defined once; totals reconciled to the source system
  • PII tagged; partitioning and clustering chosen for the main queries

Interview-ready summary

Say this in the interview

"The hardest modelling problems are rarely the diagram. They are grain, keys, history and timing."

"I start by writing the grain of every fact as one sentence and testing it for uniqueness, because mixed grain is the main cause of double counting. I use surrogate keys and conformed dimensions so the same customer is one customer everywhere, with MDM when sources disagree."

"For history I choose SCD type per attribute and join facts to the version valid at the event time. For late-arriving dimensions I insert inferred members, so no fact is dropped. Many-to-many relationships go through bridge tables with weights."

"Finally, I make definitions shared: conformed dimensions, a semantic layer for metrics, data contracts with source teams, and reconciliation against source totals, so the model stays trusted as it grows."

14. Joining Two Fact Tables

A classic interview question: "What happens when you join two fact tables, given that facts are huge?" The short answer is that you usually get wrong numbers and a very expensive query at the same time. The good answer explains why, and what to do instead.

Why fact-to-fact joins go wrong

Two fact tables usually share only dimensions (customer, product, date), not a one-to-one key. Joining on a shared dimension is a many-to-many join: every sales row for a customer pairs with every return row for that customer. Kimball calls the result a fan trap (or chasm trap): rows multiply and measures are counted many times.

fact_sales (grain: order line)          fact_returns (grain: return line)
customer  line  sales                   customer  return  amount
C1        L1    100                     C1        R1      40
C1        L2     50                     C1        R2      30
C1        L3     30
C2        L4     80

JOIN ON customer_id  ->  C1: 3 sales rows x 2 return rows = 6 rows
                         C2: no returns, so an inner join drops C2 entirely
SELECT s.customer_id,
       COUNT(*)             AS joined_rows,
       SUM(s.sales_amount)  AS total_sales,
       SUM(r.return_amount) AS total_returns
FROM fact_sales s
JOIN fact_returns r ON s.customer_id = r.customer_id
GROUP BY s.customer_id;
customerjoined_rowstotal_salestotal_returnsTruth
C16360 (doubled)210 (tripled)Sales 180, returns 70
C2missingmissingmissingSales 80, returns 0

Tested on PySpark 3.5. Each sales row is repeated once per matching return row and each return row once per sales row. No error is raised: the query looks fine and the numbers are silently wrong.

What happens to the engine at huge volume

The output size of a many-to-many join is the sum over every key of (rows on the left) × (rows on the right). With billions of rows that number becomes astronomical, and the engine has to do all the work below before it can return anything:

StageWhat happensSymptom
ShuffleNeither fact fits in memory, so broadcast is impossible. Both sides are hash-partitioned on the join key and sent across the networkTerabytes of shuffle read and write
Sort-merge or hash joinSpark chooses a sort-merge join; warehouses use a distributed hash join. Each partition pairs every left row with every right row for the same keyLong stages, high CPU
Row explosionOutput rows = Σ (left rows × right rows) per key, often 100× or 1,000× the inputsSnowflake Query Profile flags an "exploding join"; Spark shows output rows far above input rows
SkewHot keys, such as a marketplace seller or an "unknown" customer, land on one taskOne task runs for hours while the others finish in seconds
Spill and failurePartitions exceed memory and spill to diskDisk spill, out-of-memory errors, executor loss, retries
CostWarehouse credits or cluster hours scale with the exploded rows, not the inputsOne dashboard query costs more than the nightly load

A tested example at small scale: 300,000 sales rows and 30,000 return rows over 1,000 customers.

ApproachRows producedTotal sales reported
Naive join on customer_id9,000,000 (27× the 330,000 inputs)450,161,414: 30× the truth
Drill-across (below)1,00015,005,380: correct

Scale the same shape to 3 billion sales rows and the naive join would produce trillions of rows. That is why the query either runs for hours or fails, and why the answer would be wrong even if it finished.

Estimate the damage before you join

Counting the rows per key on each side tells you how big a join will be, using only cheap aggregations:

SELECT SUM(s.n * r.n) AS rows_the_join_will_produce,
       MAX(s.n * r.n) AS rows_from_worst_key
FROM (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM fact_sales   GROUP BY customer_id) s
JOIN (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM fact_returns GROUP BY customer_id) r
  ON s.customer_id = r.customer_id;

Tested: it predicted 9,000,000 rows and a worst key of 9,000, matching the real join exactly. If the result is far above the larger input, the join is many-to-many.

The right patterns

1. Drill-across: aggregate first, then join

Bring each fact to the same grain on conformed dimensions, then join the small results. This is Kimball's drill-across, and it is what BI tools such as Power BI and Looker do behind the scenes when one report uses two facts through shared dimensions.

WITH s AS (SELECT customer_id, SUM(sales_amount) AS total_sales
           FROM fact_sales GROUP BY customer_id),
     r AS (SELECT customer_id, SUM(return_amount) AS total_returns
           FROM fact_returns GROUP BY customer_id)
SELECT COALESCE(s.customer_id, r.customer_id) AS customer_id,
       COALESCE(s.total_sales, 0)             AS total_sales,
       COALESCE(r.total_returns, 0)           AS total_returns
FROM s FULL OUTER JOIN r ON s.customer_id = r.customer_id;

Result: C1 180 and 70, C2 80 and 0. Use a full outer join so customers that appear in only one fact are kept. The aggregations are cheap because engines aggregate partially before the shuffle, and the join is now one-to-one on far fewer rows.

2. Union, then aggregate (no join at all)

SELECT customer_id,
       SUM(sales_amount)  AS total_sales,
       SUM(return_amount) AS total_returns
FROM (
  SELECT customer_id, sales_amount, 0 AS return_amount FROM fact_sales
  UNION ALL
  SELECT customer_id, 0, return_amount FROM fact_returns
) t
GROUP BY customer_id;

Same correct result. Stacking the facts and grouping once avoids the join and its skew entirely, and scales well because a group-by can combine rows partially before the shuffle, unlike a join.

3. Join at the true shared grain

Sometimes two facts really are related row to row: a return points to the order line it reverses. Then join on that key (often a degenerate dimension such as order_line_id), after aggregating the side that can have several rows per key:

SELECT s.order_line_id, s.sales_amount,
       COALESCE(r.returned, 0)                  AS returned,
       s.sales_amount - COALESCE(r.returned, 0) AS net_amount
FROM fact_sales s
LEFT JOIN (SELECT order_line_id, SUM(return_amount) AS returned
           FROM fact_returns GROUP BY order_line_id) r
  ON s.order_line_id = r.order_line_id;

Tested: L1 100 − 40 = 60, L3 30 − 30 = 0, L2 and L4 unchanged. The join is now one-to-one, so no row multiplies.

4. Model it once: consolidated and accumulating facts

PatternWhen to use itExample
Consolidated factTwo facts are always analysed together at one grainfact_sales_and_returns_daily by customer, product, day
Accumulating snapshotA process with milestonesOne row per order with ordered, shipped, delivered and returned dates
Aggregate table or materialized viewCommon dashboard queriesDaily revenue and returns per store, refreshed incrementally
Semantic layer metricsMany tools need the same cross-fact metricNet revenue = sales − returns, defined once

When you really must join two large facts

TechniqueWhy it helps
Filter and prune firstRestrict dates so partition and file pruning skip most data; select only needed columns
Pre-aggregate the many sideTurns many-to-many into one-to-many before the join
Co-locate on the join keyLiquid clustering or Z-order in Delta, clustering keys in Snowflake, clustering in BigQuery, bucketing or storage-partitioned joins in Iceberg and Hive tables reduce or remove the shuffle
Adaptive Query ExecutionSpark 3.2+ enables AQE by default: it splits skewed partitions and switches to broadcast when a side turns out small after filtering
Salt hot keysSpreads one huge key across many tasks (below)
Process incrementallyJoin only new or changed partitions instead of the full history every run
# Salting: spread a hot key across 16 tasks
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
SALT = 16
fact = big_fact.withColumn("salt", (F.rand() * SALT).cast("int"))
other = small_side.crossJoin(spark.range(SALT).withColumnRenamed("id", "salt"))
joined = fact.join(other, ["customer_id", "salt"])

Tested: a key holding 150,000 of 200,000 rows was split into 16 pieces of about 9,300 rows each, and the salted join returned exactly the same count and sum as the plain join. Salt the big side randomly and copy the other side once per salt value; it only makes sense when the other side is small enough to copy.

== physical plan of the naive join, with broadcast disabled ==
SortMergeJoin [customer_id], [customer_id], Inner
:- Sort [customer_id ASC]
:  +- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id, 8)     <- shuffle of fact 1
+- Sort [customer_id ASC]
   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(customer_id, 8)     <- shuffle of fact 2

Simplified from the tested plan. Two Exchange nodes mean both facts cross the network; that is the cost you pay before a single row is matched.

Common mistakes

MistakeEffectFix
Joining facts on a shared dimension keyFan-out, inflated totalsDrill-across or union then aggregate
Inner join between factsMembers missing from one fact disappearFull outer join of the aggregates
Using COUNT(DISTINCT) or AVG to hide fan-outSome measures look right, sums stay wrongFix the grain, not the symptom
Joining full history every runCost grows every dayIncremental processing and partition filters
Ignoring skewOne task runs for hoursAQE skew handling, salting, filter out unknown keys

Interview-ready summary

Say this in the interview

"Two fact tables normally share only dimensions, so joining them on, say, customer_id is many-to-many. Every sales row pairs with every return row for that customer, so totals are multiplied. That is the fan trap. An inner join also drops customers that exist in only one fact."

"At big-data volume it is also a performance problem. Neither side can be broadcast, so both facts are shuffled on the join key and sort-merged. The output is the sum of left rows times right rows per key, so it can be hundreds of times the input. Hot keys cause skew, then spills, out-of-memory failures and high cost."

"So I avoid joining facts directly. I use drill-across: aggregate each fact to the same grain on conformed dimensions, then full outer join the small results. Or I union the facts and aggregate once. If the facts are truly related row to row, I join on that shared key, such as order_line_id, after aggregating the many side."

"If the business always needs them together, I model it once as a consolidated fact, an accumulating snapshot or an aggregate table, with the metric in the semantic layer. When a large join is unavoidable I filter early, cluster on the join key, rely on AQE for skew, salt hot keys and process incrementally."

15. Data Governance

Data governance is the set of roles, rules and processes that decide how data is owned, defined, protected and used. Tools enforce it, but governance starts with people: if nobody owns the customer table, no tool can decide who should see it.

The three parts of governance

PartWhat it coversRetailer example
PeopleOwners, stewards and a governance councilThe CRM team owns customer data
ProcessHow access is requested, how definitions are agreed, how issues are fixedAccess requests approved by the owner within 2 days
TechnologyCatalog, access control, lineage, quality and audit toolsUnity Catalog, plus a business catalog

Roles

RoleResponsible for
Data ownerA senior business person accountable for a data domain; approves access and rules
Data stewardDay-to-day definitions, quality rules and metadata for that domain
Data custodianThe technical team that stores and secures the data
Data consumerUses data within the agreed rules
Governance councilSets company-wide policies and settles disputes

Operating models

ModelHow it worksSuits
CentralisedOne team sets and enforces all rulesSmaller or highly regulated companies
FederatedA central team sets standards; domains apply themMost large companies, and data mesh
DecentralisedEach domain decides aloneRarely works: definitions drift

Our retailer chooses the federated model. A small central team defines classification levels, naming rules and security standards. The Sales, CRM and Finance domains each own their data and apply those rules.

Policies a company needs

  • Data classification policy: the sensitivity levels and how to label data
  • Access policy: who approves access, and how often it is reviewed
  • Retention policy: how long each kind of data is kept
  • Data quality policy: required checks and who fixes failures
  • Acceptable use policy: what data may be used for, including AI

Many companies follow DAMA-DMBOK, the Data Management Body of Knowledge, which puts data governance at the centre of ten other knowledge areas, including architecture, modelling, security, quality and metadata.

Governance tools

ToolTypeStrengths
Databricks Unity CatalogPlatform-native governanceEnforces access, captures lineage and audit automatically
Microsoft PurviewEnterprise catalog and complianceMicrosoft and Azure estates, classification
CollibraBusiness-focused governance platformGlossary, stewardship workflows, policy management
AlationData catalogSearch, collaboration, query-log based usage
AtlanModern active metadata platformWide connectors, collaboration
Informatica CDGCEnterprise data governance and catalogLarge estates, data quality and MDM suite
DataHub, OpenMetadataOpen-source metadata platformsFree, extensible, strong lineage
Apache AtlasOpen-source, Hadoop eraHive and Hadoop ecosystems
AWS Lake Formation, Glue Data CatalogAWS-nativePermissions and catalog for AWS data lakes
Google DataplexGoogle Cloud-nativeCatalog and governance on Google Cloud

A common pattern is two layers: the platform's own catalog, such as Unity Catalog, enforces rules where the data lives, and an enterprise catalog, such as Collibra or Purview, describes data across every system for business users.

16. Metadata and Catalogs

Governance needs metadata, meaning data about data. Without it, nobody can find a table, trust a definition or tell which column holds an email address.

KindExamplesWho uses it
TechnicalSchema, data types, location, sizeEngineers
BusinessDefinitions, glossary terms, ownersAnalysts, business users
OperationalLast refresh, row counts, job runsOperations, support
GovernanceClassification tags, access rules, retentionSecurity, compliance

How Unity Catalog organises data

Metastore (one per region)
  └─ Catalog        prod_sales            often one per domain or environment
       └─ Schema    gold
            ├─ Table     fact_order_line
            ├─ View      v_customer_masked
            ├─ Volume    raw_files           non-table files
            ├─ Function  mask_email          UDFs, masks, filters
            └─ Model     churn_model         ML models

Full name: catalog.schema.object -> prod_sales.gold.fact_order_line

Each object can carry the metadata above: a comment for the business definition, an owner, and tags for classification.

COMMENT ON TABLE prod_sales.gold.dim_customer IS
  'One row per version of a customer (SCD2). Owner: CRM team.';

ALTER TABLE prod_sales.gold.dim_customer OWNER TO `crm-owners`;

ALTER TABLE prod_sales.gold.dim_customer
  ALTER COLUMN email SET TAGS ('pii' = 'email');

A business glossary

A glossary defines business terms once, such as Active Customer: placed an order in the last 90 days, and links each term to the tables and columns that implement it. This is what stops three dashboards from showing three different numbers for the same thing.

Catalogs on other platforms

PlatformTechnical catalogEnterprise or business catalog
DatabricksUnity CatalogUnity Catalog, or an external catalog
SnowflakeSnowflake Horizon (built in)Horizon, or an external catalog
AWSGlue Data CatalogSageMaker Catalog (formerly DataZone)
AzureFabric and OneLake catalogMicrosoft Purview
Google CloudBigQuery metadataKnowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex)
Open sourceHive Metastore, Apache Polaris (Iceberg REST)DataHub, OpenMetadata, Amundsen

The architectural decision is which catalog is the source of truth for each kind of metadata. A common answer: each platform's own catalog enforces access, and one enterprise catalog collects metadata, glossary and lineage from all of them.

17. Data Classification

Before deciding how to protect data, you must know how sensitive it is. Classification gives every dataset, and ideally every column, a label that the rest of the platform can act on.

LevelMeaningRetailer exampleTypical controls
PublicSafe to publishProduct catalogueNone special
InternalFor employeesDaily sales totalsLogin required
ConfidentialLimited to certain teamsSupplier prices, marginsGroup-based access, audit
RestrictedSerious harm if leakedEmails, phone numbers, payment dataMasking, encryption, strict approval

Types of sensitive data

TermMeaningExamples
PIIPersonally identifiable informationName, email, phone, address
Sensitive personal dataHigher-risk categoriesHealth, biometrics, religion, finances
PHIProtected health information (US HIPAA)Diagnoses, prescriptions
PCI dataPayment card dataCard number, CVV
Quasi-identifiersNot identifying alone, but together they can bePostcode + birth date + gender

Classification only helps if it drives action. In Unity Catalog, a governed tag is a tag from an approved list, so it cannot be misspelled, and access policies can use it directly, as the security section shows. Databricks documents a safe default: tag every new object as unverified, block access until it is reviewed, then apply the right tags.

Finding sensitive data automatically

In a large estate you cannot tag every column by hand. Discovery tools scan data and suggest classifications, which stewards then confirm.

PlatformDiscovery tool
AWSAmazon Macie (S3)
Azure and multi-cloudMicrosoft Purview
Google CloudSensitive Data Protection
SnowflakeBuilt-in data classification
DatabricksData classification in Unity Catalog
Multi-platformBigID, Collibra, Informatica, Immuta, Privacera

18. Data Privacy

Privacy is about using personal data fairly and lawfully: collecting only what you need, using it only for the stated purpose, and respecting people's rights. Security is about protecting data from unauthorised access. A perfectly secure system can still break privacy law, for example by keeping data for too long or using it for something nobody agreed to.

Privacy principles

PrincipleMeaningArchitecture decision
Purpose limitationUse data only for the stated purposeTag tables with their allowed purpose
Data minimisationCollect and keep only what is neededDo not copy emails into gold if no report needs them
ConsentA lawful basis, often consent, for processingStore consent and filter by it
Storage limitationKeep data no longer than neededRetention rules, then delete
Rights of individualsAccess, correction and erasureBe able to find and delete one person's data
AccountabilityProve that you complyAudit logs, lineage, documentation

Laws and standards an architect meets

RegulationWhereKey points
DPDP Act 2023IndiaConsent, purpose limits and individual rights. The DPDP Rules were notified in November 2025, with most duties applying from May 2027. Penalties reach ₹250 crore
GDPREURight to erasure; breach notification within 72 hours; fines up to 4% of global turnover
CCPA / CPRACaliforniaRights to know, delete, and opt out of sale or sharing
HIPAAUS healthcareProtects health information
PCI DSSCard payments worldwideAn industry standard, not a law; strict rules for card data

This is a summary for architecture planning, not legal advice. Confirm exact obligations and dates with your legal team.

Privacy techniques

TechniqueWhat it doesReversible?Use for
MaskingHides part of a value when shownThe data is unchanged underneathShowing data to analysts
PseudonymisationReplaces an identifier with a codeYes, with the key or mappingJoining data without revealing who
TokenisationSwaps a value for a random token, kept in a vaultYes, through the vaultCard numbers
EncryptionScrambles data with a keyYes, with the keyStorage and transfer
AggregationKeeps only totalsNoReports
AnonymisationRemoves any way to identify peopleNo, if done properlySharing and research

Tested: hashing is not anonymisation

A common mistake is to hash emails with SHA-256 and call the data anonymous. We hashed two emails, then hashed a list of guessed emails and joined the two:

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

hashed = customers.select(F.sha2("email", 256).alias("email_hash"), "spend")

guesses = candidate_emails.select(
    "email", F.sha2("email", 256).alias("email_hash"))

hashed.join(guesses, "email_hash").select("email", "spend").show()
# Both customers were re-identified, with their spend.

Anyone with a list of likely emails can reverse a plain hash. A keyed hash, mixing in a secret held in a secret store, stopped the attack in our test: 0 matches. The same email still produced the same value, so joins kept working.

key = dbutils.secrets.get("privacy", "hash_key")  # never in code
pseudo = F.sha2(F.concat(F.lit(key), F.col("email")), 256)

Under laws such as GDPR, keyed hashes are still personal data, called pseudonymised data, because whoever holds the key can link them back. They lower risk; they do not remove legal duties. A dedicated keyed function such as HMAC is the stronger form of this idea.

Tested: deleting a person from a Delta table

Erasure requests are harder in a lakehouse than they look, because Delta keeps old versions for time travel. We deleted customer C200 and checked what remained:

StepResult
DELETE ... WHERE customer_id = 'C200'The current table has 2 rows
Read version 0 with time travelC200's email is still readable
VACUUM ... RETAIN 0 HOURSRefused by a safety check, unless it is turned off
VACUUM after the old files expireThe old data file is deleted
Read C200 from version 0 againFails: the data is gone
count() on version 0Still says 3, from the log's statistics, not the files
DESCRIBE HISTORYStill shows the DELETE and VACUUM, which is your evidence

So erasure is a process, not a single statement: delete from every table that holds the person, including bronze and any copies, then let VACUUM remove the old files after the retention period. Lineage tells you which tables to check.

DELETE FROM prod_sales.silver.customer WHERE customer_id = 'C200';
DELETE FROM prod_sales.gold.dim_customer WHERE customer_id = 'C200';
-- after the retention period (default 7 days), old files are removed
VACUUM prod_sales.silver.customer;
VACUUM prod_sales.gold.dim_customer;

The default retention exists to protect running readers and time travel; do not set it to zero in production. Check your retention settings against the deadline the law gives you. Raw files in bronze, exports and backups also need a deletion plan.

Erasure on other platforms

Every modern platform keeps deleted data for a while to protect against mistakes, so the Delta lesson applies everywhere: a DELETE is only the first step, and the erasure is complete once the recovery copies expire.

PlatformWhere deleted data survivesHow it is finally removed
Delta LakeOld versions for time travelVACUUM after the retention period
Apache IcebergOld snapshotsExpire snapshots, then remove orphan files
SnowflakeTime Travel (up to 90 days on Enterprise), then 7 days of Fail-safeExpires automatically; shorten Time Travel on sensitive tables
BigQueryTime travel window (up to 7 days), then fail-safeExpires automatically
S3, ADLS, GCSObject versions and soft delete, if enabledLifecycle rules for old versions
Backups and exportsSnapshots, extracts, test copiesYour own retention schedule

Document these windows in your privacy notice and erasure process, because "deleted" usually means "deleted from live use now, and from recovery copies within a known period".

Data residency and cross-border transfers

Many laws care about where personal data is stored and processed. GDPR restricts transfers outside the EU unless safeguards are in place, and India's DPDP Act lets the government restrict transfers to certain countries. For an architect this becomes concrete: choose cloud regions deliberately, keep EU customers' personal data in an EU region, and make sure backups, logs, support access and analytics copies follow the same rule. Aggregated or anonymised data can usually move more freely.

19. Data Security and How to Implement It

Security protects data from unauthorised access, change or loss. No single control is enough, so architects use defence in depth: several layers, so that one mistake does not expose everything.

LayerQuestionControls
IdentityWho are you?Single sign-on, MFA, users and groups synced from the identity provider, service principals
AccessWhat may you do?Grants to groups, least privilege, ABAC policies
Fine-grainedWhich rows and columns?Row filters, column masks, dynamic views
EncryptionCan stolen data be read?At rest, in transit (TLS), customer-managed keys
NetworkWhere can you connect from?Private connectivity, no public IPs, IP access lists
SecretsWhere are passwords kept?A secret store, never in code
MonitoringWhat happened?Audit logs, alerts, regular access reviews

Implementation steps on any platform

Whatever the vendor, security is implemented in the same order. The Databricks example below and the other platforms after it all follow these steps.

#StepDone when
1Federate identity from one identity provider (Entra ID, Okta, Ping)No local accounts; MFA everywhere
2Create role-based groups and service identitiesPeople and jobs are in groups, not granted directly
3Grant least privilege to groupsEvery grant has an owner and a reason
4Classify and tag sensitive dataPersonal data columns are tagged
5Apply masking and row-level rules, ideally by tagAnalysts cannot see raw personal data
6Encrypt at rest and in transit, with managed keys where neededKey ownership documented
7Isolate the networkNo public endpoints for data services
8Move secrets to a vaultNo passwords in code or config
9Centralise audit logs and alertsYou can answer "who read this?" in minutes
10Review access regularlyQuarterly certification by data owners

This approach is often called zero trust: never trust a request because of where it comes from, verify every identity, and give the least access needed.

Example: implementing it on Databricks

Here is how the retailer answers the auditor's question, layer by layer.

1. Connect identity. Sync users and groups from the identity provider, such as Microsoft Entra ID or Okta, with SCIM. Create groups by role, for example analysts, crm-owners and data-engineers. Production jobs run as service principals, not as people.

2. Grant to groups, with least privilege. Each group gets only what its job needs. Because grants go to groups, moving a person between teams changes their access automatically.

GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG prod_sales TO `analysts`;
GRANT USE SCHEMA  ON SCHEMA  prod_sales.gold TO `analysts`;
GRANT SELECT      ON SCHEMA  prod_sales.gold TO `analysts`;

GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON SCHEMA prod_sales.silver TO `data-engineers`;

SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE prod_sales.gold.dim_customer;

3. Protect sensitive columns. Analysts need customer counts by city, but not emails. A column mask hides the value for everyone outside an approved group, while the table stays the same.

CREATE FUNCTION prod_sales.security.mask_email(email STRING)
RETURNS STRING
RETURN CASE
  WHEN is_account_group_member('crm-owners') THEN email
  ELSE concat(left(email, 1), '***@', substring_index(email, '@', -1))
END;

ALTER TABLE prod_sales.gold.dim_customer
  ALTER COLUMN email SET MASK prod_sales.security.mask_email;

The masking expression itself was tested in Spark: asha@example.com became a***@example.com, and a card number became ************1111.

4. Limit rows where needed. Regional teams should see only their region's orders. A row filter applies that automatically to every query.

CREATE FUNCTION prod_sales.security.region_filter(region STRING)
RETURNS BOOLEAN
RETURN is_account_group_member('sales-all-regions')
    OR (region = 'IN' AND is_account_group_member('sales-india'))
    OR (region = 'EU' AND is_account_group_member('sales-europe'));

ALTER TABLE prod_sales.gold.fact_sales
  SET ROW FILTER prod_sales.security.region_filter ON (region);

5. Scale it with tags and ABAC. Writing a mask for each table does not scale to hundreds of tables. Attribute-based access control applies one policy to every column carrying a tag, including tables created later. Databricks now recommends ABAC for this, and it became generally available in April 2026.

-- tag the column once
ALTER TABLE prod_sales.gold.dim_customer
  ALTER COLUMN email SET TAGS ('pii' = 'email');

-- one policy covers every email column in the schema
CREATE POLICY mask_emails
ON SCHEMA prod_sales.gold
COLUMN MASK prod_sales.security.mask_email
TO `account users`
FOR TABLES
MATCH COLUMNS has_tag_value('pii', 'email') AS email_col
ON COLUMN email_col;

ABAC needs Databricks Runtime 16.4 or above, or serverless compute, and some parts are still in Beta. Row filters and column masks have limits: for example, they cannot be applied to views, and time travel and clones are not supported on tables that use them.
