6. Encrypt and isolate. Data is encrypted at rest and in transit. For stricter control, use customer-managed keys in the cloud key service, so that revoking the key makes the data unreadable. Use private connectivity so traffic does not cross the public internet.

7. Keep secrets out of code. Store passwords and keys in a secret scope, or in a cloud vault behind it, and read them at runtime.

password = dbutils.secrets.get(scope="etl", key="crm_db_password")

8. Audit and review. Every access is logged. Query the audit system table to answer the auditor directly, and review grants every quarter.

-- Who read the customer table in the last 30 days?
SELECT event_time, user_identity.email, action_name
FROM system.access.audit
WHERE event_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 30 DAYS
  AND request_params.full_name_arg = 'prod_sales.gold.dim_customer'
ORDER BY event_time DESC;

The Databricks grants, masks, filters, policies and audit queries above follow the Databricks documentation; they need a Unity Catalog workspace and were not run here. Check audit column names in your workspace before relying on the query.

The same controls on other platforms

Here is the email mask and the regional row filter from the Databricks example, on the other major platforms. The pattern is the same everywhere: a policy object, attached to a column or table, deciding per user at query time.

Snowflake uses masking policies and row access policies, both requiring Enterprise Edition or higher. A masking policy can also be attached to a tag, so every tagged column is masked.

CREATE OR REPLACE MASKING POLICY email_mask AS (val STRING) RETURNS STRING ->
  CASE
    WHEN CURRENT_ROLE() IN ('CRM_OWNER') THEN val
    ELSE '*********'
  END;

ALTER TABLE customers MODIFY COLUMN email SET MASKING POLICY email_mask;

CREATE OR REPLACE ROW ACCESS POLICY region_policy
AS (region VARCHAR) RETURNS BOOLEAN ->
  CURRENT_ROLE() = 'SALES_ALL'
  OR (region = 'IN' AND CURRENT_ROLE() = 'SALES_INDIA');

ALTER TABLE sales ADD ROW ACCESS POLICY region_policy ON (region);

Google BigQuery uses row access policies that grant rows to principals, and policy tags for column-level security and data masking. Data masking is applied on top of row-level security.

CREATE ROW ACCESS POLICY india_rows
ON retail.sales
GRANT TO ("group:sales-india@example.com")
FILTER USING (region = "IN");

CREATE ROW ACCESS POLICY all_rows
ON retail.sales
GRANT TO ("group:sales-all@example.com")
FILTER USING (TRUE);

In BigQuery, creating the first row access policy hides all rows from anyone not granted, which is why the second policy gives full access back to the right group.

AWS Lake Formation controls access to data in S3 through the Glue Data Catalog. Data filters provide column, row and cell-level security when granting SELECT, and are enforced in Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR and Glue. LF-Tags give tag-based access control: a user whose granted tags match a resource's tags can access it.

Microsoft offers controls in several places. Fabric's OneLake security defines roles with row-level rules, written as SQL predicates, and column-level rules on Delta tables. Azure SQL and SQL Server provide dynamic data masking and row-level security:

-- SQL Server / Azure SQL: mask a column
ALTER TABLE dbo.Customers
  ALTER COLUMN Email ADD MASKED WITH (FUNCTION = 'email()');

-- Row-level security: a predicate function plus a security policy
CREATE FUNCTION security.fn_region(@region NVARCHAR(10))
RETURNS TABLE WITH SCHEMABINDING AS
RETURN SELECT 1 AS allowed
WHERE IS_MEMBER('sales-all') = 1
   OR (@region = 'IN' AND IS_MEMBER('sales-india') = 1);

CREATE SECURITY POLICY security.RegionFilter
  ADD FILTER PREDICATE security.fn_region(Region) ON dbo.Sales
  WITH (STATE = ON);

PostgreSQL has row-level security built in:

ALTER TABLE sales ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

CREATE POLICY region_access ON sales
  USING (region = current_setting('app.region'));

These examples follow each vendor's documentation and were not run here. Masking in SQL Server is a display-level control: users with ad hoc query access can sometimes infer values, so combine it with permissions.

Cross-platform security comparison

ControlDatabricksSnowflakeBigQueryAWSMicrosoft
GrantsUnity Catalog GRANTRoles and GRANTIAM rolesLake Formation, IAMWorkspace roles, SQL GRANT
Column masksColumn masksMasking policiesPolicy tags, maskingData filtersOneLake CLS, DDM
Row filtersRow filtersRow access policiesRow access policiesData filtersOneLake RLS, SQL RLS
Tag-based policiesABAC with governed tagsTag-based maskingPolicy tagsLF-TagsPurview policies
Auditsystem.access.auditACCESS_HISTORYCloud Audit LogsCloudTrailPurview audit, Monitor

When data lives on several platforms, the risk is inconsistent rules: an email masked in Snowflake but visible in a copy on S3. Mitigations are to tag sensitive data consistently everywhere, generate policies from one definition (in code, or with a cross-platform tool such as Immuta or Privacera), and use lineage to find unprotected copies.

20. Data Lineage

Data lineage shows where data comes from, how it is transformed and where it goes. It answers the second half of the auditor's question: where does customer email data end up?

UseQuestion lineage answers
Impact analysisIf I change this column, which tables and dashboards break?
Root causeThis dashboard is wrong; which upstream job caused it?
ComplianceWhere does personal data flow, and which copies must be erased?
TrustIs this number built from approved sources?
Clean-upWhich tables does nothing read any more?

Levels of lineage

LevelShowsExample
Job or processWhich job, notebook or task ranload_fact_order_line ran at 06:00
Dataset or tableWhich tables feed whichsilver.orders → gold.fact_order_line
ColumnWhich columns feed whichorders.amount → rpt_daily_sales.revenue

How lineage is captured

MethodHow it worksTrade-off
Runtime captureThe engine reports what each query read and wroteAccurate; needs support in each engine
Parsing SQL or codeA scanner reads queries and scriptsCovers many systems; misses dynamic code
Query logsReads the warehouse's query historyNo code changes; only SQL
Manual registrationPeople add links by hand or APIFills gaps; goes out of date

Example: lineage in Databricks

Unity Catalog captures lineage automatically for queries run on Databricks through Spark DataFrames or Databricks SQL. Here is what happens when the retailer's daily job runs:

1. The job runs as usual. Nothing in the code mentions lineage.

spark.sql("""
  CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE prod_sales.gold.rpt_daily_sales AS
  SELECT f.order_date, c.city, SUM(f.net_amount) AS revenue
  FROM prod_sales.gold.fact_order_line f
  JOIN prod_sales.gold.dim_customer c ON f.customer_sk = c.customer_sk
  GROUP BY f.order_date, c.city
""")

2. Unity Catalog records the links. From the query plan it learns that rpt_daily_sales reads fact_order_line and dim_customer, that revenue comes from net_amount, and which job or notebook ran it.

3. View it in Catalog Explorer. Open the table, choose the Lineage tab, then See Lineage Graph. Click a column to see its upstream and downstream columns, and filter for the jobs and dashboards that use the table.

4. Query it with SQL. Lineage is also in system tables, so it can drive reports and automation.

-- What reads dim_customer?
SELECT DISTINCT target_table_full_name, entity_type
FROM system.access.table_lineage
WHERE source_table_full_name = 'prod_sales.gold.dim_customer'
  AND event_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 90 DAYS;

-- Where does the email column flow?
SELECT DISTINCT target_table_full_name, target_column_name
FROM system.access.column_lineage
WHERE source_table_full_name = 'prod_sales.silver.customer'
  AND source_column_name = 'email';
Unity Catalog lineage facts
CapturesTables, views, columns, notebooks, jobs, pipelines, dashboards, models
ScopeAcross all workspaces on one metastore
RetentionCatalog Explorer keeps it indefinitely (data since September 2024); system tables keep 395 days by default
Does not captureRDDs, global temp views, renamed objects, column lineage for path-based tables, column mappings inside UDFs
External systemsAdded manually or by API as external metadata, such as a Kafka topic or a Tableau report

To get full lineage, register tables in Unity Catalog and refer to them by name, not by path, and avoid RDDs. These rules are worth writing into your coding standards.

Example: lineage outside Databricks with OpenLineage

OpenLineage is an open standard for lineage events. A Spark listener sends an event when a job starts and finishes, listing the datasets it read and wrote. Marquez is its reference server, and DataHub, Purview and others can receive the same events.

spark = (SparkSession.builder
  .config("spark.jars.packages",
          "io.openlineage:openlineage-spark_2.12:1.40.1")
  .config("spark.extraListeners",
          "io.openlineage.spark.agent.OpenLineageSparkListener")
  .config("spark.openlineage.transport.type", "http")
  .config("spark.openlineage.transport.url", "http://marquez:5000")
  .config("spark.openlineage.namespace", "retail")
  .getOrCreate())

We ran this on local Spark 3.5, sending events to a file instead of a server. The result was a useful lesson:

OperationWhat OpenLineage recorded
Writing the raw orders and customers filesEach output dataset, with its schema
Joining them and writing a Delta tableBoth inputs, but no output dataset
Joining them and writing ParquetNo lineage event at all

So lineage coverage depends on the engine version, the command and the table format, and no tool catches everything. Test lineage capture for your real job types before promising an auditor complete coverage. We saw the same on Databricks' list of limitations above.

Lineage on other platforms

PlatformNative lineageNotes
DatabricksUnity Catalog, automaticSystem tables keep 395 days
SnowflakeACCESS_HISTORY view, plus a lineage graph in SnowsightColumn lineage needs Enterprise Edition; 365 days of history
Google CloudKnowledge Catalog data lineageAutomatic for BigQuery jobs; kept 30 days; accepts OpenLineage events
AzureMicrosoft PurviewScans many sources; Databricks via Unity Catalog scans
AWSSageMaker Catalog and partner toolsOften filled in with OpenLineage-based tools
Open-source SparkOpenLineage listener, SplineSends events to Marquez, DataHub or others
dbtBuilt-in model graphModel-level; dbt platform adds column-level

In Snowflake, column lineage is recorded in the objects_modified field of ACCESS_HISTORY, and can be flattened into source-to-target pairs:

SELECT ah.query_start_time,
       om.value:"objectName"::STRING    AS target_table,
       col.value:"columnName"::STRING   AS target_column,
       src.value:"objectName"::STRING   AS source_table,
       src.value:"columnName"::STRING   AS source_column
FROM snowflake.account_usage.access_history ah,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(ah.objects_modified) om,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(om.value:"columns") col,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(col.value:"directSources") src
WHERE ah.query_start_time >= DATEADD(day, -30, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP());

The Snowflake query follows the structure in Snowflake's documentation and was not run here. Retention differs widely between platforms, from 30 days to over a year, so copy lineage into your own store if audits need longer history.

Other lineage tools

ToolHow it gets lineage
dbtBuilds a model-level graph from ref() and source(), shown in dbt docs
Microsoft PurviewScans sources; Unity Catalog lineage through scans, and Spark through OpenLineage
CollibraTechnical lineage scanners, including one for Unity Catalog
DataHub, OpenMetadataConnectors for databases, Databricks, Kafka and Airflow, plus a Spark listener
MarquezReference store for OpenLineage events
Apache AtlasHooks for Hive and other Hadoop tools
AirflowThe OpenLineage provider reports what each task reads and writes

21. Building Enterprise Lineage Across Systems

Unity Catalog covers what runs on Databricks. A real company also has source databases, APIs, Kafka, other Spark clusters and Airflow, so the architect has to join them into one picture. These seven steps build on each other.

 Source DBs    APIs      Kafka       Spark jobs      Airflow DAGs
     │          │          │              │                │
 scanners    manual    schema reg.   OpenLineage    OpenLineage
 (JDBC)      / API     + topics      listener       provider
     └──────────┴──────────┴──────┬───────┴────────────────┘
                                  ▼
                  CENTRAL METADATA PLATFORM
              (Collibra, DataHub, Atlas, Purview)
       technical metadata + glossary + owners + lineage graph
                                  │
              impact analysis • visualisation • audit

1. Collect metadata from every source. Each kind of system needs a different collector:

SourceHow to collectWhat you get
Source databasesCatalog scanners connect over JDBC and read the system catalogTables, columns, types, keys
APIsRegister the API and its schema (for example OpenAPI) as a dataset, by hand or APIEndpoints and fields
KafkaRead topics and the schema registryTopics, message schemas
SparkThe OpenLineage listener, or Unity Catalog on DatabricksRuntime inputs and outputs
AirflowThe OpenLineage provider (Airflow 2.7+)Task runs and the datasets they touch

2. Capture all three levels. Job-level lineage says which run produced the data. Dataset-level lineage links tables. Column-level lineage links fields, which is what you need to trace personal data and judge the impact of a column change.

3. Use OpenLineage where it fits. Choose the open standard for anything you control, such as Spark and Airflow, so that you are not tied to one vendor. Use native connectors where they are richer, such as Unity Catalog inside Databricks. Keep dataset names consistent: OpenLineage identifies a dataset by namespace and name, so the same table must get the same name from every tool, or the graph splits.

4. Store it centrally. Send everything to one metadata platform. Collibra is strongest for business governance and stewardship workflows; DataHub is open source with strong lineage and many connectors; Apache Atlas suits Hadoop-based estates. Purview is the natural choice in Microsoft-heavy companies.

5. Connect technical and business metadata. Link each table and column to a glossary term and an owner. Then the lineage graph can say "the Revenue KPI comes from CRM and Orders data, owned by the Sales domain", not only "table A feeds table B".

6. Build impact analysis. Walk the graph upstream to find causes and downstream to find what breaks. Run it automatically: when a pull request changes a column, list the affected tables, dashboards and owners, and notify them before merging.

7. Provide visualisation and audit. Users explore the graph in the catalog. Auditors get evidence: lineage for personal data, access logs, and the history of who changed what. Keep lineage history for as long as your audit period requires.

The hard part is rarely the tools. It is coverage, naming and ownership, so measure them: the percentage of tables with an owner, and the percentage of pipelines sending lineage.

Lineage interview questions with answers

Q1. What is the difference between data lineage and data provenance?
Lineage is the map of how data flows: which sources, jobs and transformations lead to a dataset, and where it goes next. Provenance is the origin and history of specific data: where a record came from, when, from which source version, and every change made to it, often used as evidence. Lineage says "revenue comes from orders through this job"; provenance says "this row came from file orders_0612.csv, loaded at 06:02 by run 8841, and was corrected on 14 June". Delta table history and audit logs provide provenance; lineage graphs provide lineage.

Q2. What is column-level lineage?
It links each column to the source columns and transformation that produce it. For example, rpt_daily_sales.revenue comes from SUM(fact_order_line.net_amount), which comes from orders.quantity × orders.unit_price. It is needed to trace personal data such as email through every copy, to judge the impact of changing one column, and to explain a metric. Tools build it from the query plan or by parsing SQL. It breaks down inside UDFs and path-based tables, which hide the column mapping.

Q3. How do you capture lineage across 100 Spark pipelines?
Never instrument each pipeline by hand; capture lineage at the platform level so new pipelines are covered automatically. On Databricks, Unity Catalog does this, provided every pipeline uses Unity Catalog tables by name, avoids RDDs, and runs on supported compute. Elsewhere, add the OpenLineage listener once, in the cluster defaults, an init script or a shared job template, with one namespace convention. Then enforce it: a CI check rejects path-based writes and missing table registration, and a coverage report lists pipelines that sent no lineage in the last week. Finally, test each job type: in our test, OpenLineage recorded a Delta write's inputs but not its output.

Q4. How do you capture lineage from Kafka to Delta Lake?
A Structured Streaming job reads the topic and writes a bronze Delta table. On Databricks, Unity Catalog records the Delta tables, but a Kafka topic is not a Unity Catalog object, so register it as external metadata (system type Kafka, entity type Topic) and link it to the bronze table with the External Lineage API, including column mappings. That external lineage shows in Catalog Explorer, but not in the lineage system tables. With OpenLineage, the Spark listener reports the Kafka topic as an input dataset, provided your version supports the source. Also collect topic schemas from the schema registry so the columns can be matched.

Q5. How do you identify downstream impact when a source column changes?
Use column-level lineage to walk downstream from the column, then expand to the jobs, dashboards and owners attached to each result. On Databricks, query system.access.column_lineage repeatedly, starting from the changed column, and join to table_lineage for jobs and dashboards. In dbt, dbt ls --select model+ lists downstream models. Automate it in CI so a pull request that drops or renames a column shows the impact list and notifies owners, and use data contracts so breaking changes need agreement first.

# Walk downstream from one column, level by level
frontier = {("prod_sales.silver.customer", "email")}
seen = set()
while frontier:
    pairs = " OR ".join(
        f"(source_table_full_name = '{t}' AND source_column_name = '{c}')"
        for t, c in frontier)
    rows = spark.sql(f"""
        SELECT DISTINCT target_table_full_name AS t, target_column_name AS c
        FROM system.access.column_lineage
        WHERE ({pairs}) AND target_table_full_name IS NOT NULL""").collect()
    frontier = {(r.t, r.c) for r in rows} - seen
    seen |= frontier
print(sorted(seen))   # every downstream column that carries email

Q6. What is the difference between technical lineage and business lineage?
Technical lineage is system-level detail: tables, columns, jobs and SQL, for engineers. Business lineage is a simplified view in business terms: "the Monthly Revenue KPI is calculated from paid orders in the Order system, owned by Finance", for analysts, auditors and managers. Business lineage is built by linking technical assets to glossary terms and owners, and hiding intermediate steps.

Q7. How does Unity Catalog capture lineage?
Automatically, at runtime. When a query runs on Databricks compute through Spark DataFrames or Databricks SQL, Unity Catalog records which tables and columns were read and written, and which notebook, job, pipeline or dashboard ran it. It aggregates this across all workspaces on the metastore. You see it in Catalog Explorer and query it in system.access.table_lineage and column_lineage, kept 395 days by default. Tables must be registered in Unity Catalog. RDDs, global temp views, renamed objects and path-based column lineage are not captured, and external systems are added through external metadata.

Q8. What is OpenLineage, and how does it integrate with Airflow?
OpenLineage is an open standard for lineage events. Each event describes a run of a job with its input and output datasets, plus extra details called facets, such as schemas or column lineage. Airflow 2.7 and later integrate through the apache-airflow-providers-openlineage package. A listener fires when tasks start, complete or fail, and gets lineage from the operator in this order: a custom extractor, the operator's own OpenLineage methods, hook-level lineage, then manual inlets and outlets. You configure a transport, such as HTTP to Marquez or DataHub, or the console for testing. Where the operator supports it, Airflow passes parent run details to Spark, so a task links to the Spark job it launched.

Q9. How would you integrate Collibra with Databricks?
Collibra connects to Unity Catalog through an Edge site or a Collibra Cloud site. You create a Databricks Workspace connection, add the Technical Lineage for Databricks Unity Catalog capability, and synchronise manually or on a schedule, then review the ingestion report. It brings in databases, schemas, tables and columns with their lineage, with volumes and notebooks in preview, but not workflows. Use a service principal with only USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT; Collibra recommends a dedicated catalog of lineage views rather than direct access to query history tables. Then link the ingested assets to Collibra's glossary terms, owners and policies, so that business users see governed data with lineage.

Q10. How would you maintain lineage across multiple cloud platforms?
Choose one central metadata platform, such as DataHub, Collibra or Purview, and one standard, OpenLineage, for custom pipelines. Harvest native lineage from each platform: Unity Catalog per metastore, which means per region, AWS Glue, and Microsoft Fabric or Purview. Use a single naming convention for datasets, because the graph only joins up when the same dataset has the same identity everywhere. Register shared data, such as Delta Sharing recipients or cross-cloud copies, as explicit links. Run the collectors on a schedule, measure coverage per platform, and keep ownership and glossary terms in the central catalog, so the business view stays the same whichever cloud the data is in.

22. Implementing Centralised Metadata, Lineage, Governance and Security

Large companies rarely have one data platform. A bank or retailer may run Databricks for engineering, Snowflake for finance, BigQuery for marketing, Kafka for events, Oracle and SAP as sources and Power BI or Tableau on top. Each platform has its own catalog, permissions and lineage. The goal of a centralised design is one place to find, understand, trust and control all of it.

The principle that makes it work: define centrally, enforce natively. Definitions, ownership, classifications, policies and the lineage graph live in one central metadata platform (the control plane). Enforcement stays inside each platform's native engine (the data planes), because only Unity Catalog can mask a column in Databricks and only Snowflake can mask a column in Snowflake. A central tool that tries to sit in the query path for every platform becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure.

Reference architecture

 DATA PLANES (where data lives and policies are ENFORCED)
 Databricks/UC   Snowflake    BigQuery    Kafka+Registry   Oracle/SAP   Airflow, dbt   Power BI/Tableau
      |              |            |              |              |             |               |
      +------ pull: harvesters / connectors -----+---- push: OpenLineage events, APIs, CI ----+
                                        |
                                        v
 CONTROL PLANE: CENTRAL METADATA PLATFORM (Collibra, DataHub, Purview, Alation, Atlan ...)
   +-----------------+------------------+-----------------+------------------+-----------------+
   | technical       | business         | lineage graph   | governance       | quality and     |
   | metadata        | glossary, owners | job, table,     | classifications, | usage signals   |
   | (schemas)       | domains, CDEs    | column          | policies, terms  | (scores, SLAs)  |
   +-----------------+------------------+-----------------+------------------+-----------------+
                                        |
            +---------------------------+------------------------------+
            v                           v                              v
   SEARCH and DISCOVERY        POLICY SYNC (tags -> native      ACTIVATION: impact analysis,
   portal, data marketplace,   masks, row filters, grants)      alerts, PR checks, AI assistants,
   access requests             in every data plane              audit and compliance reports

 FOUNDATION: identity provider (Entra ID / Okta) + SCIM groups, KMS keys, network controls,
             audit logs -> SIEM (Splunk, Sentinel)

Types of metadata

An earlier section listed the four basic kinds. A centralised platform has to collect and connect more than that:

TypeWhat it describesExamplesMain sourceMain users
TechnicalStructure and storageSchemas, columns, types, partitions, file formats, locations, sizesPlatform catalogs, harvestersEngineers
BusinessMeaningGlossary terms, definitions, KPIs, domains, owners, stewards, critical data elementsPeople, in the catalogAnalysts, business users
OperationalWhat happened whenJob runs, durations, row counts, refresh times, failures, SLAsOrchestrators, pipelinesOperations, SRE
LineageWhere data comes from and goesJob, table and column lineage; transformation logicOpenLineage, Unity Catalog, SQL parsingEngineers, auditors
Governance / policyRules that applyClassifications, retention, policies, certifications, data contractsGovernance team, catalogCompliance, stewards
Security / accessWho can do whatGrants, roles, masks, row filters, access requests, audit logsPlatform permissions, IdPSecurity, auditors
QualityHow trustworthy it isTest results, quality scores, freshness, anomalies, incidentsDQ and observability toolsData owners, consumers
Usage / socialHow it is usedQuery counts, top users, popular joins, ratings, commentsQuery history, catalogEveryone: shows what to trust
PrivacyPersonal data and its legal basisPII categories, purpose, consent, data subject locationClassifiers, privacy toolsDPO, legal
Reference and masterShared codes and entitiesCountry codes, currencies, master IDs and hierarchiesRDM and MDM hubsAll systems
AI / MLModels and their dataModel versions, training datasets, features, metrics, model cards, promptsMLflow, feature storesData scientists, AI governance

Two more distinctions interviewers like:

  • Passive vs active metadata: passive metadata is collected and displayed in a catalog. Active metadata is used to drive actions automatically: a PII tag that creates a mask, a failed quality check that pauses a pipeline, a schema change that comments on a pull request, an unused table that is flagged for deletion
  • Descriptive, structural and administrative: the classic library-science split (what it is about, how it is organised, how it is managed). It maps loosely onto business, technical and governance metadata

The tools you need, by capability

CapabilityNative in platformsEnterprise and cross-platformOpen source
Central catalog and glossaryUnity Catalog, Snowflake Horizon, AWS Glue Data Catalog / SageMaker Catalog, Google DataplexCollibra, Alation, Atlan, Informatica CDGC, Microsoft PurviewDataHub, OpenMetadata, Apache Atlas, Amundsen
Lineage captureUnity Catalog lineage, Snowflake ACCESS_HISTORY, Dataplex lineage, Purview scansCollibra technical lineage, Manta (IBM), InformaticaOpenLineage + Marquez, Spline (Spark), dbt docs
Classification and discoveryUnity Catalog data classification, Snowflake classification, Amazon Macie, Google Sensitive Data ProtectionBigID, Purview, Securiti, OneTrustPresidio (PII detection)
Policy enforcementUnity Catalog ABAC and masks, Snowflake tag-based masking and row access policies, Lake Formation LF-Tags, BigQuery policy tagsImmuta, Privacera, Collibra ProtectApache Ranger
Identity and accessPlatform roles and groupsEntra ID, Okta, SailPoint (access reviews)Keycloak
Quality and observabilityLakeflow expectations, Databricks data quality monitoring, Snowflake data metric functionsMonte Carlo, Anomalo, Collibra DQ, Informatica DQGreat Expectations, Soda Core, dbt tests
Schema and contractsConfluent Schema RegistryCollibra, DataHub Cloud contractsOpen Data Contract Standard, dbt contracts
Encryption and secretsAWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, Google Cloud KMSHashiCorp Vault, ThalesVault
Audit and monitoringsystem.access.audit, Snowflake ACCOUNT_USAGE, CloudTrailSplunk, Microsoft SentinelOpenSearch
Privacy and consent—OneTrust, Securiti, TrustArc—

You do not need everything in this table. A typical stack is: native catalogs in each platform, one central catalog, OpenLineage for custom pipelines, native policy enforcement (or Immuta/Privacera when many platforms need identical policies), a quality tool, and the company's existing identity provider and SIEM.

Implementation roadmap

PhaseWhat to doDeliverable
0. Operating modelSponsor, governance council, domain owners and stewards; decide which metadata is mastered whereRACI, policies, first 50–200 critical data elements
1. Identity foundationOne identity provider, SCIM-synced groups, no local users, least privilege by defaultGroups such as sales-analysts usable in every platform
2. Harvest technical metadataConnect the central catalog to every platform; schedule harvesting; define naming and environment rulesSearchable inventory of all datasets
3. Business contextGlossary, domains, owners, certification; link terms to tables and columnsEvery gold asset has an owner, description and terms
4. Classify and tagAutomatic classification plus steward review; one tag vocabulary used everywherePII and confidentiality tags on all sensitive columns
5. Enforce securitySync central tags to native tags; ABAC policies use tags, not table names; access requests through the catalogMasking and row filters applied automatically to new tables
6. Lineage end to endNative lineage per platform, OpenLineage for Spark, Airflow and custom jobs, BI lineage, stitched with consistent dataset namesColumn-level lineage from source to dashboard
7. Quality and observabilityQuality results and incidents published to the catalog next to each assetTrust signals visible to every user
8. Activate and measureImpact analysis in CI, alerts, marketplace, coverage KPIs, audit reportsGovernance scorecard per domain

Security, step by step

1. Authenticate centrally. Single sign-on with MFA through the identity provider; service principals with short-lived credentials for pipelines; no shared accounts.

2. Authorise with groups and attributes. Role-based access control (RBAC) for coarse permissions such as "can use the sales catalog"; attribute-based access control (ABAC) for fine-grained rules such as "mask any column tagged pii unless the user is in pii-readers". ABAC scales because new tables are protected the moment they are tagged.

3. Flow tags from the centre to the edges. Classification happens once, in the central catalog or by a classifier; tags are synced to Unity Catalog governed tags, Snowflake object tags, Lake Formation LF-Tags and BigQuery policy tags; each platform's own policies then enforce them.

4. Protect the data itself. Encryption at rest with customer-managed keys where required, TLS in transit, private networking, tokenisation of the most sensitive identifiers.

5. Govern access requests. Users request access from the catalog; the owner approves; the grant is applied automatically and expires; periodic access reviews remove what is no longer needed.

6. Audit everything. Platform audit logs flow to the SIEM; reports show who accessed which classified data, and lineage shows where it went next.

  classifier / steward          central catalog              native platforms
  finds email column    --->    tag: pii=email      --->     UC governed tag    -> ABAC mask policy
                                 (one vocabulary)    --->     Snowflake tag      -> tag-based masking
                                                     --->     LF-Tag / policy tag-> column-level control
  user queries table in any platform  ->  sees ****@mail.com unless in pii-readers

Tested building blocks

1. Harvesting metadata with DataHub. An ingestion recipe names a source, optional transformers that add governance metadata on the way in, and a sink. This one assigns a domain and an owner to every table and a pii tag to any table whose name contains "customer":

source:
  type: sqlalchemy  # production: snowflake, unity-catalog, bigquery, kafka, dbt ...
  config:
    platform: sqlite
    connect_uri: "sqlite:///sales.db"
    env: PROD
    domain:
      "urn:li:domain:sales":
        allow: [".*"]

transformers:
  - type: simple_add_dataset_ownership
    config:
      owner_urns: ["urn:li:corpGroup:sales-data-owners"]
  - type: pattern_add_dataset_tags
    config:
      tag_pattern:
        rules:
          ".*customer.*": ["urn:li:tag:pii"]

sink:
  type: file  # production: datahub-rest with the server URL and a token
  config:
    filename: ./metadata_out.json

Run with datahub ingest -c recipe.yml (acryl-datahub 1.7). It produced 28 metadata events: both tables received the sales domain and the owner group; customer received the pii tag and orders received none. In production the sink is datahub-rest, and the same pattern applies to the Snowflake, Unity Catalog, BigQuery, Kafka and dbt sources.

2. Sending lineage from a custom job with OpenLineage. Platforms with built-in lineage report it themselves; custom Python or Java jobs should emit OpenLineage events so they appear in the same graph, down to column level:

from datetime import datetime, timezone
from uuid import uuid4
from openlineage.client import OpenLineageClient
from openlineage.client.event_v2 import RunEvent, RunState, Run, Job, InputDataset, OutputDataset
from openlineage.client.facet_v2 import column_lineage_dataset as cl
from openlineage.client.transport.file import FileConfig, FileTransport

client = OpenLineageClient(transport=FileTransport(FileConfig(log_file_path="lineage_events.jsonl")))
# production: an HTTP transport pointing at DataHub, Marquez or another OpenLineage endpoint

src = dict(namespace="postgres://crm-db:5432", name="sales.public.orders")
revenue = OutputDataset(
    namespace="databricks://prod", name="prod_sales.gold.daily_revenue",
    facets={"columnLineage": cl.ColumnLineageDatasetFacet(fields={
        "revenue": cl.Fields(
            inputFields=[cl.InputField(**src, field="amount")],
            transformationDescription="SUM(amount)", transformationType="AGGREGATION"),
        "order_date": cl.Fields(
            inputFields=[cl.InputField(**src, field="order_ts")],
            transformationDescription="CAST(order_ts AS DATE)", transformationType="TRANSFORMATION"),
    })})

client.emit(RunEvent(
    eventType=RunState.COMPLETE,
    eventTime=datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
    run=Run(runId=str(uuid4())),
    job=Job(namespace="custom-python-jobs", name="load_daily_revenue"),
    producer="https://example.com/pipelines",
    inputs=[InputDataset(**src)], outputs=[revenue]))

Tested with openlineage-python 1.55: the event recorded revenue ← sales.public.orders.amount (SUM) and order_date ← order_ts (CAST). DataHub, Marquez and other consumers accept these events over HTTP.

3. Measuring governance coverage. Export the inventory from the catalog's API and track coverage per domain; "gold assets missing an owner or classification" is the number to drive to zero:

SELECT domain,
       COUNT(*)                                                                 AS assets,
       ROUND(100 * AVG(CASE WHEN owner          IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)) AS owner_pct,
       ROUND(100 * AVG(CASE WHEN description    IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)) AS described_pct,
       ROUND(100 * AVG(CASE WHEN classification IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)) AS classified_pct,
       ROUND(100 * AVG(CASE WHEN has_lineage     THEN 1 ELSE 0 END))            AS lineage_pct,
       ROUND(100 * AVG(CASE WHEN glossary_linked THEN 1 ELSE 0 END))            AS glossary_pct,
       SUM(CASE WHEN tier = 'gold' AND (owner IS NULL OR classification IS NULL)
                THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)                                              AS gold_gaps
FROM metadata_inventory          -- exported nightly from the catalog's API
GROUP BY domain;
domainassetsowner %described %classified %lineage %glossary %gold gaps
hr2505050100500
sales475507575500

Tested on PySpark 3.5 with six sample assets. Gold tables are fully covered; the gaps are in silver and bronze, which tells stewards exactly where to work next.

Collibra vs DataHub

Both are central metadata platforms, but they come from opposite directions. Collibra started as a business governance tool, built around the glossary, stewardship workflows and policies. DataHub started as an engineering metadata platform at LinkedIn, built around automated ingestion, lineage and APIs.

CollibraDataHub
TypeCommercial SaaS platformOpen source (Apache 2.0), created at LinkedIn; managed version DataHub Cloud (formerly Acryl)
AudienceGovernance office, data stewards, business users, complianceData engineers and platform teams, plus analysts
StrengthBusiness glossary, operating model, stewardship and approval workflows, policy managementAutomated metadata ingestion, lineage, search, APIs and event-driven automation
ModelConfigurable operating model: communities, domains, asset types, attributes, relationsTyped entities with aspects (dataset, dashboard, pipeline, glossary term, domain, data product); extensible model
IngestionEdge sites and harvesters, scheduled syncs, many enterprise connectorsPython ingestion framework with YAML recipes and dozens of connectors; pull and push (REST, Kafka, SDKs)
LineageTechnical lineage via harvesters and SQL parsing; business lineage viewsTable and column lineage from connectors and SQL parsing; accepts OpenLineage events
WorkflowsStrong, configurable workflow engine: term approval, issue management, access requestsLighter: proposals and approvals; richer workflows and forms in DataHub Cloud
QualityCollibra Data Quality and Observability moduleAssertions and data contracts; integrates results from Great Expectations, dbt tests and others
SecurityCollibra Protect pushes masking and access policies to platforms such as Snowflake and DatabricksGoverns access to metadata; data enforcement stays in the platforms, driven by tags through integrations and the Actions framework
APIsREST APIs, integrations marketplaceGraphQL and REST APIs, Python and Java SDKs, Actions framework for automation, full source code
HostingSaaS; Edge component inside your network for private sourcesSelf-hosted (Kubernetes: GMS, Kafka, MySQL or PostgreSQL, Elasticsearch or OpenSearch) or DataHub Cloud
CostEnterprise licence; higher cost, lower engineering effortFree software, but you pay in engineering and infrastructure to run it; or a subscription for DataHub Cloud
Best fitRegulated enterprises (banks, insurers, pharma) needing formal stewardship, policies and audit evidenceEngineering-led companies wanting automation, openness and lineage at scale, and willing to customise

How to choose

  • Choose Collibra when the main driver is regulation and business ownership: formal glossary approval, stewardship workflows, policy evidence for auditors (BCBS 239, GDPR), and a governance office that will own the tool
  • Choose DataHub when the main driver is engineering productivity: discovery, column-level lineage, impact analysis in CI, metadata as code, and the freedom to extend and automate
  • Some large companies use both: DataHub (or native catalogs) for technical metadata and lineage, synchronised into Collibra for the business glossary and governance workflows. If you do this, decide which tool masters each kind of metadata, so there is no second source of truth
  • Also on most shortlists: Microsoft Purview (Azure and Fabric estates), Alation (catalog with strong usage-based curation), Atlan (active metadata, modern UI), Informatica CDGC (Informatica estates), OpenMetadata (open source alternative to DataHub)

Common mistakes

MistakeResultBetter approach
Buying a catalog before defining ownersAn empty catalog nobody maintainsOperating model and critical data elements first
Two sources of truth for the glossary or tagsConflicting definitions and policiesOne master per metadata type, synced one way
Policies written per tableNew tables are unprotectedABAC on tags, applied automatically
Central tool in the query path of every platformLatency, outages, vendor lock-inDefine centrally, enforce natively
Lineage only for one platformImpact analysis stops at the platform boundaryNative lineage plus OpenLineage, with consistent dataset names
Measuring tool adoption, not coverageLooks busy, governs littleCoverage KPIs: owners, classification, lineage, certified usage

Interview-ready summary

Say this in the interview

"I design centralised governance as a control plane over many data planes. One central metadata platform, such as Collibra or DataHub, holds technical, business, lineage, governance, quality and usage metadata for every system. Enforcement stays native: Unity Catalog, Snowflake, Lake Formation and BigQuery apply the masks, row filters and grants. The principle is define centrally, enforce natively."

"The metadata types I collect are technical, business, operational, lineage, governance, security, quality, usage, privacy, reference and master, and AI metadata, and I make it active: tags drive masking policies, quality failures pause pipelines and schema changes trigger impact analysis in CI."

"I implement it in phases: operating model and critical data elements; identity with SCIM groups; harvesting from every platform; glossary and owners; classification with one tag vocabulary; ABAC policies on those tags in each platform; end-to-end lineage with native capture plus OpenLineage; quality signals in the catalog; then coverage KPIs per domain."

"For tools, Collibra is a commercial, business-led platform, strongest in glossary, stewardship workflows and policy evidence for regulated firms. DataHub is open source and engineering-led, strongest in automated ingestion, column lineage, APIs and automation. I choose by the main driver, regulation or engineering productivity, and if both are used, I make sure each kind of metadata has exactly one master."

Follow-up interview questions

Q1. Why do you need a central catalog if Unity Catalog already has a catalog and lineage?

Unity Catalog governs what runs on Databricks, very well. It does not see the Oracle sources, the Snowflake finance warehouse, Kafka topics or the Power BI semantic models. A central catalog stitches those together for end-to-end lineage, one glossary and one place to search. Unity Catalog stays the enforcement point and a key metadata source for the central catalog.

Q2. How do you avoid two sources of truth between the central catalog and platform catalogs?

Decide mastership per metadata type. Technical metadata is mastered in the platforms and harvested one way into the centre. Business metadata, such as glossary terms, owners and classifications, is mastered in the central catalog and pushed one way out as tags and comments. Never let both sides edit the same field.

Q3. What is active metadata?

Metadata that triggers action instead of only being displayed: a pii tag that creates a mask, a failed freshness check that alerts the owner and marks dashboards as stale, a deprecated table that warns its users, a column change that lists downstream impact on the pull request. DataHub's Actions framework, Atlan and Collibra workflows are examples.

Q4. How do you make lineage consistent across many platforms?

Use native lineage where it exists, OpenLineage for everything you build, and a naming convention for dataset identifiers (platform, instance, database, schema, table), so the same table gets the same name from every producer and the graph joins up. Measure the share of pipelines that emit lineage.

Q5. How do you prove to an auditor that personal data is protected?

Show the classification coverage of personal data columns, the tag-based policies that mask them, access-review records, audit logs of who read classified data, and lineage showing every downstream copy is also tagged and masked. A central catalog plus SIEM produces these as repeatable reports rather than one-off spreadsheets.

23. Data Quality

Governed, secure, traceable data is still useless if it is wrong. Data quality is measured on a few standard dimensions:

DimensionQuestionExample check
CompletenessIs anything missing?customer_id is never NULL
ValidityDoes it follow the rules?Email matches a pattern; quantity > 0
UniquenessAre there duplicates?One row per order line
ConsistencyDoes it agree across systems?Fact total equals report total
AccuracyDoes it match reality?Stock matches the warehouse count
TimelinessIs it fresh enough?Loaded before 7 a.m.

Where to check, and with what

WhereToolExample
In Databricks pipelinesLakeflow Declarative Pipelines expectationsDrop rows where amount is negative
In dbtData tests and contractsunique, not_null, relationships
In any Spark jobGreat Expectations, Soda, DeequA suite of checks after each load
On tables over timeLakehouse MonitoringDrift and freshness alerts
In the table itselfDelta NOT NULL and CHECK constraintsReject bad writes
-- Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines: rules live with the table
CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE silver_orders (
  CONSTRAINT valid_amount EXPECT (amount > 0) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW,
  CONSTRAINT has_customer EXPECT (customer_id IS NOT NULL)
    ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE
) AS SELECT * FROM STREAM(bronze_orders);

Data contracts

A data contract is an agreement between the producer and consumers of a dataset: its schema, meaning, quality rules, freshness and owner. Breaking changes need notice. The dbt card shows one in practice: a model contract stops a build when a column's type changes.

Master data management

Customers often exist in several systems under different IDs, such as the CRM, the website and the loyalty app. Master data management (MDM) matches those records and creates one trusted golden record per customer, product or supplier. Tools include Informatica MDM, Reltio and Profisee, or matching rules built in Spark.

24. Data Quality KPIs at Enterprise Level

Checks catch bad rows; KPIs tell leadership whether data quality is improving across the whole company. A good enterprise scorecard measures three things: the data itself, the reliability of delivery, and how well the organisation responds when something breaks.

1. KPIs on the data (quality dimensions)

KPIFormulaTypical target for critical data
Completeness rateNon-null required values ÷ required values≥ 99.5%
Validity rateValues passing format and range rules ÷ values checked≥ 99%
Uniqueness rate1 − duplicate rows on the grain ÷ total rows100% on primary keys
Consistency rateRecords agreeing across systems ÷ records compared≥ 99%
Accuracy rateRecords matching a trusted source or audit sample ÷ records sampled≥ 98%
Referential integrityFacts with a valid dimension key ÷ facts100%; unknown members tracked separately
Reconciliation variance|platform total − source total| ÷ source total< 0.1% for financial data

2. KPIs on delivery (reliability)

KPIFormulaWhy it matters
Freshness SLA attainmentLoads landed before the SLA time ÷ scheduled loadsLate data is wrong data for a 7 a.m. dashboard
Pipeline success rateSuccessful runs ÷ total runsShows platform stability
Data downtimeΣ (time to detect + time to resolve) per incidentOne number for how long data was wrong or missing
MTTDAverage time from the issue starting to being detectedMeasures monitoring coverage
MTTRAverage time from detection to resolutionMeasures response and ownership
Schema-change breakagesUnannounced breaking changes per monthMeasures how well data contracts work

3. KPIs on the programme (governance and impact)

KPIFormulaWhat it shows
Critical data element coverageCDEs with active quality rules ÷ all CDEsWhether the important data is actually monitored
Ownership coverageCertified datasets with a named owner and steward ÷ certified datasetsAccountability
Issues found by consumersIncidents reported by users ÷ all incidentsLower is better: you find problems before the business does
Issue backlog and ageingOpen DQ issues, and how many are older than 30 daysWhether problems get fixed, not just logged
Certified dataset usageQueries on certified (gold) data ÷ all analytical queriesTrust and adoption
Cost of poor qualityRework hours, failed reports, regulatory findings, revenue lostThe business case, in money

Rolling checks up into a score

Store every check result in one table, then roll it up by domain, table and dimension. Weight rules by severity so one failed critical rule counts more than many failed optional ones.

SELECT domain,
       ROUND(100 * SUM(rows_passed) / SUM(rows_checked), 2) AS row_pass_pct,
       ROUND(100 * SUM(w * rows_passed / rows_checked) / SUM(w), 2) AS dq_score
FROM (SELECT *, CASE severity WHEN 'critical' THEN 4 WHEN 'high' THEN 3
                              WHEN 'medium' THEN 2 ELSE 1 END AS w
      FROM dq_check_results WHERE run_date = '2026-11-07') t
GROUP BY domain;
domainrow_pass_pctdq_scoreReading
crm85.0088.33Optional phone numbers drag it down; the critical rules are not the problem
sales99.9399.94Healthy: all critical rules near 100%
SELECT COUNT(*) AS incidents,
       ROUND(AVG((unix_timestamp(detected_at, 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm')
                - unix_timestamp(started_at,  'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm')) / 3600), 2) AS mttd_hours,
       ROUND(AVG((unix_timestamp(resolved_at, 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm')
                - unix_timestamp(detected_at, 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm')) / 3600), 2) AS mttr_hours,
       ROUND(SUM((unix_timestamp(resolved_at, 'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm')
                - unix_timestamp(started_at,  'yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm')) / 3600), 2) AS data_downtime_hours,
       ROUND(100 * AVG(CASE WHEN found_by = 'consumer' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 0) AS pct_found_by_consumers
FROM dq_incidents;

Tested on PySpark 3.5 with two incidents: MTTD 1.75 h, MTTR 3 h, data downtime 9.5 h, 50% found by consumers. A freshness query over the same sample gave 50% SLA attainment for gold.fact_sales (one late load out of two).

Making KPIs work in practice

  • Start with critical data elements: the 50 to 200 fields behind revenue, regulatory and customer reporting, not every column
  • Set targets per tier: gold and regulatory data strict, exploratory data relaxed
  • Publish one scorecard per domain, with an owner for each red number
  • Show trends, not snapshots: a score moving from 92% to 97% tells a better story than 97% alone
  • Collect results automatically from Lakeflow expectations, dbt tests, Great Expectations, Soda or Lakehouse Monitoring into one results table
  • Tie KPIs to business impact in the language of the business: "the finance close was late twice because of data", not "null rate 0.4%"

Interview-ready summary

Say this in the interview

"At enterprise level I measure data quality on three layers. First, the data: completeness, validity, uniqueness, consistency, accuracy, referential integrity and reconciliation to source, with targets per tier."

"Second, delivery reliability: freshness SLA attainment, pipeline success rate, MTTD, MTTR and data downtime. Data that is correct but late is still a failure for the business."

"Third, the programme: coverage of critical data elements, named owners, the share of issues found by consumers rather than by us, backlog ageing, and the cost of poor quality."

"I collect every check result in one table, weight rules by severity, roll scores up by domain and publish a trending scorecard with an owner for every red number. That turns quality from a list of failed tests into something leadership can manage."

25. Master Data Management (MDM)

Master data is the small set of core business entities that many systems share: customers, products, suppliers, employees, locations and accounts. Master data management (MDM) is the discipline, process and tooling that creates one trusted version of each of those entities, the golden record, and keeps every system linked to it.

The problem it solves: the same customer exists in the CRM as "Asha Rao", in the web shop as "asha rao" with another city, and in the loyalty app as "A. Rao" with only a phone number. Without MDM, reports count three customers, marketing sends three emails and compliance cannot answer "what do we hold about this person?"

Three kinds of data

TypeWhat it isExamplesChangesManaged by
Master dataCore entities the business runs onCustomer, product, supplier, employeeSlowlyMDM
Reference dataFixed code lists that classify other dataCountry, currency, status codes, unitsRarelyReference data management, often part of MDM
Transactional dataEvents that happen to master dataOrders, payments, clicks, shipmentsConstantly, high volumeOLTP applications, then the warehouse

MDM vs a regular database vs a data warehouse

Operational database (OLTP)Data warehouse / lakehouseMDM hub
Main purposeRun one application: take orders, store accountsAnalyse history across the businessCreate and govern one trusted version of each core entity
Data heldThat application's own records, including transactionsIntegrated history of transactions and dimensionsMaster entities only, plus links to every source record
ScopeOne systemMany sources, read-only copiesMany sources, and it can feed corrections back
DuplicatesUnaware of the same customer in other systemsInherits duplicates unless someone resolves themMatches and merges duplicates: its core job
Key outputRows for the appFacts, dimensions, reports, ML featuresGolden record, cross-reference (source ID → master ID), hierarchies
Data flowUsers and apps write to itOne way: sources → warehouse → BITwo way: sources → hub → back to sources and to the warehouse
HistoryUsually current state onlyFull history (SCD, snapshots)Current golden record plus an audit trail of every merge and edit
VolumeHigh transaction rateVery large: billions of rowsSmall: millions of entities, not billions of events
PeopleApp usersAnalysts, data scientistsData stewards who review matches and approve changes
ExamplesPostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server behind an appSnowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, FabricInformatica MDM, Reltio, SAP MDG, Profisee, Stibo STEP, Semarchy

The key point: a database stores data for one application and a warehouse analyses data from many, but neither decides which record is the real customer. MDM is the system that decides, and both of the others then use its answer. In the warehouse, the MDM master ID becomes the business key of the conformed dim_customer.

  CRM        Web shop     Loyalty app      ERP
   |            |             |             |
   +------------+------+------+-------------+
                       v
              MDM HUB  (match -> merge -> survivorship -> steward review)
              golden records + cross-reference + hierarchies
                       |
         +-------------+--------------+
         v                            v
  back to source apps         data warehouse / lakehouse
  (corrected address,         dim_customer keyed by master_id,
   master ID stamped)         so every fact joins to one customer

How MDM works: the core steps

StepWhat happensExample
1. StandardiseClean and normalise values before comparing themLower-case and trim emails; keep the last 10 digits of phones; parse addresses
2. MatchFind records that are the same entity, using exact (deterministic) and fuzzy (probabilistic or ML) rulesSame email, or same phone, or similar name in the same city
3. MergeGroup matched records under one master IDCRM-1, WEB-7 and LOY-3 become master CRM-1
4. SurvivorshipChoose the best value of each attribute from the groupName from the most trusted source; email from the most recent update
5. Steward reviewPeople resolve uncertain matches and conflicts"Ravi Kumar" vs "Ravi Kumarr": same person?
6. Publish and syncShare golden records and the cross-reference with every consumerAPIs or events to apps; tables to the warehouse

A tested match, merge and survivorship example

Five customer records from three systems. Step 1 standardises the values and gives each source a trust rank:

CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW std AS
SELECT *,
       NULLIF(LOWER(TRIM(email)), '')                         AS email_n,
       RIGHT(REGEXP_REPLACE(phone, '[^0-9]', ''), 10)         AS phone_n,
       CASE source WHEN 'CRM' THEN 1 WHEN 'LOY' THEN 2 ELSE 3 END AS trust
FROM customer_sources;

Steps 2 and 3 match on email, then on phone, so records linked through either one end up under the same master ID:

CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW matched AS
WITH pass1 AS (
  SELECT *, MIN(source_id) OVER (PARTITION BY COALESCE(email_n, source_id)) AS g1
  FROM std),
pass2 AS (
  SELECT *, MIN(g1) OVER (PARTITION BY COALESCE(phone_n, source_id)) AS g2
  FROM pass1)
SELECT *, MIN(g2) OVER (PARTITION BY g1) AS master_id
FROM pass2;
source_idemail (standardised)phone (standardised)master_id
CRM-1asha.rao@mail.com9845012345CRM-1
WEB-7asha.rao@mail.com (was " ASHA.RAO@MAIL.COM ")—CRM-1 (same email)
LOY-3—9845012345 (was "98450-12345")CRM-1 (same phone)
CRM-2ravi@mail.com9000000001CRM-2
WEB-9ravi.k@other.com9000000002WEB-9

Step 4 builds the golden record with survivorship rules, one per attribute:

SELECT master_id,
       MIN_BY(name, trust)                                                AS name,
       MAX_BY(email_n, CASE WHEN email_n IS NOT NULL THEN updated_at END) AS email,
       MIN_BY(phone_n, CASE WHEN phone_n IS NOT NULL THEN trust END)      AS phone,
       MAX_BY(city, updated_at)                                           AS city,
       COUNT(*)                                                           AS source_records
FROM matched
GROUP BY master_id;
master_idnameemailphonecitysource_records
CRM-1Asha Rao (CRM is most trusted)asha.rao@mail.com9845012345Mumbai (latest update)3
CRM-2Ravi Kumarravi@mail.com9000000001Delhi1
WEB-9Ravi Kumarrravi.k@other.com9000000002Delhi1

Step 5 sends uncertain pairs to a data steward instead of merging them automatically:

SELECT a.master_id AS record_a, b.master_id AS record_b, a.name AS name_a, b.name AS name_b,
       LEVENSHTEIN(LOWER(a.name), LOWER(b.name)) AS name_distance
FROM matched a JOIN matched b
  ON a.master_id < b.master_id AND a.city = b.city
WHERE LEVENSHTEIN(LOWER(a.name), LOWER(b.name)) <= 2;

Tested on PySpark 3.5: five source records became three golden records, and one pair (CRM-2 and WEB-9, "Ravi Kumar" vs "Ravi Kumarr", distance 1) went to the review queue. The two-pass match is a teaching simplification: real MDM tools and libraries such as Splink or Zingg use blocking, weighted probabilistic scores and graph connected components, so chains of links of any length are merged.

The cross-reference table

MDM never throws the source IDs away. A cross-reference (xref) table maps every source record to its master ID, which is what lets the warehouse, the apps and auditors trace any golden record back to where it came from:

master_idsourcesource_id
CRM-1CRMCRM-1
CRM-1LOYLOY-3
CRM-1WEBWEB-7
CRM-2CRMCRM-2
WEB-9WEBWEB-9

MDM implementation styles

StyleHow it worksGolden record livesWhen to use it
RegistryHub stores only match links and IDs; data stays in the sourcesAssembled on readQuick start, read-only analytics, least disruption
ConsolidationHub copies and merges source data; sources are not updatedIn the hub, for analyticsBetter reporting and a single customer view in the warehouse
CoexistenceHub merges data and syncs corrections back to sourcesIn the hub and the sourcesSeveral systems keep editing, but should agree
Centralised (transaction hub)Master data is created and edited only in the hubIn the hub onlyStrict control, such as product or supplier onboarding

Tools

CategoryExamples
Enterprise MDM platformsInformatica MDM (IDMC), Reltio, SAP Master Data Governance, Profisee (integrates with Microsoft Purview and Fabric), Stibo Systems STEP, Semarchy, TIBCO EBX
Customer data platforms with identity resolutionSegment, mParticle, Salesforce Data Cloud: identity stitching for marketing, lighter on governance
Open-source entity resolution on SparkSplink (probabilistic record linkage), Zingg (ML-based matching), often run on Databricks
Cloud servicesAWS Entity Resolution

Common challenges

ChallengeHow to handle it
Over-matching: two people merged into oneConservative automatic thresholds, steward review for the grey zone, and an unmerge capability
Under-matching: duplicates remainBetter standardisation, more match attributes, fuzzy and ML matching
No business ownershipNamed data owners and stewards per domain; MDM is a governance programme, not just a tool
Trying to master everything at onceStart with one domain, usually customer or product, and a few critical attributes
PrivacyGolden records concentrate personal data: classify, mask and apply consent and deletion across the xref
Keeping sources in syncEvent-driven updates and stamping the master ID back into source systems

Types of MDM

"Types of MDM" can mean four different things, so a strong answer names the angle first. The two most often asked are by domain and by usage.

Classified byTypesWhat it means
Domain (which entity is mastered)Customer or party, product, supplier or vendor, employee, location or site, asset, financial (chart of accounts, cost centres), reference dataSingle-domain MDM masters one entity; multidomain MDM masters several on one platform and links them, such as customer ↔ product ↔ location
UsageOperational, analytical, collaborativeOperational feeds golden records to live applications in real time; analytical feeds the warehouse and BI; collaborative runs workflows where several teams create and approve master data, such as new product or supplier onboarding
Implementation styleRegistry, consolidation, coexistence, centralisedWhere the golden record lives and whether sources are updated (table above)
DeploymentOn-premises, cloud SaaS, hybridReltio and Informatica IDMC are cloud-native; SAP MDG often runs with SAP S/4HANA
DomainTypical attributesMain consumers
Customer / partyName, identifiers, addresses, contacts, consent, segment, householdCRM, marketing, service, risk, analytics
ProductSKU, description, category, attributes, pricing, packagingE-commerce, ERP, supply chain (often with a PIM tool)
Supplier / vendorLegal name, tax ID, bank details, certifications, risk ratingProcurement, payables, compliance
EmployeePerson, role, org unit, manager, locationHR, IT access, payroll
LocationSites, stores, warehouses, geocodesLogistics, sales territories
AssetEquipment, serial numbers, maintenance hierarchyOperations, maintenance
FinancialChart of accounts, legal entities, cost centresFinance, consolidation, regulatory reporting

Interview-ready summary

Say this in the interview

"MDM, master data management, creates one trusted golden record for core shared entities such as customer, product and supplier, which otherwise exist as different, conflicting copies in many systems."

"It works in steps: standardise, match with exact and fuzzy rules, merge under a master ID, apply survivorship rules to pick the best value of each attribute, send uncertain matches to data stewards, then publish the golden record and a cross-reference of source IDs to master IDs."

"It differs from an operational database, which stores data for one application and does not know about duplicates elsewhere, and from a data warehouse, which integrates high-volume transactions for analysis but does not decide which record is the real customer. MDM handles a small volume of master data, is governed by stewards, and often flows two ways, sending corrections back to source systems."

"The three work together: MDM decides who the customer is, the master ID becomes the business key of the conformed customer dimension, and the warehouse joins every fact to it, so reports count each customer once."

Follow-up interview questions

Interviewers rarely stop at "what is MDM?". These are the follow-ups that usually come next, with answers at the depth a senior or architect role expects.

Q1. What is the difference between MDM and data governance?

Data governance is the framework for all data: policies, standards, roles (owners, stewards), decision rights and quality rules. MDM is one programme that applies that framework to master data, with its own processes and tools.

Data governanceMDM
ScopeAll data: master, transactional, analytical, AIMaster and reference data only
OutputPolicies, glossary, ownership, quality standards, access rulesGolden records, cross-reference, hierarchies
NatureOrganisational: people and decisionsOperational: processes and a platform
ToolsCollibra, Purview, Unity Catalog, AlationInformatica MDM, Reltio, SAP MDG, Profisee

They depend on each other: governance decides who owns customer data, which attributes are critical and which source is trusted; MDM enforces those decisions in its match and survivorship rules. MDM without governance becomes an expensive duplicate-matching tool that nobody trusts.

Q2. What is a golden record?

The golden record (also "best version of truth") is the single, most accurate version of an entity, built by matching records from several sources and choosing the best value for each attribute. It usually does not equal any one source record: in the example above, Asha's golden record takes the name from the CRM, the email from the web shop and the latest city.

  • A stable master ID that never changes, even when sources do
  • Best attribute values, each with lineage: which source supplied it and when
  • Links to every contributing source record (the cross-reference)
  • Status and history: active, merged, retired; versions over time
  • Relationships and hierarchies: household, parent company, product family

Q3. What is the difference between MDM and a Customer 360 platform?

MDM answers "who is this customer?": a governed, high-precision identity with core attributes. A Customer 360 answers "everything about this customer": the identity plus orders, payments, service cases, marketing interactions, web behaviour and scores, usually for front-office users.

MDMCustomer 360 / CDP
FocusIdentity and core attributesFull profile: identity + transactions + interactions + behaviour
MatchingHigh precision, steward-reviewed; false merges are costlyOften probabilistic identity stitching of cookies and devices, tolerant of some error
UsersOperational systems, data teams, complianceSales, service, marketing
GovernanceStrong: owners, stewards, auditLighter, driven by activation needs
ExamplesInformatica MDM, Reltio, SAP MDGSalesforce Data Cloud, Segment, Adobe Real-Time CDP

Best practice: build the Customer 360 on top of MDM. The master ID is the spine that every transaction and interaction is attached to. A 360 without MDM shows three half-profiles of the same person.

Q4. What are matching and survivorship rules?

Matching rules decide whether two records are the same entity. Survivorship rules decide which value wins for each attribute once they are matched.

Matching approachHow it worksExample
DeterministicExact match on standardised strong identifiersSame tax ID, LEI, passport number or verified email
ProbabilisticWeighted score across many attributes (Fellegi-Sunter model); fuzzy measures such as Jaro-Winkler, edit distance, phonetic codesName 0.92 similar + same date of birth + same postcode → score 0.95
ML-basedA model trained on steward decisions predicts match probabilityZingg, Reltio and Informatica use ML matching

Scores fall into three bands: auto-merge above an upper threshold, steward review in the grey zone, no match below. Blocking compares only records sharing a cheap key, such as postcode or the first letters of a surname, to avoid comparing every record with every other.

Survivorship rulePicksTypical use
Source trustValue from the most trusted source for that attributeLegal name from the KYC system
Most recentLatest updated valueEmail, phone, address
Most completeLongest or most populated valueFull name over an initial
Most frequentValue most sources agree onDate of birth
ValidatedValue that passed external verificationPostal-verified address
Steward overrideA human decision, which always winsResolved conflicts

Two golden rules: never let a NULL overwrite a real value, and define survivorship per attribute, not per record.

Q5. What is the difference between registry and consolidation MDM?

RegistryConsolidation
StoresOnly IDs, match links and the cross-referenceA physical copy of the cleansed, merged golden records
Golden viewAssembled at read time from the sources (virtual)Pre-built and stored in the hub
Source systemsUntouchedUntouched: corrections do not flow back
Data qualitySources stay as they are; view is only as good as runtime rulesCleansed and enriched in the hub
PerformanceDepends on calls to every sourceFast reads from the hub
Effort and riskLowest; quickest to startModerate
Best forQuick single view, many systems you cannot change, data that must stay in placeAnalytics, reporting and a trusted dim_customer in the warehouse

Both are read-only towards the sources. If sources must also be corrected, move to coexistence; if all creation must be controlled, move to centralised. Many companies start with registry or consolidation and evolve.

Q6. How do you handle conflicting customer records from different systems?

  • Standardise first: many "conflicts" are formatting, such as "+91 98450 12345" vs "98450-12345"
  • Agree source trust per attribute with the data owners: KYC system for legal name and date of birth, billing for address, CRM for contact preferences
  • Apply survivorship rules, recording which source won each attribute and why
  • Route true conflicts to stewards: two trusted sources with different dates of birth should not be auto-resolved
  • Keep everything: losing values stay in history and the cross-reference, so decisions can be audited and reversed
  • Support unmerge: a wrong merge must be undoable, with facts re-pointed to the right master IDs
  • Fix at source: in coexistence style, send corrections back so the conflict does not return tomorrow
  • Measure: duplicate rate, false-merge rate, steward backlog and time to resolve

Q7. How do you maintain historical changes in master data?

Master data needs three kinds of history: attribute history (Asha moved from Pune to Mumbai), identity history (records merged or unmerged) and an audit trail (who changed what, and which steward approved it).

Attribute history is usually kept as SCD Type 2 on the golden record. This Delta Lake MERGE closes the old version and inserts the new one in one atomic step:

MERGE INTO golden_customer_hist t
USING (
  -- every incoming record, keyed so it meets its current row
  SELECT u.master_id AS merge_key, u.* FROM golden_updates u
  UNION ALL
  -- changed records again with a NULL key, so they fall through to INSERT
  SELECT NULL AS merge_key, u.*
  FROM golden_updates u
  JOIN golden_customer_hist h
    ON h.master_id = u.master_id AND h.is_current
   AND h.attr_hash <> sha2(concat_ws('|', u.name, u.email, u.city), 256)
) s
ON t.master_id = s.merge_key AND t.is_current
WHEN MATCHED AND t.attr_hash <> sha2(concat_ws('|', s.name, s.email, s.city), 256) THEN
  UPDATE SET valid_to = CAST(s.changed_at AS TIMESTAMP), is_current = false
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (master_id, name, email, city, attr_hash, valid_from, valid_to, is_current)
  VALUES (s.master_id, s.name, s.email, s.city,
          sha2(concat_ws('|', s.name, s.email, s.city), 256),
          CAST(s.changed_at AS TIMESTAMP), NULL, true);
master_idcityvalid_fromvalid_tois_current
CRM-1Pune2026-01-102026-09-01false
CRM-1Mumbai2026-09-01NULLtrue
CRM-2Delhi2026-02-01NULLtrue (unchanged, untouched)
CRM-7Chennai2026-09-01NULLtrue (new customer)

Tested on PySpark 3.5 with Delta Lake 3.2: 1 row updated, 2 inserted. Re-running the same batch changed nothing, because the attribute hash detects that nothing changed. Asking for CRM-1's city on 2026-05-01 returned Pune.

  • Identity history: keep the cross-reference with valid_from and valid_to too, so a merge or unmerge on a date can be replayed and old reports reproduced
  • Audit trail: an append-only change log of every edit, merge and steward decision with user and reason
  • Bitemporal history for regulated industries: valid time (when it was true in the real world) and system time (when we recorded it), so you can answer "what did we know on 31 March?"
  • Do not rely on Delta time travel for business history: VACUUM and retention settings remove old versions

Q8. What is the difference between MDM and a data warehouse?

A data warehouse integrates large volumes of transactional history from many systems for analysis. It is one-way and read-only towards the sources, and it inherits whatever duplicates arrive. MDM manages a small volume of core entities to resolve and govern identity: it matches, merges and applies survivorship, involves human stewards, and can push corrections back to operational systems in real time.

They are complementary, not alternatives: MDM produces the master ID and golden attributes; the warehouse uses them as the business key and attributes of conformed dimensions such as dim_customer, then adds the facts. The full comparison is in the table at the top of this section.

Q9. How do you integrate MDM with Kafka and a lakehouse?

SOURCES                     KAFKA                        MDM HUB
CRM, core banking,   CDC   crm.customer.cdc      --->   match, merge,
web, loyalty   ----------> web.customer.cdc             survivorship,
(Debezium, GoldenGate)     loyalty.customer.cdc         stewardship
                                                             |
                           mdm.customer.golden   <-----------+  compacted topic,
                           mdm.customer.xref     <-----------+  key = master_id
                              |            |
               +--------------+            +--------------------+
               v                                                v
     operational apps update                LAKEHOUSE (Structured Streaming)
     their local copies                     bronze: raw golden and xref events
                                            silver: golden_customer_hist (SCD2 MERGE)
                                                    xref_hist
                                            gold:   dim_customer, Customer 360
  • Inbound: change data capture (Debezium, Oracle GoldenGate, Qlik) streams every source change into one topic per source, so MDM sees changes in seconds instead of nightly files
  • Outbound: the hub publishes golden-record events to a log-compacted topic keyed by master_id, so the topic always holds the latest state of every customer and new consumers can rebuild from it. Merges and unmerges go to a separate xref topic
  • Ordering: keying by master_id puts all events for one customer in one partition, which keeps them in order
  • Contracts: Avro or Protobuf schemas in a schema registry, with compatibility rules, so producers cannot break consumers
  • Lakehouse: Spark Structured Streaming reads the topics into bronze, then each micro-batch runs the SCD2 MERGE above in foreachBatch; the checkpoint plus an idempotent MERGE gives exactly-once results in Delta
  • Merges in facts: store source IDs in facts and resolve master IDs through the cross-reference when building gold, so a later merge or unmerge re-points history without rewriting fact tables
def upsert_golden(batch_df, batch_id):
    batch_df.createOrReplaceTempView("golden_updates")
    batch_df.sparkSession.sql(HIST_MERGE_SQL)  # the SCD2 MERGE shown above

(spark.readStream.format("kafka")
   .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "broker:9092")
   .option("subscribe", "mdm.customer.golden")
   .load()
   .select(F.from_json(F.col("value").cast("string"), golden_schema).alias("e"))
   .select("e.*")
   .writeStream
   .foreachBatch(upsert_golden)
   .option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/golden_customer_hist")
   .start())

The MERGE inside foreachBatch is the one tested above. The Kafka reader follows the standard Spark Structured Streaming API but was not run here, as it needs a broker. If one batch can hold several events for the same master_id, keep only the latest per key before the MERGE.

Q10. How would you implement MDM for customer and counterparty data in a global bank?

Start with why the bank needs it: regulation and risk. Credit exposure must be aggregated per counterparty and per group (BCBS 239, large-exposure rules), KYC and anti-money-laundering rules require knowing the customer and its beneficial owners, and sanctions screening needs one reliable identity. A false merge in a bank is not a marketing nuisance: it can misstate risk or leak one client's data to another.

Design areaWhat I would do
Data modelA party model: one party (person or legal entity) with many roles (customer, counterparty, guarantor, issuer, beneficial owner) and relationships, rather than separate customer and counterparty silos
IdentifiersDeterministic matching on strong IDs: LEI (ISO 17442, 20 characters), SWIFT BIC, company registration and tax numbers; national IDs for individuals, tokenised
HierarchiesLegal-entity hierarchy with direct and ultimate parent, enriched from GLEIF Level 2 "who owns whom" data and vendors such as Dun & Bradstreet or Moody's Orbis, so exposure rolls up to the group
MatchingDeterministic first, then probabilistic on name and address with legal-suffix normalisation (Ltd, Limited, GmbH) and transliteration of non-Latin scripts; conservative auto-merge thresholds and four-eyes steward approval
SurvivorshipKYC system authoritative for legal identity and date of birth; GLEIF for legal name and parent; CRM for contact preferences; steward overrides audited
StyleCentralised or coexistence for counterparty onboarding, run as a collaborative KYC workflow; consolidation first for retail customers across many legacy core systems
Data residencyRegional hubs where law requires local storage (for example EU GDPR transfer rules, India's RBI payment-data localisation, China's PIPL), with a global index holding only pseudonymised keys and links
HistoryBitemporal history and a full audit trail, kept for the regulatory retention period
IntegrationCDC from core banking, cards, lending and trading into Kafka; golden and xref events back to them; a lakehouse for risk aggregation, regulatory reporting and Customer 360
ScreeningSanctions and PEP screening (OFAC, UN, EU lists) runs on the golden record and its owners, re-run on every change
SecurityPII encrypted and tokenised, attribute-level access by role and region, consent tracked
GovernanceA client data office with owners per domain, critical data elements, data quality KPIs (duplicate rate, false-merge rate, LEI coverage, KYC completeness) and BCBS 239 evidence

Roadmap: (1) legal-entity counterparty master for risk, with the highest regulatory value; (2) hierarchies and beneficial ownership; (3) retail customer master region by region; (4) real-time operational sync and Customer 360. Each phase ships golden records that a regulator-facing report actually uses.

26. Observability and Operations
