A platform in production needs the same discipline as any software system. Data observability watches the data itself, not just whether jobs succeeded, because a job can succeed while writing wrong data.

PillarQuestionSignal
FreshnessIs the data up to date?Time since last update
VolumeDid we get the expected amount?Row counts against history
SchemaDid the structure change?Added, removed or retyped columns
DistributionDo the values look normal?Null rates, ranges, category mix
LineageWhat is affected?Upstream causes, downstream impact

SLIs, SLOs and SLAs

TermMeaningExample
SLI (indicator)What you measureMinutes after 06:00 that gold sales tables were ready
SLO (objective)Internal targetReady by 07:00 on 99% of days
SLA (agreement)Promise to consumers, often with consequencesReady by 08:00 or the business is notified

Tools

NeedOptions
Data observabilityMonte Carlo, Bigeye, Soda, Elementary (dbt), Lakehouse Monitoring
Pipeline and infrastructure monitoringDatadog, Grafana, cloud monitoring services
Platform usage and costSystem tables and account usage views on each platform
IncidentsPagerDuty, Opsgenie, ServiceNow

Operating model

  • Everything as code: infrastructure with Terraform, Bicep or CloudFormation; jobs with Asset Bundles, dbt or similar; permissions as code where possible
  • Environments: dev, test and prod separated by account, workspace or catalog, with production data access restricted
  • CI/CD: every change reviewed and tested before deployment, including data tests on representative data
  • Runbooks and on-call: a documented response for each critical pipeline, and blameless reviews after incidents
  • Change management: data contracts and lineage-based impact checks before breaking changes

27. Resilience, Lifecycle and Cost

Disaster recovery

Recovery is designed from the two numbers agreed earlier. RPO, the recovery point objective, is how much data you can afford to lose. RTO, the recovery time objective, is how long you can be down.

ApproachRPO and RTOCost
Backups restored when neededHours to daysLow
Copy data to a second region on a scheduleHoursMedium
Warm standby in a second regionMinutes to an hourHigh
Active in two regionsNear zeroHighest
-- A full, independent copy of a Delta table, for backup or another region
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE dr_sales.gold.fact_order_line
DEEP CLONE prod_sales.gold.fact_order_line;
PlatformRecovery features
DatabricksDeep clone, cloud storage replication, workspace configuration as code
SnowflakeTime Travel and Fail-safe, database replication and failover across regions
BigQueryTime travel window, cross-region dataset replication
Object storageS3 cross-region replication, Azure geo-redundant storage, GCS dual and multi-region buckets
DatabasesRead replicas, point-in-time restore, cross-region replicas

Delta time travel helps with mistakes such as a bad overwrite, but it is not a backup: the data is in the same storage, and VACUUM removes old versions. Also store infrastructure and jobs as code, so the platform itself can be rebuilt.

Data lifecycle and retention

StageRetailer rule
HotLast 13 months of orders in gold for fast queries
WarmOlder orders in a cheaper storage tier
ArchiveUp to the legal retention period, rarely read
DeleteAfter retention ends, or when the law requires it

Cost as an architecture concern

  • Tag compute and tables by team and project, so every cost has an owner
  • Report spend from billing data, for example the Databricks system.billing.usage table
  • Use serverless or autoscaling for uneven workloads, and job compute rather than all-purpose clusters for scheduled work
  • Set budgets and alerts, and remove tables that lineage shows nothing reads
  • Review the biggest jobs every month: a few usually cause most of the bill

Sharing data

Instead of copying data to partners, Delta Sharing, an open protocol, gives them read access to live tables, with the same governance and audit. Data mesh takes the idea further inside a company: each domain publishes data products, which are documented, owned and quality-checked datasets that others can use. The Data Architecture Patterns card covers data mesh in more detail.

28. Data Architecture for AI

AI raises the stakes for everything above. A model trained on personal data, or a chatbot that retrieves documents a user should not see, turns a governance gap into a visible incident.

ComponentPurposeExamples
Feature storeReusable, consistent features for training and servingDatabricks Feature Store, SageMaker Feature Store, Vertex AI Feature Store, Feast
Vector databaseStores embeddings for semantic search and retrievalpgvector, OpenSearch, Azure AI Search, Mosaic AI Vector Search, Pinecone
Model registryVersioned models with lineage to data and codeMLflow, SageMaker, Vertex AI, Azure ML
MonitoringDrift, quality and safety of predictionsPlatform monitoring tools, Evidently

Governance rules for AI data

  • Permission-aware retrieval: a retrieval-augmented (RAG) assistant must only return documents the asking user may read; filter by the user's permissions at query time, not when building the index
  • Redact before embedding: remove or mask personal data before documents become embeddings, since embeddings are hard to delete selectively
  • Lineage from data to model: record which data version trained each model, so you can retrain after an erasure request or a quality issue
  • Purpose and consent: data collected for orders may not be lawful to use for training without a proper basis
  • Regulation: the EU AI Act sets duties by risk level, phased in from 2025, so classify AI use cases as well as data

How to evaluate a platform

Score options against agreed criteria rather than preferences. Weight the criteria first, with stakeholders, then score each option, and record the result in an ADR.

CriterionQuestions

Total cost of ownershipLicences, compute, storage, people, training and migration together
OpennessOpen formats and APIs? How hard is it to leave?
Security and complianceCertifications, regions, encryption, audit
SkillsCan the current team use it, or hire for it?

Build, buy or assemble

OptionGood whenRisk

30. Implementing an Enterprise Data Lake

A data lake is cheap object storage plus the rules that stop it becoming a data swamp: files nobody can find, trust or delete. The storage is the easy part; the conventions are the architecture.

Zones

ZoneContentsWho writesWho reads
LandingFiles exactly as delivered, kept brieflyIngestion toolsIngestion jobs only
Raw (bronze)Immutable copy of every source, with load metadataIngestion jobsEngineers
Curated (silver)Cleaned, typed, deduplicated, conformedPipelinesEngineers, analysts
Consumption (gold)Business-ready, modelled, documentedPipelinesEveryone with access
SandboxPersonal and team experiments, auto-expiringAnalysts, scientistsTheir owners
ArchiveOld data kept for legal reasonsLifecycle rulesRarely, on request

Storage layout

Separate by environment and zone at the bucket or container level, because that is where cloud permissions, encryption keys and lifecycle rules apply. Use a fixed path convention below that.

s3://acme-lake-prod-raw/       one bucket per environment and zone
  crm/customers/ingest_date=2026-11-07/part-0000.parquet
  orders_db/orders/ingest_date=2026-11-07/...
s3://acme-lake-prod-curated/
  sales/orders/                  table format folder (Delta or Iceberg)
s3://acme-lake-prod-gold/
  sales/fact_order_line/

pattern: <env>-<zone> / <source or domain> / <dataset> / <partition>

Implementation steps

1. Set up the landing zone. Cloud accounts or subscriptions per environment, network isolation, encryption with managed keys, central logging. Do this before any data arrives.

2. Create zones with their own permissions. Ingestion roles can write raw; only pipelines write curated and gold; analysts read gold. Deny public access everywhere.

3. Register everything in a catalog. Glue Data Catalog, Unity Catalog, Purview or Knowledge Catalog. A file that is not in the catalog does not exist for consumers.

4. Standardise ingestion. One framework, with a metadata contract per source: owner, classification, schema, frequency, retention. Reject sources without an owner.

5. Choose formats. Keep raw in the delivered format or Parquet; use an open table format from curated onwards, so you get updates, deletes and schema evolution.

6. Apply lifecycle rules. Landing files expire in days, sandbox in weeks, raw moves to cheaper storage classes after months, archive follows legal retention.

7. Add quality and lineage. Checks between zones; lineage captured automatically where possible.

8. Publish and measure. Track the share of datasets with an owner, a description and a classification. Falling numbers are the first sign of a swamp.

Building blockAWSAzureGoogle Cloud
StorageS3ADLS Gen2Cloud Storage
Catalog and permissionsGlue Data Catalog, Lake FormationPurview, storage RBAC and ACLsKnowledge Catalog, IAM
QueryAthena, Redshift SpectrumSynapse serverless, FabricBigQuery external and BigLake tables
ProcessingGlue, EMRDatabricks, Fabric SparkDataproc, Dataflow

31. Implementing an Enterprise Data Warehouse

A warehouse gives the business one trusted, modelled version of its data, optimised for SQL and BI. Three classic design approaches still shape how it is built:

ApproachIdeaStrengthsWeaknesses
Kimball (bottom-up)Build star-schema marts per business process, joined by conformed dimensionsFast value, easy for BI usersNeeds discipline to keep dimensions conformed
Inmon (top-down)A normalised enterprise warehouse first, then marts from itIntegrated, consistent coreSlow to deliver
Data Vault 2.0Hubs (keys), links (relationships) and satellites (history) in the core, marts on topAuditable, absorbs source changes, parallel loadingComplex; still needs marts for users
 Sources ─► Staging ─► Integration layer ─► Data marts ─► Semantic layer ─► BI
            (as is)    (3NF or Data Vault)   (star schemas)  (metrics)

The bus matrix

Kimball's bus matrix is the planning tool: business processes as rows, shared dimensions as columns. Each tick is a fact table that must use that conformed dimension, and the matrix becomes the delivery roadmap.

Business processDateCustomerProductStoreSupplier
Orders✓✓✓✓
Returns✓✓✓✓
Inventory✓✓✓✓
Purchasing✓✓✓

Implementation steps

1. Start from business questions. Interview stakeholders, list the key metrics and decisions, and build the bus matrix.

2. Choose the core approach and platform. Kimball for speed, Data Vault when sources change often and audit matters; then a platform from the evaluation criteria in this card.

3. Build conformed dimensions first. Date, customer and product, with surrogate keys and SCD rules agreed per attribute.

4. Deliver one process at a time. Typically the highest-value row of the bus matrix, end to end, including tests and a dashboard.

5. Load incrementally. CDC or watermarks into staging, MERGE into the core, idempotent at every step.

6. Manage workloads. Separate compute for loading, BI and ad hoc queries; materialised views for hot aggregates.

7. Secure and govern. Role-based access, masking of personal data, documented metrics in the semantic layer.

The Data Warehouse card covers star and snowflake schemas, SCDs and normal forms; the Data Modelling card builds a full mart with DDL and PySpark.

32. Implementing a Lakehouse on Delta Lake

A lakehouse combines the lake's cheap open storage with the warehouse's reliability, using an open table format. Here is an enterprise implementation on Delta Lake with Unity Catalog, followed by the Iceberg equivalent.

 Ingestion           Storage and catalog            Consumption
 ─────────           ───────────────────            ───────────
 CDC, Auto Loader ─► prod catalog               ─►  SQL warehouses, BI
 Kafka streams       ├─ bronze  raw, append-only    ML, feature store
 Batch connectors    ├─ silver  cleaned            Delta Sharing
                     └─ gold    marts, products    Semantic layer, AI
                     Unity Catalog: access, lineage, audit, tags

Step 1: lay out catalogs and schemas

Decide early how catalogs map to the organisation, because permissions and isolation follow this structure. Two common designs: one catalog per environment with schemas per layer, or one catalog per domain per environment.

CREATE CATALOG IF NOT EXISTS prod_sales
  MANAGED LOCATION 's3://acme-lakehouse-prod/sales';

CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS prod_sales.bronze;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS prod_sales.silver;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS prod_sales.gold;

GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG prod_sales TO `sales-analysts`;
GRANT USE SCHEMA, SELECT ON SCHEMA prod_sales.gold TO `sales-analysts`;

Step 2: set table standards

Write the defaults once and apply them to every table through templates or code review.

CREATE TABLE prod_sales.silver.orders (
  order_id     STRING NOT NULL COMMENT 'Business key from the order system',
  customer_id  STRING,
  order_ts     TIMESTAMP COMMENT 'UTC',
  amount       DECIMAL(18,2),
  _ingested_at TIMESTAMP COMMENT 'Load time, for audit'
)
CLUSTER BY (order_ts)
COMMENT 'One row per order. Owner: sales-domain'
TBLPROPERTIES (
  'delta.enableChangeDataFeed'      = 'true',
  'delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration' = 'interval 7 days',
  'delta.logRetentionDuration'      = 'interval 30 days'
);
StandardWhy
Managed tables in Unity CatalogGovernance, lineage and automatic maintenance
Liquid clustering, not partitioning, for most tablesDatabricks guidance for tables under 1 TB, and flexible later
Comments and owners on every tableDiscoverability and accountability
Retention properties set deliberatelyThey decide time travel and how long deleted personal data survives
UTC timestamps, DECIMAL money, audit columnsConsistency across domains

Step 3: ingestion and processing

  • Bronze: Auto Loader for files, Lakeflow Connect or CDC tools for databases, Structured Streaming for Kafka; append-only
  • Silver: deduplicate, type and conform; MERGE for idempotency
  • Gold: dimensional models or data products, built with SQL, dbt or Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines
  • Orchestrate with Lakeflow Jobs or Airflow; deploy with Asset Bundles through CI/CD

Step 4: operate it

  • Maintenance: enable predictive optimization, or schedule OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and ANALYZE
  • Quality: expectations, dbt tests or monitoring on gold tables
  • Cost: tagged compute per team, serverless where usage is uneven
  • Security: groups, tag-based masking, audit reviews

The same lakehouse on Iceberg

ConcernDelta Lake on DatabricksIceberg (open or multi-engine)
CatalogUnity CatalogGlue Data Catalog, Apache Polaris, Snowflake Horizon, Unity Catalog
EnginesDatabricks, SparkSpark, Trino, Flink, Athena, Snowflake, BigQuery
LayoutLiquid clusteringHidden partitioning, sort orders, partition evolution
CompactionOPTIMIZErewrite_data_files procedure
Removing old dataVACUUMexpire_snapshots, then remove_orphan_files
Change feedChange data feedIncremental reads between snapshots; row lineage in v3

33. Implementing a Data Mesh

Data mesh is mostly an organisational change, not a product you install. It answers a scaling problem: one central data team becomes a bottleneck when hundreds of sources and consumers depend on it.

PrincipleMeaningIn practice
Domain ownershipThe teams who know the data own it end to endSales owns sales data products, including quality and support
Data as a productData is published with the care of a productOwner, documentation, SLOs, contract, version
Self-serve platformA platform team makes publishing easyTemplates for pipelines, catalogs, CI/CD, access
Federated computational governanceShared rules, enforced automaticallyPolicies as code, tag-based security, standard checks

Is it right for you?

SignalMesh helpsMesh is premature
OrganisationMany domains, many data teamsOne small data team
BottleneckCentral team backlog of monthsDelivery is fast enough
Domain skillsDomains have or can hire engineersDomains have no technical staff
Platform maturityStrong platform and governance automationBasics such as a catalog are missing

A data product specification

Every product is described in a standard, machine-readable file, so the platform can validate it, publish it to the catalog and enforce its policies.

name: sales.orders_daily
domain: sales
owner: sales-data-team@acme.example
description: Daily orders by store and product, net of returns
output_ports:
  - type: table
    location: prod_sales.gold.orders_daily
  - type: share
    name: orders_daily_partners
schema_contract: contracts/orders_daily.yaml  # columns, types, compatibility
classification: internal
slo:
  freshness: "07:00 daily"
  completeness: ">= 99.9% of stores"
version: 2.1.0

Implementation steps

1. Pick two or three domains. Choose domains with strong teams and real consumers, not the hardest problem first.

2. Build the self-serve platform. A product template that creates storage, a catalog or schema, CI/CD, quality checks and access groups from the specification above.

3. Define global standards. Naming, classification tags, security policies, interoperability formats and SLO reporting, enforced by the platform rather than by review meetings.

4. Publish products to a marketplace. A catalog where consumers find products, read contracts and request access.

5. Share between domains without copying. Use the platform's sharing features, so domains consume each other's products in place.

6. Measure and expand. Track product usage, SLO compliance and time-to-publish; add domains as the platform matures.

PlatformDomain boundarySharing between domains
DatabricksCatalog per domain in Unity CatalogGrants across catalogs, Delta Sharing
SnowflakeDatabase or account per domainSecure data sharing, listings
AWSAccount per domainLake Formation cross-account grants, SageMaker Catalog
AzureFabric domains and workspacesOneLake shortcuts, Purview
Google CloudProject per domainBigQuery sharing (Analytics Hub), Knowledge Catalog

Common failures: renaming central teams as "domains" without giving them ownership, building no platform so each domain reinvents pipelines, and skipping governance so products are incompatible. Many companies end up with a hybrid: a central platform and core data, with domains owning their products.

34. Modernising Legacy Systems

Most enterprises do not start from scratch. They have a warehouse appliance, a Hadoop cluster, decades of ETL jobs and perhaps a mainframe. Modernisation moves these to a cloud platform without breaking the business while it happens, which is why it is a programme of waves, not a single project.

Why modernise

  • Hardware or licence end of life, and rising support costs
  • Fixed capacity that cannot scale for month-end or AI workloads
  • Skills scarcity for old technologies
  • No support for streaming, unstructured data or machine learning
  • Governance gaps: no lineage, coarse access control

Typical legacy estates and where they go

LegacyCommon targetApproach and tools
Teradata, Netezza, Exadata, Oracle or SQL Server warehousesSnowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Redshift or FabricAutomated SQL conversion (Databricks Lakebridge, Snowflake SnowConvert, BigQuery SQL translation, AWS Schema Conversion Tool), then manual fixes
Hadoop: Hive, Impala, HDFSLakehouse on Delta or IcebergCopy data to object storage, convert Parquet tables in place, port HiveQL, replace Oozie with Airflow or jobs
ETL tools: Informatica PowerCenter, DataStage, SSIS, Ab Initiodbt, Spark, Data Factory, GlueConverters where available, or rebuild using lineage to prioritise
Mainframe: DB2, IMS, VSAM, COBOL batchCloud data platform, mainframe kept as system of record at firstCDC replication of DB2; parse EBCDIC files with COBOL copybooks, for example with the Cobrix library for Spark
On-premise OLTP databasesManaged cloud databasesDatabase migration services plus CDC into analytics
Reporting: Business Objects, Cognos, MicroStrategy, SSRSPower BI, Tableau, LookerRebuild on a semantic layer; retire unused reports

Migration tools change quickly: Databricks made the BladeBridge conversion technology free as Lakebridge in 2025, and Snowflake now centres on SnowConvert AI. Always run a proof of concept on your own code, because conversion rates vary widely by source.

Modernisation patterns

PatternHow it worksWhen
Strangler figReplace the legacy system piece by piece, routing one domain or report at a time to the new platformDefault for large estates: low risk, value early
Coexistence with CDCKeep the legacy source running and stream its changes to the new platformMainframes and core databases that cannot move yet
Big bangMove everything and switch over at onceSmall, simple estates only
Lift and shift firstMove as is, modernise laterA hard data-centre exit date

The six Rs of migration

StrategyMeaningExample
Rehost (lift and shift)Move as is to cloud serversOracle on a cloud VM
ReplatformSmall changes to use managed servicesOracle to a managed database service
Refactor or re-architectRedesign for the cloudTeradata warehouse to a lakehouse
RepurchaseReplace with a SaaS productCustom CRM to Salesforce
RetireSwitch off what nobody usesOld reports found through lineage
RetainKeep on premise for nowMainframe with strict constraints

A modernisation programme, phase by phase

1. Discover. Inventory every table, job, report and user. Usage logs and lineage show what is really used; it is common to find a large share of reports and tables nobody reads, which can be retired instead of migrated.

2. Assess and plan. Score each workload by business value and migration complexity, group them into waves by domain, and build the business case on total cost, including running both systems in parallel.

3. Build the foundation. Landing zone, network, identity, catalog, security policies, CI/CD and the ingestion framework, before the first wave.

4. Migrate a pilot wave. One domain end to end: bulk-load history, keep it current with CDC, convert and test the code, and rebuild its reports.

5. Validate by reconciliation. Prove the new platform gives the same answers as the old one, at several levels (below).

6. Run in parallel, then cut over. Both systems run side by side for an agreed period; consumers switch domain by domain once results match.

7. Decommission. Switch off legacy jobs and hardware wave by wave. Savings only appear when the old system is actually turned off.

Tested: converting legacy Parquet tables in place

Hadoop estates often hold Hive tables already stored as Parquet. Delta can adopt them without rewriting any data, which makes migrating very large tables fast and cheap:

CONVERT TO DELTA parquet.`s3://legacy/warehouse/sales`
  PARTITIONED BY (region_id INT);
Check on 100,000 rows in 3 partitionsResult
Converting without PARTITIONED BYRejected: partition columns found in folder names
Converting with PARTITIONED BYSucceeded
Data filesAll 6 untouched; only a transaction log was added
Reading as DeltaAll 100,000 rows
Table historyOne CONVERT operation

Iceberg offers similar procedures, such as migrate and snapshot, which add Iceberg metadata over existing files. Test them on a copy first: an in-place conversion changes how the folder must be written from then on.

Tested: reconciling source and target

Reconciliation proves the migration is correct. We copied a table, then deliberately deleted one row and changed one amount in the target. A layered check caught both:

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

def profile(df, key, cols):
    row_hash = F.xxhash64(*[F.col(c) for c in cols])
    return df.agg(F.count("*").alias("rows"),
                  F.countDistinct(key).alias("keys"),
                  F.sum("amount").alias("sum_amount"),
                  F.sum(row_hash).alias("hash_sum")).first()

s = profile(source, "order_id", ["order_id", "region_id", "amount"])
t = profile(target, "order_id", ["order_id", "region_id", "amount"])
for k in ("rows", "keys", "sum_amount", "hash_sum"):
    print(k, "match" if s[k] == t[k] else f"DIFF {s[k]} vs {t[k]}")

missing = source.join(target, "order_id", "left_anti")
changed = source.exceptAll(target).join(target.select("order_id"), "order_id")
CheckResultWhat it found
Row count100,000 vs 99,999Something is missing
Sum of amountDiffersA value changed or is missing
Hash of all columnsDiffersAny change in any column
Missing keysorder 7The deleted row
Changed rowsorder 4242The edited amount

Use the cheap aggregate checks on every table and every load; run the row-level comparison when aggregates disagree, or on a sample. Finish with report-level checks: the top business reports must show the same numbers on both platforms.

What usually goes wrong

ProblemExamplePrevention
SQL semantics differInteger division, NULL ordering, case-insensitive comparison defaults, date functionsAutomated conversion plus targeted tests on edge cases
Data types differOracle DATE includes a time; legacy NUMBER precision; CHAR paddingExplicit type mapping document, reviewed per table
Time zonesLegacy stored local time without a zoneConvert to UTC once, at ingestion
Mainframe encodingsEBCDIC text and packed decimalsCopybook-driven parsing, validated against known totals
Hidden dependenciesA spreadsheet macro reading a legacy tableUsage logs, lineage, and asking users before switching off
Running two systems too longCost doubles and attention splitsFixed parallel-run periods and decommission dates per wave
Copying old problemsMigrating unused tables and bad models as isRetire first; redesign where it matters

35. Putting It Together: The Retailer's Plan

Back to the auditor's question. Here is how the architect turns this card into a plan, in an order where each phase makes the next one possible.

PhaseWorkAnswers
1. FoundationA central catalog per platform (Unity Catalog, Lake Formation, Purview, Horizon); identity sync; groupsWhere is all our data?
2. OwnershipOwners and stewards per domain; glossary of key termsWho is responsible?
3. ClassificationOne tag scheme on every platform; discovery scans; unverified-by-defaultWhat is sensitive?
4. ProtectionLeast-privilege grants; tag-based masks and row filters; secretsWho can see emails?
5. VisibilityNative lineage per platform, OpenLineage for custom jobs, one enterprise catalogWhere does email data go?
6. TrustQuality checks, contracts, monitoringIs the data right?
7. ComplianceRetention, erasure process, audit reports, access reviewsCan we prove it?

After phase 5, the auditor's question has a one-query answer: the grants and policies show who can see the email column unmasked, and lineage shows every table it reaches, on every platform. That is the measure of a good data architecture: hard questions get quick, provable answers.

36. Common Mistakes

MistakeWhat goes wrongInstead
Buying a tool before defining ownersAn empty catalog nobody maintainsRoles and processes first
Granting access to individualsAccess piles up as people moveGrant to groups
Treating hashing as anonymisationEmails can be re-identifiedKeyed hashing, and treat it as personal data
Deleting rows and calling it erasureOld versions and copies keep the dataDELETE everywhere, then VACUUM
Masks written table by tableNew tables are missedTags with ABAC policies
Path-based tablesWeak lineage and governanceRegister tables, use names
Secrets in notebooksLeaks through Git and logsSecret scopes or vaults
Assuming lineage is completeGaps appear in an auditTest capture and measure coverage
Time travel as a backupLost with the storage, or after VACUUMDeep clones or replication
No written decisionsThe same debates repeatArchitecture decision records

37. Project Walkthrough Questions

After the theory, most architect interviews switch to your project: "explain your architecture", "why Databricks?", "what happens when a job fails?". Interviewers check that you really built it, that you understand why each choice was made, and that you know its weak points.

The model answers below describe one realistic project: an enterprise lakehouse on Azure Databricks for a retailer with about 40 source systems. Replace every number, tool and example with your own. Interviewers follow up on details, and an answer you cannot defend hurts more than a simpler true one.

How to structure any project answer

PartWhat to coverExample
ContextBusiness goal, users, scale"Retail group, 40 sources, about 2 TB a day, 600 BI users, daily and near-real-time reporting"
ArchitectureFlow from source to consumer, in layersSources → ingestion → bronze/silver/gold → serving
Your roleWhat you personally designed or built"I designed the ingestion framework and the governance model"
DecisionsTwo or three choices and why, with the alternative rejectedDelta over Parquet; Auto Loader over custom file listing
ResultsMeasurable outcomes"Daily load from 6 hours to 90 minutes; 40% lower compute cost"
LessonsWhat you would do differently"Introduce data contracts earlier"

Say this in the interview

"We built a lakehouse on Azure Databricks with ADLS Gen2 and Delta Lake, organised in bronze, silver and gold layers and governed by Unity Catalog. About 40 sources come in through four patterns: CDC for databases, managed connectors for SaaS, Event Hubs for point-of-sale and web events, and Auto Loader for partner files. Silver holds cleansed, conformed entities with SCD2 history; gold holds star schemas and aggregates served to Power BI through SQL warehouses, plus feature tables for ML. Everything is orchestrated with Lakeflow Jobs, deployed through Git and Asset Bundles, and monitored through system tables and alerts. My part was the ingestion framework and the governance model."

Q2. Why did you choose Databricks?

Never answer "because the company already had it" alone. Show that you compared options against requirements:

RequirementWhy Databricks fitted
Mixed workloads: ETL, streaming, BI and ML on the same dataOne platform and one copy of data for engineering, SQL analytics and ML (MLflow, feature tables)
Open formats, no lock-in for storageData stays in our own ADLS account as Delta; readable by other engines, and as Iceberg through UniForm
Large and semi-structured dataSpark scales out for TB-sized daily loads, JSON events and files
Streaming and batchStructured Streaming and Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines use the same tables and largely the same code
GovernanceUnity Catalog gives access control, tags, masking, row filters, lineage and audit for tables, files and models
Azure fitFirst-party Azure service, Entra ID integration, private networking
AlternativeWhy not chosen (in this project)
SnowflakeExcellent for SQL and BI, but our heavy Python, streaming and ML workloads and open-format requirement fitted Databricks better
Microsoft Fabric / SynapseEvaluated; at the time Databricks was more mature for large-scale engineering and ML
Self-managed Spark (HDInsight, EMR)More operations work; no Unity Catalog governance or serverless SQL

Also name the trade-offs honestly: cost needs active management (cluster policies, autoscaling, serverless, auto-stop on SQL warehouses), and teams need Spark skills. Mentioning how you controlled cost shows maturity.

Say this in the interview

"We needed one platform for batch and streaming ETL, BI and ML on large, partly semi-structured data, with open formats in our own storage and strong governance. Databricks met all of those: Delta on ADLS, Spark for scale, SQL warehouses for Power BI, MLflow for ML and Unity Catalog for security and lineage. We compared Snowflake, which is excellent for SQL and BI but fitted our Python, streaming and ML-heavy workloads less well. The main trade-off is cost control, which we handled with cluster policies, serverless compute and monitoring through system billing tables."

Q3. How do you handle incremental data?

StageTechniqueHow it works
Source databasesCDCRead inserts, updates and deletes from the transaction log; no full extracts
Sources without CDCWatermark columnLoad rows where updated_at > last stored watermark (tested in the design questions section)
FilesAuto LoaderTracks which files were processed in its checkpoint; only new files are read
Bronze → silverStructured Streaming with availableNowProcesses only new bronze data each run, then stops
Silver → goldDelta Change Data FeedReads row-level changes since the last processed version
Applying changesMERGE by business keyUpsert; SCD2 or apply-changes APIs for history; deletes applied from CDC flags
Late dataReprocess a rolling windowFor example, recompute the last 3 days of gold aggregates each run
-- Enable once on the silver table
ALTER TABLE silver_orders SET TBLPROPERTIES (delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true);

-- Each run reads only what changed since the last processed version
SELECT order_id, amount, status, _change_type, _commit_version
FROM table_changes('silver_orders', 2);      -- 2 = last processed version + 1
order_idamountstatus_change_type_commit_version
1100.00NEWupdate_preimage2
190.00SHIPPEDupdate_postimage2
345.00NEWdelete3
4300.00NEWinsert4

Tested on Delta Lake 3.2: after an update, a delete and an insert, the change feed returned exactly those changes, with before and after images of the update. Store the last processed version per consumer, or let a streaming read with readChangeFeed track it in its checkpoint.

Say this in the interview

"We never reload full tables when we can avoid it. Databases come in through CDC, sources without CDC through a watermark column, and files through Auto Loader, which remembers processed files in its checkpoint. Bronze to silver runs as Structured Streaming with availableNow, so each run handles only new data, and silver to gold reads Delta Change Data Feed. Changes are applied with MERGE by business key, with SCD2 where history matters, and gold aggregates recompute a rolling window to absorb late data."

Q4. How do you manage data quality?

WhereWhat we checkToolAction on failure
IngestionFile arrived, schema matches the contract, row count in expected rangeAuto Loader schema tracking, custom checksAlert; hold the load
Bronze → silverNot null keys, valid types and ranges, valid codes, duplicatesLakeflow expectationsBad rows to a quarantine table; good rows continue
SilverReferential integrity, uniqueness of business keysExpectations, dbt-style testsFail the update for critical rules
GoldReconciliation to source totals, KPI movement within thresholdsSQL checksBlock publishing; notify the owner
Over timeFreshness, volume and distribution driftDatabricks data quality monitoring, alertsIncident with the owner
  • Rules are agreed with data owners and stored with the table, not hidden in code
  • Severity decides the action: warn, drop and quarantine, or fail
  • The quarantine pattern keeps bad rows for investigation instead of losing them; the medallion section shows a tested run where one corrupt row was quarantined and the rest loaded
  • Quality results go into one table and a dashboard, with KPIs per domain (see Data Quality KPIs at Enterprise Level)
Say this in the interview

"Quality is checked at every layer. At ingestion we validate schema and volumes against the data contract. Between bronze and silver, Lakeflow expectations validate keys, types, ranges and codes; failing rows go to a quarantine table, and critical rules stop the pipeline. In gold we reconcile totals to the source and check KPI movements before publishing. Results feed a quality dashboard per domain, and owners get alerts with the failing rule and sample rows."

Q5. How do you ensure data consistency?

  • ACID tables: every write to Delta is a transaction, so readers never see a half-finished load
  • Idempotent loads: MERGE by business key, with a version or timestamp guard so replays and late events never overwrite newer data
  • One system of record per entity, and CDC rather than dual writes
  • Conformed dimensions and one semantic layer, so every report uses the same customer and the same revenue definition
  • Publish together: gold tables for one business process are refreshed in one job and exposed only after all succeed, so a dashboard never mixes today's facts with yesterday's dimensions
  • Reconciliation: counts, totals and row hashes against sources every day

The tested version-guarded MERGE and reconciliation queries are in the next section, under How would you ensure data consistency across systems?

Say this in the interview

"Delta gives us atomic writes, so no reader sees partial data. Loads are idempotent: MERGE by business key with a version guard, so retries and late events are harmless. Each entity has one system of record fed by CDC, dimensions are conformed and metrics live in one semantic layer. Related gold tables publish together after the whole job succeeds, and we reconcile counts, totals and row hashes against sources daily."

Q6. How do you handle failures and recovery?

FailureHow we prevent or recover
Transient task failure (network, spot loss)Automatic task retries in Lakeflow Jobs; repair run re-runs only the failed tasks
Job rerun after a partial writeIdempotent writes: MERGE by key, or txnAppId / txnVersion for appends, so a retried batch is not written twice
Streaming job crashRestart from the checkpoint; exactly-once results into Delta
Bad data or bad deploymentQuarantine stops most bad rows; if a bad load lands, RESTORE the table to the last good version, fix, and reprocess from bronze
Source outage or late filesFreshness alerts; when the source returns, watermarks and checkpoints catch up automatically
Schema change at sourceSchema tracking and contracts detect it; additive changes evolve, breaking ones alert
Region or workspace outageDisaster recovery: infrastructure as code (Terraform, Asset Bundles), storage replication or Deep Clone to a secondary region, agreed RPO and RTO, tested failover
Human error (dropped table)UNDROP for managed tables in Unity Catalog within the retention period, plus least-privilege permissions
def write_batch(df, batch_id):
    (df.write.format("delta").mode("append")
       .option("txnAppId", "gold_daily_loader")  # stable id of this writer
       .option("txnVersion", batch_id)  # increasing batch number
       .saveAsTable("gold_daily"))

write_batch(day1, 1)
write_batch(day1, 1)  # retry after a failure: Delta skips it, no duplicates
write_batch(day2, 2)
DESCRIBE HISTORY silver_orders;                       -- find the last good version
RESTORE TABLE silver_orders TO VERSION AS OF 4;       -- undo the bad load in seconds

Tested on Delta Lake 3.2: a batch written twice with the same txnAppId and txnVersion produced one copy (2 rows after 3 writes). A bad UPDATE that multiplied every amount by 100 was undone with RESTORE; the table history shows the UPDATE and the RESTORE as separate versions, so the audit trail is kept. Remember that VACUUM limits how far back RESTORE and time travel can go.

  • Alerting: job failure and SLA alerts to the on-call channel; data quality and freshness alerts to owners
  • Runbooks for common failures, so anyone on call can recover
  • Post-incident reviews that fix the cause, add a test or check, and update the runbook
Say this in the interview

"We design for failure. Tasks retry automatically and we repair only failed tasks. Every write is idempotent, using MERGE by key or Delta's txnAppId and txnVersion for appends, so reruns never duplicate data. Streams restart from checkpoints. If bad data lands, we RESTORE the table to the last good version and reprocess from bronze, which keeps the raw history. For larger outages we have infrastructure as code, replication to a secondary region and tested RPO and RTO targets. Alerts, runbooks and post-incident reviews close the loop."

38. Project Walkthrough 2: Bank Risk Lakehouse on Apache Iceberg

A second model project, deliberately different from the first: a risk data platform for a global bank, built on Apache Iceberg with open-source and multi-vendor engines instead of Databricks, integrating 50 source systems. It also answers the questions architects get about metadata: which tool maintains which metadata, who is responsible, and how it stays up to date. As before, adapt the numbers and tools to your own experience.

1. Context and requirements

AreaRequirement
BusinessMarket risk (VaR, Expected Shortfall), credit risk (exposure per counterparty and group), IFRS 9 expected credit loss, liquidity, stress testing, regulatory reporting
RegulationBCBS 239: accurate, complete, timely, adaptable risk data with lineage and reconciliation; model risk management (SR 11-7 in the US, SS1/23 in the UK); data residency
Scale50 sources, about 3 TB a day, 7–10 years of history, intraday positions every 15 minutes, official end-of-day by 06:00
ReproducibilityAny past risk run must be re-creatable exactly, for auditors and regulators
Architecture principleOpen formats and no single-vendor lock-in; several engines on one copy of data; runs on AWS with on-premises sources

2. Why Iceberg (and not Databricks) for this bank

ReasonDetail
Multi-engine by designSpark for batch ETL, Flink for streaming, Trino for interactive SQL, and Snowflake for finance all read and write the same Iceberg tables through one REST catalog
Open and vendor-neutralBank architecture policy required an open table format and an open catalog API, to avoid lock-in and allow engines to change over a 10-year horizon
End-of-day tags and time travelEach official end-of-day is a named tag; risk runs and reports read the tag, so results are reproducible
Hidden partitioning and partition evolutionUsers filter on business_date, not on partition columns; partitioning can change without rewriting years of data
Existing skills and platformThe bank already ran Kubernetes, Kafka and Spark; Databricks would have added a platform rather than replaced one

Trade-offs to state honestly: you assemble and operate more components yourself (catalog, engines, security plugins, table maintenance), and features that Databricks bundles, such as lineage capture, quality monitoring and serverless SQL, need separate tools. Managed options such as AWS S3 Tables, Snowflake-managed Iceberg or a managed Polaris service reduce that operational load.

3. Architecture

 50 SOURCES                 INGESTION                       LAKEHOUSE: S3 + Apache Iceberg
 trading, loans, cards ---> Debezium CDC -> Kafka    ---+   bronze  raw, append-only, as delivered
 treasury, collateral       (Schema Registry)           |
 market data vendors   ---> Airflow API jobs         ---+-> silver  conformed trade model, golden
 GL, reference, KYC    ---> EOD files -> S3 landing  ---+           counterparty and instrument keys
                                                            gold    positions and exposures by
                                                                    business date, EOD tags

 STREAMING: Flink (Kafka -> Iceberg, intraday)                     business date, EOD tags
 BATCH:     Spark on Kubernetes / EMR, dbt for SQL models

 CATALOG:   Iceberg REST catalog (Apache Polaris or AWS Glue) - one catalog for every engine
 ENGINES:   Spark (ETL)  |  Flink (streaming)  |  Trino (SQL, BI)  |  Snowflake (finance, read)
 RISK:      risk engines and Python grid read gold EOD tags -> results tables (Iceberg)
 SERVING:   Tableau / Power BI on Trino, regulatory reporting tool, limit monitoring

 METADATA:  DataHub (technical metadata, lineage)  <->  Collibra (glossary, CDEs, policies)
 SECURITY:  Lake Formation or Apache Ranger policies from tags, KMS, Vault, audit to SIEM
 QUALITY:   Great Expectations / Soda in pipelines, results published to the catalogs
 OPS:       Airflow, Prometheus + Grafana, Terraform, GitLab CI
LayerToolWhy
StorageAmazon S3 with Apache Iceberg (format v2)Cheap, durable, open; ACID and time travel from Iceberg
CatalogIceberg REST catalog: Apache Polaris or AWS Glue Data CatalogOne catalog API every engine understands; credential vending
Change captureDebezium + Kafka + Schema RegistryLog-based CDC from Oracle, SQL Server, DB2; schemas versioned
StreamingApache Flink with the Iceberg sinkIntraday positions and trades into bronze and silver with exactly-once commits
BatchSpark on Kubernetes or EMR; dbt (dbt-spark or dbt-trino) for SQL modelsScales for EOD loads; SQL models versioned and tested in Git
SQL and BITrino (or Starburst), Tableau or Power BIInteractive queries on Iceberg; federated access to legacy stores
OrchestrationApache AirflowDependencies across 50 sources, SLAs, OpenLineage provider
QualityGreat Expectations or Soda; reconciliation SQLRules as code; results stored and published
MetadataDataHub for technical metadata and lineage; Collibra for business governanceSee the metadata model below
SecurityLake Formation (with Glue) or Apache Ranger (with Trino and Spark plugins); KMS; VaultTag-based access, encryption, secrets

4. Integrating the 50 sources

CategorySourcesExamplesPattern
Trading and front office12Murex, Calypso, Summit, in-house pricing and booking systemsCDC for trades intraday + EOD position files
Loans and credit8Corporate lending, retail mortgages, credit approval, ratingsCDC; nightly files from older cores
Cards and retail banking5Cards, current accounts, overdraftsCDC and files
Treasury and liquidity5Funding, deposits, liquidity buffers, FTPFiles and APIs
Market data6Bloomberg, LSEG (Refinitiv) prices and curves, volatility surfaces, FX ratesVendor files and APIs, snapshot at the EOD cut-off
Reference and master data6Counterparty MDM, instrument master, GLEIF LEI, legal-entity hierarchy, calendars, org hierarchyAPIs and CDC
Finance3General ledger, sub-ledgers, chart of accountsEOD files for reconciliation
Collateral and netting3Collateral management, CSA and netting agreements, marginCDC and files
Operations and compliance2KYC, limit managementAPIs
Total50
  • Five patterns, not 50 pipelines: CDC, EOD files, vendor APIs, streams and reference APIs, each a reusable, tested template
  • Metadata-driven: a config table lists source, object, target, load type, keys, watermark, owner and SLA; the generic loader is the one tested in the design questions section, here writing Iceberg tables
  • Onboarding checklist per source: data contract signed by the source owner, schema registered, owner and steward named, classification done, quality rules agreed, lineage verified, reconciliation in place
  • Waves: wave 1 is the 15 sources behind market risk VaR; wave 2 credit exposure; wave 3 IFRS 9 and liquidity; each wave ends with parallel runs against the legacy system
  • One cut-off: every source declares when its EOD is complete; the EOD process waits for all critical sources or runs with an approved fallback and flags it

5. Iceberg table design, tested

CREATE TABLE risk.silver.positions (
  position_id     STRING        COMMENT 'Unique position key from the trading system',
  book            STRING        COMMENT 'Trading book',
  counterparty_id STRING        COMMENT 'Golden counterparty ID from MDM',
  notional        DECIMAL(18,2) COMMENT 'Notional in book currency',
  currency        STRING        COMMENT 'ISO 4217 currency code',
  business_date   DATE          COMMENT 'Risk business date (end-of-day cut-off)',
  updated_at      TIMESTAMP     COMMENT 'Last change time in the source'
) USING iceberg
PARTITIONED BY (days(business_date), bucket(16, counterparty_id))   -- hidden partitioning
COMMENT 'Positions by business date, conformed from 12 trading systems'
TBLPROPERTIES (
  'data_owner'        = 'market-risk-data-owner',
  'steward'           = 'risk-data-stewards',
  'classification'    = 'confidential',
  'cde'               = 'true',
  'source_systems'    = 'murex,calypso,summit',
  'format-version'    = '2',
  'write.merge.mode'  = 'copy-on-write',
  'write.update.mode' = 'copy-on-write',
  'write.delete.mode' = 'copy-on-write'
);

Tested on Spark 3.5 with Iceberg 1.6.1. Two lessons from the test: Spark reserves the owner table property for the current user, so store the business owner as data_owner; and Iceberg 1.6 cannot build a changelog over merge-on-read delete files ("Delete files are currently not supported in changelog scans"), so tables whose changes feed downstream jobs use copy-on-write.

-- Load and amend positions, then freeze the official end-of-day view
MERGE INTO risk.silver.positions t
USING staged_positions s
ON t.position_id = s.position_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_at > t.updated_at THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;

ALTER TABLE risk.silver.positions CREATE TAG `eod_2026_11_07`;

-- Any engine can reproduce exactly what the risk run used
SELECT position_id, notional
FROM risk.silver.positions VERSION AS OF 'eod_2026_11_06';
QueryResult
Current tableP1 1,200,000 (amended), P2, P3, P4 (new)
VERSION AS OF 'eod_2026_11_06'P1 1,000,000, P2, P3: exactly what the 6 November risk run used

Incremental processing between two end-of-day tags uses the changelog view:

CALL risk.system.create_changelog_view(
  table              => 'risk.silver.positions',
  options            => map('start-snapshot-id', '<eod_2026_11_06 snapshot>',
                            'end-snapshot-id',   '<eod_2026_11_07 snapshot>'),
  identifier_columns => array('position_id'),
  changelog_view     => 'positions_changes');

SELECT position_id, notional, _change_type FROM positions_changes;
position_idnotional_change_type
P11,000,000.00UPDATE_BEFORE
P11,200,000.00UPDATE_AFTER
P4500,000.00INSERT
-- Undo a bad load
CALL risk.system.rollback_to_snapshot('risk.silver.positions', <last good snapshot id>);

-- Daily maintenance: compact small files, expire old snapshots (tagged EOD snapshots are kept)
CALL risk.system.rewrite_data_files(table => 'risk.silver.positions');
CALL risk.system.expire_snapshots(table => 'risk.silver.positions',
                                  older_than => TIMESTAMP '2026-11-01 00:00:00', retain_last => 5);
CALL risk.system.remove_orphan_files(table => 'risk.silver.positions');

-- Inspect any table through its metadata tables
SELECT * FROM risk.silver.positions.snapshots;   -- every commit
SELECT * FROM risk.silver.positions.refs;        -- branches and tags
SELECT * FROM risk.silver.positions.partitions;  -- rows and files per partition
SELECT * FROM risk.silver.positions.files;       -- every data file

Tested: an UPDATE that multiplied every notional by 1,000 was undone with rollback_to_snapshot. After adding book as a new partition field, old files kept spec 0 and new files used spec 1, and one query read both. Compaction rewrote 4 small files; expire_snapshots removed the untagged history but kept both EOD tags, and the 6 November view still returned the original figures. Tag retention can be limited with RETAIN n DAYS to match the regulatory retention period.

6. Where data modelling happens

Modelling is not one step. It starts before anything is built, and then each layer uses a different kind of modelling: almost none in bronze, the main conformed model in silver, dimensional models in gold, and metric definitions in the semantic layer.

Stage or layerModelling styleIn the risk projectWho leads it
Design phase (before build)Conceptual and logical modelEntities and relationships: trade, position, counterparty, legal-entity hierarchy, instrument, book, collateral, market data, risk measure; CDEs per report; bus matrixData architect with risk SMEs and data owners
BronzeSource-aligned: no business modelEach of the 50 sources as delivered, plus load metadata; physical choices only (append-only, partitioned by load date)Data engineers
SilverConformed / canonical model, often Data Vault in banksOne trade and position model across Murex, Calypso and Summit; golden MDM keys; SCD2 history; business_date; bitemporal where regulators need itData architect and modellers
GoldDimensional (star schemas) and report martsfact_position_eod, fact_exposure, fact_risk_result with conformed counterparty, book, instrument, date and currency dimensions; COREP and IFRS 9 martsModellers with analytics engineers
Semantic layerMetric definitionsVaR, Expected Shortfall, exposure at default, expected credit loss defined once (Trino views or a semantic layer)Analytics engineers with risk owners

Design phase. Before the first pipeline, agree the conceptual and logical model with risk analysts, finance and data owners: which entities exist, how they relate (a counterparty belongs to a legal-entity hierarchy; a trade sits in a book; a position is a trade valued on a business date) and which critical data elements each regulatory report needs. Keep it in an ER tool (erwin, SqlDBM) or in Collibra next to the glossary, so the physical layers are built from one agreed picture.

Bronze. Do not model business meaning here. Bronze must reflect each source exactly, so that silver can be rebuilt when the model changes. Modelling bronze couples you to source quirks too early.

Silver: where the real modelling happens. The 50 sources become one consistent model. Many banks choose Data Vault 2.0 here, because new sources add satellites without redesign, and every row keeps its load time and record source for audit. Hubs hold business keys, links hold relationships, and satellites hold descriptive history:

-- Hub: one row per business key (LEI), whichever source sent it first
CREATE TABLE risk.silver.hub_counterparty (
  counterparty_hk STRING, lei STRING, load_dts TIMESTAMP, record_source STRING) USING iceberg;

INSERT INTO risk.silver.hub_counterparty
SELECT sha2(lei, 256), lei, MIN(load_dts), MIN_BY(source, load_dts)
FROM bronze_counterparty b
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM risk.silver.hub_counterparty h WHERE h.lei = b.lei)
GROUP BY lei;

-- Satellite: descriptive attributes, a new row only when they really change
INSERT INTO risk.silver.sat_counterparty_details
SELECT counterparty_hk, load_dts, hash_diff, name, rating, record_source FROM (
  SELECT sha2(lei, 256) AS counterparty_hk, load_dts,
         sha2(concat_ws('|', upper(name), rating), 256) AS hash_diff,
         name, rating, source AS record_source,
         LAG(sha2(concat_ws('|', upper(name), rating), 256))
           OVER (PARTITION BY lei ORDER BY load_dts, source) AS prev_hash
  FROM bronze_counterparty)
WHERE prev_hash IS NULL OR prev_hash <> hash_diff;
TableRowsWhy
hub_counterparty2LEI-ACME-UK arrived from both Murex and the loans system but is one business key; LEI-ACME-DE is the second
sat_counterparty_details3UK at rating A, UK downgraded to BBB on 3 November, DE at A. The loans system's upper-case copy of the same name produced no new row, because the hash of the upper-cased values was unchanged

Tested on Spark 3.5 with Iceberg 1.6.1. Data Vault is optional: a conformed 3NF-style model with SCD2 works too, and is simpler for smaller teams. Choose Data Vault when there are many sources, frequent source changes and strict audit requirements, which describes most bank risk platforms.

Gold: dimensional modelling for consumers. Each fact table has a declared grain, and conformed dimensions are shared by every fact, so exposures, positions and risk results can be compared and combined (see Joining Two Fact Tables for why facts are combined through dimensions, not joined directly):

                    dim_counterparty (SCD2)                dim_book
                    counterparty_sk, lei, rating,          book_sk, book, desk,
                    ultimate_parent_lei,                   legal_entity
                    valid_from, valid_to                        |
                              |                                 |
                              +-----------+     +---------------+
                                          |     |
   dim_date  ------------------  fact_position_eod  ------------------  dim_currency
                                 grain: one row per position per business date
                                 notional, market_value
                                          |
                                     dim_instrument
Fact tableGrainMain measures
fact_position_eodOne row per position per business dateNotional, market value, sensitivities
fact_exposureOne row per counterparty, netting set and business dateExposure at default, potential future exposure, collateral
fact_risk_resultOne row per risk run, book and risk measureVaR, Expected Shortfall, stress losses
fact_eclOne row per facility and reporting dateStage, PD, LGD, EAD, expected credit loss
CREATE TABLE risk.gold.fact_position_eod (
  business_date   DATE,
  position_id     STRING,
  counterparty_sk BIGINT,
  book_sk         BIGINT,
  currency        STRING,
  notional        DECIMAL(18,2),
  market_value    DECIMAL(18,2))
USING iceberg
PARTITIONED BY (days(business_date))
COMMENT 'Grain: one row per position per business date';

INSERT INTO risk.gold.fact_position_eod
SELECT p.business_date, p.position_id, c.counterparty_sk, b.book_sk,
       p.currency, p.notional, p.market_value
FROM silver_positions p
JOIN risk.gold.dim_counterparty c
  ON  c.lei = p.lei
  AND p.business_date BETWEEN c.valid_from AND c.valid_to   -- version valid on the business date
JOIN risk.gold.dim_book b ON b.book = p.book;

ALTER TABLE risk.gold.fact_position_eod CREATE TAG `eod_2026_11_03`;

Querying the 3 November end-of-day tag, rolled up to the ultimate parent through the counterparty hierarchy:

SELECT c.ultimate_parent_lei, b.desk,
       SUM(f.notional)     AS notional,
       SUM(f.market_value) AS market_value
FROM risk.gold.fact_position_eod VERSION AS OF 'eod_2026_11_03' f
JOIN risk.gold.dim_counterparty c ON f.counterparty_sk = c.counterparty_sk
JOIN risk.gold.dim_book b         ON f.book_sk = b.book_sk
WHERE f.business_date = DATE '2026-11-03'
GROUP BY c.ultimate_parent_lei, b.desk;
ultimate_parent_leidesknotionalmarket_value
LEI-ACME-GRPFX1,000,000.0015,000.00
LEI-ACME-GRPRates3,250,000.00-2,000.00

Tested on Iceberg 1.6.1: the grain test found 0 duplicates on (business_date, position_id). Position P1 picked counterparty version 1 (rating A) on 2 November and version 2 (rating BBB) on 3 November, because the surrogate key is resolved for the business date at load time. The roll-up adds both Acme entities to one group, which is the aggregation BCBS 239 and large-exposure rules require.

Semantic layer. Risk measures are defined once, for example as governed Trino views or in a semantic layer, so Tableau, Power BI and the regulatory reporting tool compute VaR or exposure at default the same way. The definitions link to the CDEs in Collibra.

Physical modelling runs through every layer: Iceberg partitioning (business date, buckets on counterparty), sort order for common filters, copy-on-write or merge-on-read per table, and table properties carrying owner and classification. All models are versioned in dbt and must pass the metadata CI gate below.

Say this in the interview

"Modelling starts before the build: I agree a conceptual and logical model with risk SMEs and data owners, anchored on the critical data elements behind each report. Bronze is not modelled; it mirrors the 50 sources. Silver is where the real modelling happens: a conformed trade and position model with golden MDM keys and SCD2 history, often as Data Vault in banks because it absorbs many changing sources and keeps full auditability. Gold is dimensional: star schemas with a declared grain, such as one row per position per business date, and conformed counterparty, book and instrument dimensions with SCD2 keys resolved for the business date. Risk metrics are defined once in the semantic layer. Every model is versioned in dbt and passes the metadata CI gate."

7. The metadata model: which tool maintains which metadata

The golden rule: every kind of metadata has exactly one master. Other tools receive copies, never edit them.

MetadataMaster (system of record)Captured howCopied to
Table schemas, partitions, snapshots, file statisticsIceberg metadata via the REST catalogAutomatically on every commitDataHub (harvested hourly)

Classification (PII, confidential)Collibra (approved), proposed by scanners such as Amazon Macie or BigIDScanner proposes, steward approvesDataHub tags, Lake Formation or Ranger tags

Data quality rules and resultsRules: Git (Great Expectations or Soda); results: DQ results tablePipelines publish after every runDataHub assertions, Collibra DQ scores

Who does what for the most common metadata activities (RACI):

ActivityOwnerStewardEngineerPlatformGovernance office
