9. How we keep metadata up to date

Metadata goes stale when it depends on people remembering. The rule is: automate what can be captured, make the rest part of the delivery process, and measure staleness.

MechanismWhat it keeps currentHow
Automatic captureSchemas, snapshots, statistics, freshnessIceberg writes metadata on every commit; DataHub harvests the REST catalog hourly and on events
Runtime lineageJob, table and column lineageOpenLineage integrations in Spark, Flink, Airflow and dbt emit lineage on every run, so it cannot fall behind the code
Metadata as codeDescriptions, owners, classification, testsStored in dbt YAML next to the SQL; a pull request cannot merge without them (CI check below)
Properties set by pipelinesOwner, steward, CDE flag on each tableThe ingestion framework writes table properties from the config table, so every new table is born with metadata
Contracts and Schema RegistrySource schemasCompatibility rules block breaking changes; new versions are registered automatically
Stewardship workflowsGlossary, CDEs, classificationCollibra workflows route proposals to stewards and owners for approval, with deadlines and escalation
ScannersClassification of new dataMacie or BigID scans new tables; findings become proposals, not silent changes
Periodic attestationOwnership, definitions, accessOwners re-certify their CDEs and datasets every quarter; uncertified assets lose the certified badge
People changesOwners and stewardsHR leaver and mover events create tasks to reassign ownership within 10 days
Impact analysis in CIDownstream awarenessA pull request that changes a column lists affected tables, reports and owners from lineage
DecommissioningDead assetsTables with no reads for 90 days are flagged; owners archive or justify them
Metadata KPIsEverything aboveCoverage and staleness per domain (owners, descriptions, classification, lineage, last review date) on a dashboard

The CI gate that makes metadata part of "done":

# check_metadata.py: runs in CI on every pull request; a non-zero exit blocks the merge
import sys, yaml

REQUIRED_META = ("data_owner", "steward", "classification")

def check(path):
    errors = []
    for m in yaml.safe_load(open(path))["models"]:
        name, meta = m["name"], m.get("meta", {})
        if not m.get("description"):
            errors.append(f"{name}: missing description")
        for key in REQUIRED_META:
            if not meta.get(key):
                errors.append(f"{name}: missing meta.{key}")
        for c in m.get("columns", []):
            if not c.get("description"):
                errors.append(f"{name}.{c['name']}: missing description")
            if c.get("meta", {}).get("pii") and not c.get("meta", {}).get("masking_policy"):
                errors.append(f"{name}.{c['name']}: PII column without masking_policy")
        if meta.get("cde"):  # critical data elements need tests
            for c in m.get("columns", []):
                if not c.get("data_tests"):
                    errors.append(f"{name}.{c['name']}: CDE column without data tests")
    return errors

errors = check(sys.argv[1])
for e in errors:
    print("ERROR", e)
sys.exit(1 if errors else 0)
ModelResult
positionsPasses: description, data_owner, steward, classification, column descriptions and tests present
counterparty_exposureBlocked with 7 errors: no description, no data_owner, no steward, a PII column (client_name) without description or masking policy, and two CDE columns without data tests

Tested with Python 3.10 and PyYAML; the script exited with code 1, which fails the CI job. The same check can read Iceberg table properties for tables created outside dbt.

10. More metadata questions interviewers ask

QuestionAnswer
How do Collibra and DataHub stay in sync?One-way flows per metadata type: technical metadata and lineage flow DataHub → Collibra; terms, owners and classifications flow Collibra → DataHub and to table tags. Integration jobs run hourly and on change events; a nightly comparison reports drift
What happens when a source adds a column?The registry accepts it if compatible; bronze evolves the Iceberg schema (adding a column is metadata-only); DataHub picks it up on the next harvest; the CI gate forces a description and classification before the column reaches silver or gold
How do you prove BCBS 239 lineage to a regulator?From a report cell, Collibra shows the CDE and its definition; DataHub shows column lineage back to source tables; the EOD tag shows the exact data used; DQ results and reconciliations show it was complete and accurate
How do you know metadata is wrong or stale?Staleness KPIs (last review date), harvest failures, assets without owners, lineage gaps (tables with no upstream), and user feedback in the catalog
Who pays for metadata work?It is part of every delivery: a dataset is not "done" until its metadata passes the gate; stewards have stewardship written into their objectives

11. The six walkthrough questions, for this project

QuestionAnswer for the Iceberg project
Explain your end-to-end architecture50 sources via CDC, EOD files and APIs into S3 Iceberg bronze, silver and gold; Spark and dbt for batch, Flink for intraday; one REST catalog shared by Spark, Flink, Trino and Snowflake; risk engines read gold EOD tags; DataHub and Collibra for metadata; Lake Formation or Ranger for security
Why Iceberg and not Databricks?Multi-engine access to one copy of data, open catalog API, no vendor lock-in required by policy, EOD tags for reproducibility; trade-off is more components to operate
How do you handle incremental data?CDC into bronze, watermark loads where CDC is impossible, MERGE into silver, Iceberg changelog views between EOD tags for gold, Flink for intraday
How do you manage data quality?Contracts at ingestion, Great Expectations or Soda between layers with quarantine, reconciliation to front office and GL before each risk run, results in DataHub and Collibra
How do you ensure consistency?Iceberg snapshot isolation, one REST catalog for all engines, MERGE with version guards, golden reference keys from MDM, every risk run reads one EOD tag, daily reconciliation
How do you handle failures and recovery?Airflow retries, idempotent MERGE, Flink checkpoints, rollback_to_snapshot for bad loads, reprocessing from bronze, S3 cross-region replication and catalog backups for disaster recovery

Interview-ready summary

Say this in the interview

"I built a risk data platform for a bank on Apache Iceberg on S3, with one Iceberg REST catalog shared by Spark, Flink, Trino and Snowflake. Fifty sources (trading, lending, cards, treasury, market data, reference data and the general ledger) come in through five reusable patterns: CDC through Debezium and Kafka, end-of-day files, vendor APIs, streams and reference APIs, driven by a metadata config."

"Silver holds a conformed trade model with golden counterparty and instrument keys. Gold holds positions and exposures by business date, and every official end of day is an Iceberg tag, so any risk run or regulatory report can be reproduced exactly. That is central to BCBS 239."

"For metadata, each type has one master. Iceberg and the catalog own schemas and snapshots. dbt in Git owns transformation documentation. DataHub owns technical metadata and runtime lineage from OpenLineage. Collibra owns the glossary, critical data elements, owners and classifications, which flow out as tags that Lake Formation or Ranger enforce. Data owners are accountable, stewards maintain business metadata, engineers maintain technical metadata, and the platform team runs the tooling."

"We keep it current through automation (catalog harvesting and runtime lineage), metadata as code with a CI gate that blocks incomplete models, stewardship workflows, quarterly owner attestation, HR-driven ownership changes, and staleness KPIs per domain."

39. Architecture Design Interview Questions

Design questions have no single right answer. Interviewers look for a structured approach: clarify requirements, propose an architecture, justify key decisions and trade-offs, and cover governance, security and operations. Use the same five steps for every question below.

StepWhat to sayTime
1. ClarifyUsers, use cases, data volumes, latency, regulations, existing tools, constraints3–5 min
2. High-level designSources → ingestion → storage layers → processing → serving, on a whiteboard5–10 min
3. Deep diveTwo or three hard parts: the ones specific to this problem10–15 min
4. Non-functionalQuality, lineage, security, reliability, cost, scaling5 min
5. Trade-offs and roadmapWhat you chose, what you rejected and why, and how you would deliver in phases3–5 min

Q1. Design a risk data platform

Clarify first. Which risks: market, credit, liquidity, operational? Which outputs: daily VaR and Expected Shortfall, credit exposure per counterparty and group, IFRS 9 expected credit loss, regulatory reports? Which deadlines: overnight (T+1) or intraday? Volumes: millions of trades and positions, plus scenario vectors that can reach billions of values. Regulation: BCBS 239, the Basel Committee's principles for risk data aggregation and reporting, which demand accuracy, completeness, timeliness, adaptability and traceability.

 SOURCES                      INGEST                LAKEHOUSE (Delta / Iceberg)
 trading (Murex, Calypso) --> CDC + Kafka   -->     bronze: raw trades, positions, loans,
 loans, cards, treasury   --> batch EOD files               market data, as delivered
 market data (Bloomberg,  --> vendor feeds          silver: conformed trade model, cleansed,
   Refinitiv), curves                                       joined to golden reference data
 counterparty MDM, instrument master, GL  ------>   gold:   positions by business date + snapshot
                                                          |
                                     RISK CALCULATION (Spark, compute grid, Python/QuantLib)
                                     VaR / ES, sensitivities, exposures, PD-LGD-EAD, ECL
                                                          |
                                     RESULTS STORE: risk cube by business date, run id,
                                     legal entity, desk, counterparty hierarchy, scenario
                                                          |
                     risk dashboards  |  limit monitoring  |  regulatory reports (COREP, FR Y-14)

 CROSS-CUTTING: CDEs and DQ rules, lineage to every report cell, reconciliation to front office
                and general ledger, four-eyes sign-off, bitemporal history, access control
Design decisionWhat I would do and why
Business date and snapshotsEvery record carries a business date and an official end-of-day snapshot (cut-off). Risk runs read a frozen snapshot, so results can be reproduced exactly, even years later
Reference dataCounterparty and legal-entity hierarchy from MDM (LEI, ultimate parent), instrument master, market data snapshots; exposures must roll up to the group correctly
Common trade modelMap every trading system into one conformed model (inspired by FpML or ISDA CDM) in silver, so calculations do not depend on each source format
Calculation layerSpark for aggregation and scenario processing; a compute grid or Spark with pandas UDFs for pricing; versioned models and parameters stored with every run
Results storePartition by business date and run id; keep each run immutable; restatements create a new run, never overwrite
HistoryBitemporal: valid date plus recorded time, so "what did we report on 31 March?" and "what do we now know about 31 March?" are both answerable
Quality and reconciliationCompleteness checks per source (did every desk send its file?), reconciliation of positions to front office and balances to the general ledger, before a run starts
Adaptability (ad hoc requests)Granular results kept at trade or position level, so new aggregations for supervisors can be produced without new pipelines
ControlsLineage from report cell to source, data quality dashboards per critical data element, sign-off workflow, audit trail
SecurityEntitlements by legal entity, desk and region; masking of client identifiers; data residency for regional regulators
Say this in the interview

"I would build a lakehouse with medallion layers and an explicit business date and snapshot model, so every risk run is reproducible. Trades, positions and loans arrive by CDC and end-of-day files, are mapped into one conformed trade model and enriched with golden counterparty, instrument and market data. A calculation layer produces VaR, Expected Shortfall, exposures and expected credit loss into an immutable results store keyed by business date and run. Around it I put BCBS 239 controls: critical data elements with quality rules, reconciliation to front office and the general ledger before each run, lineage to every report cell, bitemporal history and sign-off workflows."

Q2. How would you integrate 50 different source systems?

The wrong answer is "build 50 pipelines". The right answer is an ingestion factory: classify the sources, build one reusable pattern per source type, and drive everything from metadata.

Source typePatternTools
Relational databases (OLTP)Change data capture from the transaction log; initial snapshot, then changesDebezium + Kafka, Oracle GoldenGate, Qlik Replicate, AWS DMS, Lakeflow Connect
SaaS applicationsManaged connectors using the vendor APIFivetran, Airbyte, Lakeflow Connect, Azure Data Factory
Files from partners and mainframesLanding zone + incremental file ingestionAuto Loader, Snowpipe, SFTP to cloud storage
Events and IoTStreaming into the lakehouseKafka, Kinesis, Event Hubs + Structured Streaming
Internal APIsScheduled API extraction with pagination and retriesCustom Python, Airflow, Data Factory
Legacy with no accessAgreed extract files with a data contractFile drops, then the file pattern
  • Metadata-driven framework: one config table holds source, object, target, load type (full or incremental), keys and watermark column. One generic, tested loader reads it, so adding a source is a config row, not new code
  • Standard landing and bronze: every source lands the same way with load metadata (_source, _loaded_at, file name), so downstream logic is uniform
  • Data contracts per source: schema, keys, frequency, owner, quality rules; schema drift is detected and alerted, not silently loaded
  • Onboarding in waves: prioritise by business value and complexity; build the patterns with the first 5 sources, then onboard the rest quickly
  • Operations: one monitoring dashboard for all 50 (freshness, row counts, failures), secrets in a vault, retries and dead-letter handling, lineage registered automatically
# One config row per source object; one generic loader for all of them
# ingest_config: source | source_object | target | load_type | keys | watermark_col | active
def ingest(cfg):
    df = spark.table(cfg.source_object)  # or JDBC, files, API, CDC feed
    if cfg.load_type == "incremental":
        wm = spark.sql(f"SELECT MAX(last_value) FROM ingest_watermark "
                       f"WHERE target = '{cfg.target}'").first()[0]
        if wm:
            df = df.filter(F.col(cfg.watermark_col) > wm)
    df = (df.withColumn("_source", F.lit(cfg.source))
            .withColumn("_loaded_at", F.current_timestamp()))
    n = df.count()
    if not spark.catalog.tableExists(cfg.target) or cfg.load_type == "full":
        df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").saveAsTable(cfg.target)
    else:
        df.createOrReplaceTempView("incoming")
        on = " AND ".join(f"t.{k} = s.{k}" for k in cfg.keys.split(","))
        spark.sql(f"MERGE INTO {cfg.target} t USING incoming s ON {on} "
                  "WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET * WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *")
    if cfg.load_type == "incremental" and n:
        new_wm = df.agg(F.max(cfg.watermark_col)).first()[0]
        spark.sql(f"DELETE FROM ingest_watermark WHERE target = '{cfg.target}'")
        spark.sql(f"INSERT INTO ingest_watermark VALUES ('{cfg.target}', '{new_wm}')")
    return n

for cfg in spark.table("ingest_config").filter("active").collect():
    ingest(cfg)

Tested on PySpark 3.5 with Delta Lake 3.2 and three sources (two incremental, one full). Run 1 loaded 2, 2 and 2 rows. Run 2, with no source changes, loaded 0 and 0 incremental rows (the full-refresh table reloaded 2). Run 3 picked up exactly one changed and one new customer and merged them by key.

Say this in the interview

"I would not build 50 pipelines. I would classify the sources into a handful of types (databases, SaaS, files, events, APIs) and build one reusable pattern each: CDC for databases, managed connectors for SaaS, Auto Loader for files, streaming for events. A metadata-driven framework makes onboarding a configuration change. Every source lands in a standard bronze format with a data contract, schema-drift alerts and one monitoring view. I would deliver in waves, proving the patterns on the first few sources."

Q3. How would you build a centralised data catalog?

The full design, with tools, metadata types and tested examples, is in the section Implementing Centralised Metadata, Lineage, Governance and Security. In an interview, answer in this order:

StepKey point
1. Purpose and ownersStart from use cases: discovery, trust, compliance, impact analysis. Set up domain owners and stewards before buying a tool
2. Choose the platformCollibra or Alation for business-led governance, DataHub or OpenMetadata for engineering-led and open source, Purview for Microsoft estates; native catalogs (Unity Catalog, Glue, Dataplex) stay as sources
3. Harvest automaticallyConnectors for every platform on a schedule; push lineage with OpenLineage; register Kafka topics, APIs and BI reports
4. Add business contextGlossary terms, owners, domains and certification on the most used and most critical assets first
5. Classify and connect to securityOne tag vocabulary; tags synced to platforms where ABAC policies enforce them
6. Show trust signalsQuality scores, freshness, usage and certification next to each dataset
7. Drive adoptionAccess requests through the catalog, catalog links in BI tools and pull requests, search in chat tools
8. MeasureCoverage of owners, descriptions, classification and lineage per domain; active users; time to find data
Say this in the interview

"A catalog succeeds through ownership and automation, not the tool. I would set up domain owners first, choose a central platform that fits the culture, harvest metadata and lineage automatically from every system, add business context starting with critical data, connect classifications to native security policies, show quality and usage signals, and measure coverage per domain."

Q4. How would you handle batch and streaming data?

ArchitectureHow it worksVerdict
LambdaSeparate batch layer (accurate) and speed layer (fast); results merged at query timeTwo codebases that drift apart; mostly legacy today
KappaEverything is a stream; reprocessing means replaying the logSimple model, but replaying years of history from Kafka is expensive
Unified lakehouseStreams and batch both read and write the same ACID tables (Delta, Iceberg); one engine and often the same codeThe common modern choice
  • Decide per use case, by latency need: fraud scoring and alerts need seconds; most reporting is fine hourly or daily. Streaming everything raises cost and complexity for no benefit
  • Same tables, same logic: Spark Structured Streaming runs continuously for low latency, or with trigger(availableNow=True) to process only new data as an incremental batch job, using the same code and checkpoint. The medallion section shows a tested run: 10 rows, then 0 new on re-run, then only the 3 new rows
  • Late and out-of-order data: event-time windows with watermarks; idempotent MERGE by key and version (Q5)
  • Backfills: rerun the batch path over historical partitions into the same tables, without touching the live stream
  • Exactly-once results: checkpoints plus transactional sinks (Delta) or idempotent writes
  • Serving: real-time needs may go to a low-latency store (Redis, Cassandra, Druid, Pinot) fed from the stream, while analytics reads the lakehouse
Say this in the interview

"I choose latency per use case rather than streaming everything. Architecturally I prefer a unified lakehouse over Lambda: streaming and batch jobs write the same Delta or Iceberg tables, often with the same Structured Streaming code, running continuously where seconds matter and as incremental availableNow jobs elsewhere. I handle late data with watermarks and idempotent merges, backfill through the batch path, and serve real-time lookups from a low-latency store when needed."

Q5. How would you ensure data consistency across systems?

First clarify which consistency: copies of the same data agreeing (source vs warehouse vs cache), meaning agreeing (the same "revenue" everywhere), or transactions spanning several systems.

TechniqueProblem it solves
One system of record per entityEveryone knows which copy wins; others are read-only replicas
CDC instead of dual writesAn application writing to its database and to Kafka separately loses messages when one write fails; CDC reads the committed log instead
Transactional outboxThe service writes the change and an outbox event in one database transaction; a relay publishes the event, so state and events never disagree
Idempotent, version-guarded upsertsRetries, duplicates and out-of-order events cannot overwrite newer data
ACID table formatsReaders never see half-written data (Delta, Iceberg)
SagasMulti-service business processes use compensating steps instead of distributed transactions
MDM, conformed dimensions, semantic layerSame customer and same metric definitions everywhere
Data contractsProducers cannot change schemas or meaning without notice
ReconciliationDetects drift that slipped through: counts, totals and row hashes compared regularly
Consistency SLAsAgree how stale a replica may be (eventual consistency within, say, 5 minutes) and monitor it

A version-guarded MERGE makes replays and late events harmless:

MERGE INTO account_balance t
USING (
  SELECT account_id, balance, version FROM (
    SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY version DESC) AS rn
    FROM events) WHERE rn = 1           -- latest event per key within the batch
) s
ON t.account_id = s.account_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.version > t.version THEN UPDATE SET *   -- older or repeated events change nothing
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;

Tested on Delta Lake 3.2: versions 1 and 2, then 3, then a late duplicate of version 2, then a replay of version 3. The final balance is 120.00 at version 3, as it should be.

Reconciliation catches what prevention misses. Compare totals first, then rows:

-- Level 1: counts and totals
SELECT 'source' AS side, COUNT(*) AS row_count, SUM(amount) AS total_amount FROM source_orders
UNION ALL
SELECT 'target', COUNT(*), SUM(amount) FROM target_orders;

-- Level 2: row-level differences by hash
WITH s AS (SELECT order_id, sha2(concat_ws('|', customer_id, amount), 256) AS h FROM source_orders),
     t AS (SELECT order_id, sha2(concat_ws('|', customer_id, amount), 256) AS h FROM target_orders)
SELECT COALESCE(s.order_id, t.order_id) AS order_id,
       CASE WHEN t.order_id IS NULL THEN 'missing in target'
            WHEN s.order_id IS NULL THEN 'extra in target'
            ELSE 'values differ' END AS issue
FROM s FULL OUTER JOIN t ON s.order_id = t.order_id
WHERE s.h IS DISTINCT FROM t.h;
CheckResult in the testLesson
CountsSource 4, target 4Counts alone said everything was fine
TotalsSource 265.5, target 267.5Something is wrong
Row hashesOrder 11 values differ, order 13 missing in target, order 14 extra in targetExactly what to fix
Say this in the interview

"I start by clarifying which consistency we need. Then: one system of record per entity; CDC or the transactional outbox instead of dual writes; idempotent, version-guarded upserts so retries and out-of-order events are harmless; ACID tables; sagas for cross-service processes; MDM and a semantic layer for consistent meaning; and data contracts. Finally I reconcile counts, totals and row hashes regularly, because matching counts can hide wrong values, and I monitor freshness against an agreed consistency SLA."

40. Scenario-Based Trade-off Questions

"X vs Y" questions test judgement, not memory. A strong answer has three parts: the real difference in one sentence, a comparison on the dimensions that matter, and a decision for the scenario with the reason. Avoid "it depends" without saying what it depends on.

1. Delta Lake vs Apache Iceberg

Scenario: A company runs Databricks for engineering, but finance queries the same data from Snowflake and analysts use Trino. Which table format?

Delta LakeApache Iceberg
OriginDatabricks; now a Linux Foundation projectNetflix; Apache Software Foundation project
Core featuresACID, time travel, schema evolution, MERGE, Change Data Feed, liquid clustering, deletion vectorsACID, time travel, schema and partition evolution, hidden partitioning, branching and tagging
Engine supportBest in Databricks and Spark; readable by many engines through connectorsBroadest multi-engine support: Spark, Flink, Trino, Snowflake, BigQuery, Athena, Dremio
CatalogsUnity CatalogREST catalog standard: Polaris, Unity Catalog, Glue, Nessie and others
InteroperabilityUniForm writes Iceberg metadata as well, so Iceberg engines can read Delta tablesNative format for most non-Databricks engines
Best fitDatabricks-centric platforms wanting the deepest optimisationMulti-engine, vendor-neutral platforms
Say this in the interview

"For this scenario I would choose Iceberg if no single engine dominates, because Snowflake, Trino and Spark all read and write it natively. If Databricks is the main engine, I would keep Delta with UniForm, so Databricks gets full Delta optimisations and Snowflake and Trino read the same tables as Iceberg. Either way the key decision is the catalog, since the formats are converging."

The section Choosing an Open Table Format covers the formats in more depth.

2. MongoDB vs PostgreSQL

Scenario: An e-commerce company needs a product catalogue where each category has different attributes, and an order and payment system. Which database for each?

MongoDBPostgreSQL
ModelDocuments (BSON), flexible schema per documentRelational tables with a defined schema; also JSONB for semi-structured data
QueriesRich document queries and aggregation pipeline; joins via $lookup are limitedFull SQL: joins, window functions, CTEs, constraints, foreign keys
TransactionsSingle-document atomic; multi-document ACID transactions since version 4.0, with more overheadMature ACID transactions across any tables
ScalingBuilt-in horizontal sharding and replica setsVertical scaling, read replicas, partitioning; horizontal via extensions such as Citus
IntegrityEnforced mostly by the application (optional schema validation)Enforced by the database: constraints, foreign keys, types
ExtrasAtlas Search, vector search in Atlas, time series collectionsExtensions: PostGIS (geo), pgvector (vectors), TimescaleDB
Best fitVaried, evolving document-shaped data at high scale: catalogues, content, user profiles, event dataRelational, consistency-critical data: orders, payments, ledgers, inventory
Say this in the interview

"I would use PostgreSQL for orders and payments, because they are relational and need strict transactions, constraints and joins. For the product catalogue, MongoDB fits well because attributes vary by category and documents map directly to the API. If the team wants one database, PostgreSQL with JSONB columns for the variable attributes is a strong alternative. For analytics, both feed the lakehouse through CDC."

3. Data lake vs data warehouse

Scenario: A retailer wants BI dashboards on sales, plus data science on clickstream logs, images and customer reviews. Lake, warehouse, or both?

Data lakeData warehouse
DataAny: structured, semi-structured, unstructured (logs, images, text)Structured, modelled data
SchemaSchema on readSchema on write
StorageCheap object storage in open file formatsManaged, optimised storage (often proprietary)
UsersData engineers, data scientists, MLAnalysts, BI users, finance
StrengthsScale, flexibility, low cost, ML and AI workloadsFast SQL, concurrency, governance, ease of use
RiskBecomes a "data swamp" without governance; weak transactions (before table formats)Expensive for raw and unstructured data; less suited to ML
Say this in the interview

"Today I would build a lakehouse: open table formats such as Delta or Iceberg on object storage give lake flexibility for clickstream, images and reviews, plus warehouse features (ACID, SQL performance, governance) for the sales dashboards, on one copy of the data. A separate warehouse is still reasonable if the company already runs one well for BI; then the lake feeds it with curated gold data."

4. Batch vs streaming

Scenario: A bank wants card-fraud detection and a daily regulatory report. Batch or streaming?

BatchStreaming
LatencyMinutes to hoursMilliseconds to seconds
ComplexitySimpler: bounded data, easy rerunsHarder: state, late events, watermarks, exactly-once, 24×7 operations
CostCompute runs only when scheduledAlways-on compute
CorrectnessComplete data, easy to reconcileNeeds care for late and out-of-order data
Use casesReporting, finance close, model training, backfillsFraud, alerts, IoT monitoring, real-time personalisation
Say this in the interview

"Fraud detection must be streaming: the decision is needed before the payment completes, so Kafka plus a stream processor or a low-latency model service. The regulatory report should be batch: it needs a complete, reconciled, reproducible snapshot. I would let both write to the same lakehouse tables, so fraud events and transactions are also available for the daily report and for retraining the model."

5. Microservices vs monolithic architecture

Scenario: A startup with eight engineers is building a new trading app. A large bank with 40 teams is modernising its payments platform. Which architecture for each?

MonolithMicroservices
StructureOne deployable application and usually one databaseMany small services, each owning its data and deployed independently
DevelopmentSimple to build, test and debug at firstTeams work and release independently
ScalingScale the whole applicationScale each service separately
OperationsOne thing to deploy and monitorService discovery, API gateways, tracing, Kubernetes; much more complexity
DataOne database: joins and transactions are easyDatabase per service: needs events, sagas and eventual consistency
FailureOne bug can bring down everythingFailures isolated, but network failures become normal
Best fitSmall teams, new products, unclear domain boundariesLarge organisations with many teams and clear domain boundaries
Say this in the interview

"For the startup, a modular monolith: one deployable application with clean internal modules, so the team moves fast and can split services out later when boundaries are clear. For the bank, microservices aligned to business domains, because 40 teams need to release independently. From the data side, microservices mean many databases, so I would use CDC or the outbox pattern to publish changes to Kafka and the lakehouse, rather than letting services query each other's databases."

6. Data mesh vs centralised data platform

Scenario: A global insurer has 15 business domains and a central data team that has become a bottleneck. Should it move to a data mesh?

Centralised platformData mesh
OwnershipCentral data team owns pipelines and modelsDomain teams own their data as products
PlatformBuilt and run by the central teamSelf-serve platform provided centrally, used by domains
GovernanceCentral and directFederated: global standards, applied by domains
StrengthsConsistency, simpler control, efficient for small or medium organisationsScales with the organisation; domain expertise close to the data
RisksBottleneck, slow delivery, weak domain knowledgeDuplication, inconsistent quality, needs mature domains and a strong platform
PrerequisitesA capable central teamDomain teams with data engineers, a self-serve platform, federated governance, product thinking
Say this in the interview

"With 15 domains and a central bottleneck, a data mesh direction makes sense, but gradually and as a hybrid. The central team becomes a platform team providing self-serve ingestion, storage, catalog, quality and security. Two or three mature domains start publishing data products with owners, contracts and SLAs, under federated governance with global standards for identity, classification and interoperability. Less mature domains stay supported centrally. A small company with one data team should usually stay centralised."

The section Implementing a Data Mesh covers the implementation in detail.

41. Common Interview Questions

QuestionShort answer
What does a data architect do?Designs how data is collected, stored, connected, secured and used across the company, and sets the standards teams build on
What is data governance?The roles, rules and processes for owning, defining, protecting and using data
Data owner vs data steward?The owner is accountable and approves access; the steward maintains definitions and quality day to day
Privacy vs security?Security protects data from unauthorised access; privacy makes sure personal data is used lawfully and fairly
Masking vs tokenisation vs encryption?Masking hides values when displayed; tokenisation swaps values for tokens kept in a vault; encryption scrambles data with a key
Is a hashed email anonymous?No. It can be guessed by hashing likely emails, and even a keyed hash is still pseudonymised personal data
How do you handle a right-to-erasure request on Delta?Find every copy through lineage, DELETE from each, then VACUUM after retention so old versions are physically removed
RBAC vs ABAC?RBAC grants by role or group; ABAC applies policies based on attributes such as tags, so they scale to new tables
How do row filters and column masks work in Unity Catalog?A SQL function attached to a table filters rows or changes a column's value per user at query time
What is defence in depth?Several security layers, identity, access, encryption, network and monitoring, so one failure does not expose everything
What is data lineage used for?Impact analysis, root cause analysis, compliance, trust and finding unused tables
What are RPO and RTO?RPO is how much data you can lose; RTO is how long recovery may take
Is Delta time travel a backup?No. It lives in the same storage and VACUUM removes old versions; use deep clones or replication
What is a data contract?An agreement on a dataset's schema, meaning, quality and freshness between producer and consumers
What is MDM?Matching records about the same entity across systems into one golden record
What is an ADR?An architecture decision record: the context, decision, options and impact, written down
How do you make governance scale?Federated ownership, governed tags, ABAC policies, automated lineage and access by group
Warehouse vs lake vs lakehouse?A warehouse holds modelled data in one SQL engine; a lake stores any files cheaply; a lakehouse adds transactions and governance to lake storage with open table formats
Data mesh vs data fabric?Mesh is an organisational model, with domains owning data products; fabric is a technology layer that uses metadata to connect and govern data across systems
How do you avoid vendor lock-in?Open table formats, open catalogs, standard SQL, infrastructure as code, and keeping data in storage you control
ETL vs ELT?ETL transforms before loading; ELT loads raw data and transforms inside the target platform
Why use CDC?It streams inserts, updates and deletes from the transaction log with little load on the source, and keeps copies current
How do you keep security consistent across Snowflake, Databricks and S3?One classification scheme, the same tags everywhere, policies generated from one definition, central audit, and lineage to find unprotected copies
How do you handle data residency?Choose regions per law, keep personal data in-region including backups and logs, and move only aggregated or anonymised data across borders
How would you migrate an on-premise warehouse to the cloud?Inventory with usage data, design the target, move data then sync with CDC, convert logic, run in parallel and reconcile, then cut over by domain and decommission
How do you choose between cloud platforms?Weighted criteria agreed with stakeholders: fit, total cost, openness, security, skills, ecosystem and vendor, recorded in an ADR
What changes for AI workloads?Permission-aware retrieval, redaction before embedding, lineage from data to model, and checking the purpose and consent of training data
What is zero trust?Never trusting a request because of its network location: verify every identity and grant least privilege
Delta, Iceberg or Hudi?Delta when Databricks or Fabric is the main engine; Iceberg when many engines share data or on AWS, Snowflake and BigQuery; Hudi or Paimon for heavy upserts and Flink streaming
Backward vs forward compatibility?Backward: new readers read old data, so upgrade consumers first. Forward: old readers read new data, so upgrade producers first
Which schema changes are safe?Adding optional fields with defaults. Renames, removing required fields and narrowing types break someone
How do you make a breaking change safely?Expand and contract: add the new field, dual-write, migrate consumers using lineage, deprecate, then remove
How do you make pipelines idempotent?MERGE on a business key or overwrite whole partitions, so a rerun produces the same result
What is write-audit-publish?Write to a hidden branch, clone or staging table, validate, then publish atomically
How do you isolate workloads?Separate compute per workload over shared storage, with each tagged and budgeted
What is a semantic layer?Business metrics defined once and reused by every BI and AI tool, so numbers agree
What are the pillars of data observability?Freshness, volume, schema, distribution and lineage
SLI vs SLO vs SLA?The measurement, the internal target, and the external promise
Why keep personal data out of Kafka topics?Retained logs are hard to erase selectively; send IDs and keep details in governed tables
How do you stop a data lake becoming a swamp?Zones with permissions, a mandatory catalog entry with owner and classification at ingestion, lifecycle rules, and quality checks between zones
Kimball, Inmon or Data Vault?Kimball for fast value with conformed star schemas; Inmon for an integrated normalised core; Data Vault for auditable history when sources change often, always with marts on top
What is a bus matrix?Business processes against conformed dimensions; it plans the warehouse and keeps dimensions shared
How do you structure catalogs in a lakehouse?By environment and layer, or by domain and environment; permissions and isolation follow that choice
What are the four principles of data mesh?Domain ownership, data as a product, a self-serve platform, and federated computational governance
When is data mesh a bad idea?Small organisations, domains without technical staff, or a platform that lacks basic governance
What is the strangler fig pattern?Replacing a legacy system piece by piece, routing one part at a time to the new platform
How do you validate a migration?Layered reconciliation: counts, aggregates, column hashes, row-level differences, then the top business reports
How do you migrate Hive tables to a lakehouse?Copy to object storage and convert Parquet tables in place to Delta or Iceberg, adding metadata without rewriting files
How do you modernise a mainframe data estate?Keep it as the system of record at first, replicate with CDC, parse files with copybooks, and move consumers gradually
What is the medallion architecture?Layers of increasing quality in a lakehouse: bronze keeps raw data, silver holds cleaned and conformed entities, gold holds business-ready models
Why keep a bronze layer?It is the replay point and audit record: fix silver logic and rebuild from bronze without asking the source to resend
What is the difference between landing and bronze?Landing holds files exactly as delivered and is short-lived; bronze is a queryable, append-only table of the same data with load metadata, kept long term
What is a landing zone?Either the first drop area for incoming data, or the secure cloud foundation of accounts, networks, identity and policies; know both meanings
What is the edge layer?Devices, sites and systems outside the platform where data is produced; edge gateways buffer, filter, translate and encrypt before sending
Where do you apply data quality in medallion?Silver: expectations validate rows and quarantine failures; bronze keeps everything; gold gets reconciliation and certification
Is medallion the same as Kimball?No. Medallion is about layers of refinement; Kimball is a modelling technique, usually used for gold
How do you avoid loading a file twice?Use tools that track loaded files, such as Auto Loader, COPY INTO or Snowpipe, or a streaming checkpoint
What are the biggest challenges in data modelling?Grain, keys, history and timing: mixed grain, inconsistent IDs across sources, changing attributes, late-arriving data, many-to-many relationships and inconsistent metric definitions
How do you handle a late-arriving dimension?Insert an inferred placeholder member, key the fact to it, and update the placeholder when the real dimension row arrives
What happens if you join two fact tables directly?They usually share only dimensions, so the join is many-to-many: rows multiply, measures are double counted, and an inner join drops members missing from one side
Why is a fact-to-fact join slow at scale?Both sides are shuffled on the join key, the output is the sum of left × right rows per key, hot keys cause skew, and partitions spill or fail
How do you combine two facts correctly?Drill-across: aggregate each fact to the same grain on conformed dimensions, then full outer join; or union the facts and aggregate once
What KPIs measure enterprise data quality?Data KPIs (completeness, validity, uniqueness, consistency, accuracy, reconciliation), delivery KPIs (freshness SLA, MTTD, MTTR, data downtime) and programme KPIs (CDE coverage, ownership, issues found by consumers)
What is data downtime?The total time data was wrong, missing or late: the sum of time to detect plus time to resolve across incidents
What is a golden record?The single best version of an entity, built by matching source records and choosing the best value per attribute, with a stable master ID and lineage
What is the difference between MDM and data governance?Governance sets policies, ownership and standards for all data; MDM applies them to master data to produce governed golden records
What are the types of MDM?By domain (customer, product, supplier, employee, location, asset, financial), by usage (operational, analytical, collaborative) and by style (registry, consolidation, coexistence, centralised)
What is MDM?Master data management: the process and tools that create one trusted golden record for core entities such as customer and product across all systems
How is MDM different from a data warehouse?A warehouse integrates high-volume transactional history for analysis; MDM resolves and governs a small set of core entities and can sync corrections back to source systems. The warehouse uses MDM master IDs as dimension keys
What is survivorship in MDM?Rules that choose the best value of each attribute from matched records, such as the most trusted source, the most recent update or the most complete value
What are the MDM implementation styles?Registry, consolidation, coexistence and centralised (transaction hub), from least to most intrusive
What does "define centrally, enforce natively" mean?Metadata, classifications and policies are defined once in a central catalog; each platform's native engine (Unity Catalog, Snowflake, Lake Formation, BigQuery) enforces them
What are the types of metadata?Technical, business, operational, lineage, governance, security, quality, usage, privacy, reference and master, and AI/ML metadata; plus passive vs active
What is the difference between Collibra and DataHub?Collibra is commercial and business-led (glossary, stewardship workflows, policies); DataHub is open source and engineering-led (automated ingestion, lineage, APIs, automation)
What is active metadata?Metadata that drives automatic actions, such as a tag that applies a mask or a failed check that pauses a pipeline
How do you integrate 50 source systems?Classify sources, build one reusable pattern per type (CDC, connectors, files, streams), drive it from a metadata config, standardise landing, add contracts and onboard in waves
How do you ensure consistency across systems?One system of record, CDC or outbox instead of dual writes, idempotent version-guarded upserts, ACID tables, sagas, MDM and contracts, plus reconciliation of counts, totals and row hashes
Lambda vs Kappa vs unified lakehouse?Lambda has separate batch and speed layers; Kappa treats everything as a stream; a unified lakehouse lets batch and streaming write the same ACID tables with the same code
Delta Lake or Iceberg?Delta for Databricks-centric platforms (with UniForm for Iceberg readers); Iceberg for multi-engine, vendor-neutral platforms
How do you process only changed data in Delta Lake?Enable Change Data Feed and read table_changes (or readChangeFeed in a stream) from the last processed version; use MERGE by key to apply
How do you make a Delta append idempotent?Use the txnAppId and txnVersion writer options; Delta skips a batch whose version was already committed by that app id
How do you recover from a bad load in Delta?Find the last good version with DESCRIBE HISTORY, RESTORE the table to it, fix the cause and reprocess from bronze
At which layer do you do data modelling?Conceptual and logical model before the build; none in bronze; the conformed model (often Data Vault in banks) in silver; dimensional star schemas in gold; metric definitions in the semantic layer
How do you make risk runs reproducible on Iceberg?Tag each official end-of-day snapshot and have every risk run and report read the tag; tagged snapshots survive snapshot expiry
Who is responsible for metadata?Data owners are accountable; business stewards maintain definitions and classifications; technical stewards maintain technical metadata and lineage; the platform team runs the tools; the governance office sets standards
How do you keep metadata up to date?Automate capture (harvesting, runtime lineage), treat metadata as code with CI gates, route business changes through stewardship workflows, attest periodically, and track staleness KPIs
